short_definition: Passive or instructed viewing of emotionally valenced images (IAPS, GAPED, NAPS, OASIS) while physiological, neural, or rating responses to valence and arousal are recorded.
description: Participants passively view color photographs from the International Affective Picture System (IAPS), a validated database of 1,182 images varying in emotional valence (pleasant, unpleasant, neutral) and arousal (calm to exciting). Images are presented for 3-5 seconds each without requiring an overt response. Post-viewing, participants rate valence and arousal on 9-point scales. The task serves as a standardized emotion elicitation tool in neuroimaging, consistently activating amygdala (for high-arousal images), visual cortex (enhanced processing of emotional stimuli), and prefrontal regions.

procedure: Participants view emotionally valenced images (e.g., IAPS) presented for several seconds each.
Participants may rate valence and arousal or simply view while physiological signals are recorded.
manipulations: Emotional valence (positive, negative, neutral) and arousal level of the images

variations.name: Category-Specific Selection
variations.description: Instead of a mixed set of pleasant, unpleasant and neutral pictures, the images are chosen to evoke one specific emotion at a time, such as fear, disgust or sadness, and are usually shown in blocks of a single emotion. The participant still views them passively or rates them afterwards.
variations.justification: Restricts stimuli to specific emotional categories (e.g., fear, disgust), creating category-structured event blocks distinct from mixed viewing

families.rationale: View valenced images

short_definition: Target evaluation (good/bad) preceded by a briefly presented affective prime; response facilitation on congruent trials indexes automatic evaluation.
description: Participants categorize target stimuli (e.g., judge words as "good" or "bad") that are immediately preceded by briefly presented prime stimuli (words, faces, or images) of matching or mismatching emotional valence. The affective priming effect (faster RT for congruent vs. incongruent prime-target pairs) reflects automatic activation of evaluative representations. Subliminal variants (very brief prime exposure) provide evidence for unconscious emotional processing.

procedure: A briefly presented prime (word, face, or image with positive or negative valence) is followed by a target that participants evaluate as good/bad or classify.
manipulations: Congruence between prime valence and target valence
measurements: RT and accuracy for target evaluation
Congruency effect (faster on congruent trials) indexes automatic affective evaluation

variations.name: Evaluative Decision (Good/Bad)
variations.description: A brief positive or negative prime (a word or picture) is followed by a target word, and the participant presses one key if the target is good or pleasant and another if it is bad or unpleasant. Responses are faster when prime and target share the same valence. This is the most common form of the task.
variations.justification: Participant makes explicit valence judgment; changes response task from standard LDT

variations.name: Pronunciation/Naming
variations.description: After the prime, the participant reads the target word aloud as quickly as possible instead of judging it. Naming time is shorter when the prime and target have the same valence, so priming is measured without asking the participant to evaluate anything.
variations.justification: Vocal naming response instead of evaluative judgment; different output modality and response event

variations.name: Subliminal Priming
variations.description: The prime is flashed so briefly (typically under 30 ms) and is immediately covered by a mask, so the participant cannot consciously see it. The participant then evaluates the visible target as usual. Any priming effect must arise from processing the participant is not aware of.
variations.justification: Prime below conscious threshold; changes stimulus timing structure and awareness conditions

variations.name: Picture-Word Priming
variations.description: The prime is an emotional photograph rather than a word, and the target is a word to be evaluated. The participant sees a picture briefly, then a word, and judges the word as good or bad.
variations.justification: Visual picture prime instead of word; different stimulus type with distinct semantic processing

variations.name: Face-Face Priming
variations.description: Both the prime and the target are faces with emotional expressions. The participant sees a brief face, then a second face, and judges the second face's expression (for example happy or angry).
variations.justification: Social/facial stimuli as both prime and target; structurally distinct from word-prime paradigm

variations.name: Cross-Modal Affective Priming
variations.description: The prime is heard rather than seen, for example a spoken word or an emotional sound, and the target is a visible word. The participant judges the written target while the prime arrives through headphones.
variations.justification: Auditory prime + visual target; cross-modal structure creates distinct event types

variations.name: Masked vs. Unmasked Priming
variations.description: The same prime-target pairs are run in two conditions: one where the prime is clearly visible and one where it is masked and too brief to be seen. Comparing the two separates fast automatic priming from priming that depends on the participant noticing the prime and using it strategically.
variations.justification: Systematic masking manipulation changes prime visibility and conscious access to prime

families.rationale: Evaluative priming; the congruence structure could argue for conflict and interference

short_definition: Participants must suppress a prepotent saccade toward a peripheral cue and generate a voluntary saccade to the opposite location; errors and saccade latency index oculomotor inhibition.
description: The Anti-Saccade Task measures voluntary control over reflexive eye movements. Participants fixate centrally while a peripheral stimulus suddenly appears in the left or right visual field. Instead of looking toward the stimulus (the reflexive prosaccade), participants must look in the opposite direction (antisaccade). This requires inhibiting the automatic orienting response and generating a volitional saccade. Performance is measured by antisaccade accuracy, latency, and the rate of prosaccadic intrusions (errors). The task indexes voluntary oculomotor control and prefrontal inhibitory function.

procedure: A peripheral cue appears.
Participants must suppress the reflexive saccade toward it and instead generate a voluntary saccade to the mirror-opposite location.
manipulations: Prosaccade vs. antisaccade blocks or interleaved trials
measurements: Saccade direction errors (% erroneous prosaccades on antisaccade trials)

variations.name: Standard Anti-Saccade
variations.description: The participant fixates a central point. A cue flashes to the left or right, and the participant must look to the opposite side, at the same distance from center, as quickly as possible. Looking toward the cue by mistake is counted as an error.
variations.justification: Canonical paradigm: participant inhibits reflexive saccade and redirects gaze to mirror location

variations.name: Prosaccade (Control Condition)
variations.description: The same display, but the participant is told to look toward the flashing cue rather than away from it. This is the reflexive, easy response and serves as a baseline for eye-movement speed and accuracy.
variations.justification: Opposite stimulus-response mapping (look toward cue); different response requirement from anti-saccade

variations.name: Interleaved Pro/Anti-Saccade
variations.description: Look-toward and look-away trials are mixed unpredictably within the same block, with a cue on each trial (often fixation color) saying which rule applies. The participant must switch rules from trial to trial.
variations.justification: Mixed trial types require on-trial task-set switching; distinct from blocked presentation

variations.name: Blocked Pro/Anti-Saccade
variations.description: Look-toward trials and look-away trials are run in separate blocks, so the participant keeps the same rule throughout a block and never has to switch.
variations.justification: Separate blocks of pro- and anti-saccade trials; different cognitive context from interleaved

variations.name: Gap vs. Overlap Conditions
variations.description: Varies what happens to the central fixation point when the cue appears. In the gap condition it disappears about 200 ms before the cue, which speeds up eye movements and increases errors. In the overlap condition it stays on while the cue is shown.
variations.justification: Fixation offset timing changes saccade initiation dynamics and error rates

variations.name: Delayed Anti-Saccade
variations.description: The cue appears, but the participant must keep looking at the center and wait for a go signal (often the fixation point going off) before looking away from where the cue was. Holding the eyes still through the delay adds a waiting and memory demand.
variations.justification: Memory-guided response after delay period; adds working memory component

variations.name: Emotional Anti-Saccade
variations.description: The peripheral cue is a face with an emotional expression (or another emotional picture) instead of a plain dot. The participant still looks away from it; the question is whether emotional cues are harder to look away from.
variations.justification: Emotional stimuli as saccade targets; retained per section 5.1 (EMOT retired)

variations.name: Memory-Guided Anti-Saccade
variations.description: The cue flashes and then disappears, and the participant must remember where it was during a delay before making the look-away eye movement to the opposite location on a later signal.
variations.justification: Target location must be retained in memory before response; distinct memory demand

variations.name: Double-Step Anti-Saccade
variations.description: Two cues appear in quick succession, or the target jumps to a new place just as the eye movement starts. The participant has to correct an eye movement that is already planned or under way.
variations.justification: Two-step target displacement requires online motor reprogramming

families.rationale: Suppress the reflexive saccade and look away

short_definition: Exposure to letter strings generated by a finite-state grammar followed by a grammaticality judgment on novel strings; indexes implicit rule learning.
description: Participants are first exposed to letter strings (e.g., "MXRVXT," "VXTTRM") generated by a finite-state grammar, often under the cover story that they are memorizing the strings. In a subsequent test phase, they classify novel letter strings as grammatical or non-grammatical, performing above chance despite being unable to articulate the underlying rules. Reber (1967) introduced this paradigm as the first laboratory demonstration of implicit learning - the acquisition of complex, rule-governed knowledge without conscious awareness. The paradigm has been central to debates about the nature of implicit vs. explicit knowledge, the role of consciousness in learning, and the neural systems supporting rule abstraction.

procedure: Participants study letter strings generated by a finite-state grammar during a training phase, then classify novel strings as grammatical or not.
manipulations: Surface features (same vs. changed letter set at test)

variations.name: Standard AGL (Reber)
variations.description: The participant first studies a set of letter strings (such as VXTVPS) that were generated by hidden rules, usually by copying or memorizing them. They are then told the strings followed rules and asked to judge whether new strings follow the same rules. Above-chance judgments show learning the participant usually cannot describe.
variations.justification: Canonical implicit grammar learning: exposure to strings, then grammaticality judgment

variations.name: Transfer Version
variations.description: Training strings use one set of letters, but the test strings use a different set of letters arranged by the same underlying rules. Because the surface letters are new, the participant can only succeed by having learned the abstract structure rather than memorizing letter fragments.
variations.justification: Novel surface elements at test; isolates abstract rule knowledge from surface memorization

variations.name: Chunk Strength Control
variations.description: The test strings are built so that rule-following and rule-breaking strings contain equally familiar pairs and triples of letters from training. This stops the participant from judging strings just by how familiar their pieces feel.
variations.justification: Stimuli equated for associative chunk strength; controls for alternative explanation

variations.name: Production Task
variations.description: After training, instead of judging strings, the participant writes or types new strings they believe follow the rules. What they produce shows which parts of the structure were learned.
variations.justification: Participant generates grammatical strings rather than judging them; different output requirement

variations.name: Sequential AGL
variations.description: Each string is shown one letter at a time rather than all at once, and the participant may be asked to predict or respond to each next letter as it arrives. This turns the task into learning what tends to follow what over time.
variations.justification: Motor/spatial sequential learning of grammar; different modality and response type

variations.name: Hierarchical AGL
variations.description: The hidden rules include nested, center-embedded structure (like A1 A2 B2 B1), so elements pair up across the string rather than only with their immediate neighbors. Tests whether implicit learning can pick up this longer-range structure.
variations.justification: Nested recursive grammar; structurally distinct grammar type requiring different parsing

variations.name: Cross-Modal AGL
variations.description: The strings are presented as sequences of sounds (tones or syllables) or touches rather than as letters, or training is in one modality and testing in another. The participant still judges which new sequences follow the rules.
variations.justification: Stimulus modality change (visual->auditory or vice versa) at test; cross-modal transfer paradigm

families.rationale: Implicit rule learning from exposure to strings

short_definition: Identify the direction of a central arrow flanked by congruent or incongruent arrows, preceded by various cue types; RT differences across cue and flanker conditions index three independent attention networks (alerting, orienting, executive).
description: The Attention Network Test (ANT) combines elements of the Posner cueing paradigm and the Eriksen flanker task to provide separate measures of three attention networks in a single task. Participants respond to the direction of a central arrow flanked by congruent or incongruent flankers, with the target preceded by no cue, a center cue, a double cue, or a spatial cue. The ANT yields three independent efficiency scores: alerting (double cue benefit over no cue), orienting (spatial cue benefit over center cue), and executive control (incongruent flanker cost). The task operationalizes Posner's attention network model.

procedure: Flanker task with preceding spatial and temporal cues.
Participants identify the direction of a central arrow flanked by congruent or incongruent arrows.
manipulations: Cue type (no cue, center cue, double cue, spatial cue)
measurements: Alerting network score (double-cue minus no-cue RT)
Orienting network score (center-cue minus spatial-cue RT)
Executive network score (incongruent minus congruent RT)

variations.name: Standard ANT (Fan et al., 2002)
variations.description: On each trial a cue (none, a central alerting cue, cues at both possible locations, or a cue at the target location) is followed by a row of five arrows above or below fixation. The participant reports the direction of the middle arrow. Comparing cue types gives alerting and orienting scores; comparing matching and mismatching flankers gives an executive score.
variations.justification: Canonical ANT with three cue types and flanker congruency; measures alerting, orienting, executive

variations.name: ANT-I (Callejas et al.)
variations.description: Same arrows and flankers, but the alerting cue is a tone and the location cue is a separate visual cue, with each manipulated independently on every trial. This design lets the three network effects be tested for interactions with each other, which the original cannot do.
variations.justification: Revised cue design with interaction effects measure; different trial structure and network scoring

variations.name: ANT-R (Revised)
variations.description: A revised design with more cue conditions, including a cue that points to the wrong location, and longer and varied intervals between cue and target. It separates orienting into moving and disengaging attention and gives more reliable executive scores.
variations.justification: Revised version with separate conflict and inhibition measures; different trial protocol

variations.name: Lateralized ANT (LANT)
variations.description: The arrow rows appear to the left or right of fixation rather than above or below it, so each target is delivered first to one hemisphere of the brain. The participant still reports the middle arrow's direction.
variations.justification: Stimuli presented laterally to test hemispheric contributions; different spatial arrangement

variations.name: Child ANT
variations.description: Arrows are replaced by a row of cartoon fish, and the child presses a key for the direction the middle fish is swimming. Trials are slower, there is feedback, and the task is framed as feeding the fish.
variations.justification: Fish stimuli, simplified flanker; procedure genuinely adapted for children per section 5.3

variations.name: ANT with Emotional Stimuli
variations.description: Emotional pictures or faces are used as cues, or emotional images replace the neutral flankers, so the participant must report the central target while emotional content competes for attention.
variations.justification: Emotional flanker content; retained per section 5.1 (EMOT retired)

families.rationale: Cueing combined with a flanker; filed by its cue manipulation

short_definition: Detect, discriminate, or identify a target sound in the presence of a masking sound; threshold shifts between masked and unmasked conditions index frequency selectivity, temporal resolution, and auditory scene analysis.
description: A target sound (tone, speech token, or noise burst) is presented alongside, before, or after a masking sound, and participants detect, discriminate, or identify the target. By varying the temporal and spectral relationship between target and masker, the paradigm dissociates peripheral (energetic) masking - where masker and target excite overlapping auditory filters - from central (informational) masking - where the masker is spectrally remote but introduces perceptual uncertainty. Threshold shifts, psychometric functions, and comodulation masking release are the core dependent measures. The paradigm is foundational to auditory psychophysics and clinical audiology, and maps onto distinct subcortical and cortical processing stages.

procedure: A target sound is presented alongside, before, or after a masker.
Participants detect, discriminate, or identify the target.
manipulations: Spectral overlap between target and masker

variations.name: Simultaneous masking
variations.description: The target sound and the masking sound play at the same time. The participant reports whether the target was present, and its level is adjusted to find the quietest level still detectable in the masker. Used to measure how finely the ear separates frequencies.
variations.justification: Masker and target overlap in time; fundamental temporal configuration of masking

variations.name: Forward masking
variations.description: The masker plays first and stops, and the target sound follows after a short silent gap (a few to a few hundred milliseconds). The participant reports whether the target was heard. The closer the target follows the masker, the harder it is to hear.
variations.justification: Masker precedes target; different temporal relationship produces distinct masking mechanism

variations.name: Backward masking
variations.description: The brief target sound plays first and the masker follows it. Even though the target comes first, a masker arriving soon enough afterwards makes it harder to detect.
variations.justification: Masker follows target; different temporal order from forward masking

variations.name: Energetic masking (peripheral)
variations.description: The masker is a noise or tone that overlaps the target in frequency, so the two sounds physically compete in the same region of the inner ear. Detection thresholds can be predicted from the acoustics alone.
variations.justification: Peripheral auditory overlap; mechanistically distinct from informational masking

variations.name: Informational masking (central)
variations.description: The masker does not overlap the target in frequency, but it is similar or unpredictable enough (for example random tone complexes or other speech) that the listener has trouble telling target from masker. The difficulty comes from confusion and attention rather than from the ear itself.
variations.justification: Central/cognitive masking mechanism; different stimulus and processing demands

variations.name: Comodulation masking release (CMR)
variations.description: The target tone is masked by a narrow band of noise, and additional noise bands are added at other frequencies. When those bands rise and fall in loudness together with the masker, the target becomes easier to hear; when they fluctuate independently, it does not.
variations.justification: Comodulated flanking bands release target from masking; unique stimulus configuration

variations.name: Speech-in-noise
variations.description: The target is spoken words or sentences, and the masker is other talkers, babble or steady noise. The participant repeats or identifies what was said, and the signal-to-noise ratio at which half the words are correct is the measure.
variations.justification: Speech target in noise background; distinct task with different linguistic processing demands

variations.name: Tone-in-noise detection
variations.description: The target is a pure tone and the masker is broadband or narrowband noise. The participant reports whether the tone was present in each noise burst, often choosing which of two intervals contained it. The basic version of the task.
variations.justification: Pure tone detection in wideband noise; different target type from speech or complex stimuli

variations.name: Modulation masking
variations.description: Rather than detecting a sound, the participant detects whether a sound's loudness is fluttering (amplitude modulated). A masker with its own loudness fluctuations at a nearby rate makes the target flutter harder to notice.
variations.justification: Masking of temporal amplitude modulation; different perceptual dimension

variations.name: Spatial release from masking
variations.description: The target and masker are played from different directions, either from separate loudspeakers or with headphone cues that place them apart. The participant's detection threshold is compared with the same sounds played from the same location.
variations.justification: Spatial separation of target and masker; binaural processing distinguishes it from monaural variants

families.rationale: Detection or discrimination of a sound in noise

short_definition: Sequential pumping of a virtual balloon for monetary reward with stochastic popping; average pumps per un-popped balloon indexes risk-taking.
description: Participants inflate a virtual balloon by clicking a pump button, earning money with each pump. The balloon may explode at any point, causing loss of all accumulated earnings for that trial. Participants can cash out at any time to save their earnings. The average number of pumps before cashing out indexes risk-taking propensity. BART risk-taking correlates with real-world risky behaviors. fMRI reveals activation in ventromedial PFC, anterior insula, and striatal regions during risk assessment.

procedure: Participants sequentially pump a virtual balloon for incremental monetary reward.
Each pump risks the balloon popping and losing that trial's earnings.
They can stop and bank at any time.
measurements: Adjusted average pumps on un-popped balloons (risk-taking index)

variations.name: Standard BART (30 balloons)
variations.description: A balloon appears on screen. Each press of a pump key inflates it slightly and adds a small amount of money to a temporary bank. The participant can stop at any time and collect, but if the balloon pops the money for that balloon is lost. There are typically 30 balloons, each with a hidden random pop point.
variations.justification: Canonical BART: pump balloon for accumulating reward, risk of explosion

variations.name: BART-Y (Youth Version)
variations.description: A version for children and adolescents that uses points toward a prize rather than money, a simpler display, and a progress meter so the child can see what has been earned. The pump-or-collect decision is unchanged.
variations.justification: Modified pumping interface and simplified feedback for youth; procedure adapted per section 5.3

variations.name: Variable Explosion Probability
variations.description: Different balloons (often shown in different colors) pop according to different hidden rules, for example one color tends to pop early and another late. The participant can learn to pump more on the safer color.
variations.justification: Explicitly communicated explosion probabilities; changes decision-making structure

variations.name: High-Stakes vs. Low-Stakes
variations.description: The amount of money earned per pump is varied, for example one cent versus 25 cents, in different blocks or balloon colors. Tests whether people take fewer risks when more money is on the line.
variations.justification: Reward magnitude manipulation changes risk-reward trade-off context

variations.name: Social Context BART
variations.description: The participant plays while being watched by a peer or experimenter, or is shown how other people pumped, instead of playing alone. Measures whether an audience or peer information changes risk taking.
variations.justification: Observer or peer performance information present; changes social decision-making context

variations.name: Automatic BART
variations.description: Before each balloon the participant types how many pumps they want, and the balloon then inflates by itself to that number (or pops first). This removes the moment-to-moment decision to keep going and captures only the planned level of risk.
variations.justification: Balloon pumps automatically; removes active pumping decision, isolates risk tolerance

variations.name: BART with Loss Domain
variations.description: Each balloon starts with money already in it, and every pump removes some of that money while raising the chance of a pop that would lose a larger amount. The participant decides how much loss to accept rather than how much gain to chase.
variations.justification: Losses instead of gains; loss framing changes motivational structure of decisions

families.rationale: Sequential risk taking for reward

short_definition: Judgment of human action or identity from sparse point-light displays attached to major joints; indexes recognition of biological motion from kinematic cues alone.
description: Participants view point-light display stimuli, animations created by placing markers on the joints of a person performing actions and capturing only the light points. The resulting stimuli (12-15 dots representing joints) convey complex human actions (walking, running, dancing) from minimal motion cues. Participants may recognize actions, judge coherence (upright vs. inverted), or discriminate biological from scrambled motion. The task measures perception of complex human movement and activates the posterior superior temporal sulcus, a region specialized for biological motion processing.

procedure: Participants view point-light displays (dots at major joints) and identify actions, discriminate facing direction, or detect biological motion embedded in noise dots.
manipulations: Display type (intact vs. scrambled vs. inverted)
measurements: Accuracy and RT for action identification, direction discrimination, or detection
Noise-dot threshold for biological motion detection

variations.name: Intact Biological Motion
variations.description: The participant watches a display of about a dozen moving dots placed at the joints of a walking person. The dots alone are enough to see a walker, and the participant reports what is seen, for example whether a person is present or which way they are walking.
variations.justification: Standard point-light walker; canonical biological motion stimulus

variations.name: Scrambled Displays
variations.description: Each dot keeps its own movement pattern but is shifted to a random starting position, so the dots no longer line up as a body. The participant sees the same local motions without the overall figure, which serves as a control.
variations.justification: Spatially scrambled dots preserve local motion but destroy global form; control condition with different percept

variations.name: Inverted Displays
variations.description: The point-light walker is shown upside down. Recognition becomes much harder, which shows that the visual system expects figures in their usual orientation.
variations.justification: Walker inverted; disrupts configural processing while preserving motion signals

variations.name: Reversed (Backward) Motion
variations.description: The walking animation is played in reverse, so the body shape is intact but the movements unfold in an unnatural order. The participant judges the display as usual.
variations.justification: Temporal reversal disrupts action identity while preserving form

variations.name: Action Recognition
variations.description: The point-light figure performs one of several actions, such as walking, running, jumping, throwing or kicking, and the participant names or chooses which action it was.
variations.justification: Participant identifies specific action (running, kicking); classification task beyond detection

variations.name: Detection in Noise
variations.description: The walker's dots are hidden among extra randomly moving dots, and the participant reports whether a walker is present or where it is. The number of noise dots sets the difficulty.
variations.justification: Walker embedded in noise dots; detection task with varying signal-to-noise

variations.name: Gender/Identity Discrimination
variations.description: The participant judges whether the point-light walker is male or female, or which of several known people it is, using only the way the dots move.
variations.justification: Discrimination of walker gender or identity; different judgment dimension

variations.name: Emotion from Body Motion
variations.description: The point-light figure moves in a way that expresses an emotion, such as angry, sad or happy walking, and the participant names the emotion from the movement alone.
variations.justification: Emotional state judged from body kinematics; different recognition task

variations.name: Partial/Occluded Displays
variations.description: Only some of the joint dots are shown, or parts of the figure pass behind an invisible occluder, and the participant must still judge the figure from the incomplete display.
variations.justification: Subset of dots visible; tests perceptual completion of biological motion

variations.name: Comparison with Mechanical Motion
variations.description: Point-light displays of a person are mixed with displays of rigid or mechanical motion, such as a rotating object or a machine, and the participant decides which kind of motion each display shows.
variations.justification: Mechanical motion control alongside biological; category discrimination task

variations.name: Facing Direction Discrimination
variations.description: The walker walks in place, and the participant reports whether it is facing left or right. Judging facing direction depends on recovering the body's shape from the moving dots.
variations.justification: Ambiguous facing direction judgment; different perceptual task

families.rationale: Judgment of point-light displays

short_definition: Learn target faces across viewpoints, then identify them among distractors under increasingly difficult conditions (novel viewpoints, visual noise); accuracy indexes face recognition ability and configural face processing.
description: The Cambridge Face Memory Test is the standard measure of face recognition ability for both clinical and individual-difference research. Participants study six target faces shown in three different viewpoints. Testing occurs in three phases of increasing difficulty: in Phase 1, targets are tested in studied viewpoints; in Phase 2, targets appear in novel viewpoints and lighting conditions; in Phase 3, Gaussian visual noise is added to the images. Each phase has 12 trials (one target face among five distractor faces), yielding a total score of 72. The CFMT specifically indexes holistic and configural face processing, is relatively culture-fair, and has become the benchmark for diagnosing prosopagnosia and studying "super-recognizers."

procedure: Participants learn a set of target faces during study, then identify them among distractor faces in increasingly difficult test phases (same image, novel viewpoint, plus noise).
manipulations: Test phase difficulty (same view, novel view, contrast-degraded)

variations.name: CFMT-Original
variations.description: The participant learns six unfamiliar male faces, then picks each from sets of three in three stages: the same images, new images with different views and lighting, and new images degraded with visual noise. Seventy-two trials in all.
variations.justification: Canonical 72-item CFMT with novel face learning phases

variations.name: CFMT-Australian (CFMT+)
variations.description: The same procedure with a different set of faces and an added fourth stage of harder, noisier trials, which prevents the best performers from hitting the maximum score.
variations.justification: Australian race face set; assesses own-race advantage with matched procedure

variations.name: CFMT-Cars
variations.description: The same learn-and-recognize procedure using images of cars instead of faces. Comparing it with the face version shows whether a person's difficulty is specific to faces or extends to visual memory in general.
variations.justification: Cars instead of faces; object recognition control condition with same task structure

variations.name: CFMT-Inverted
variations.description: All face images are shown upside down throughout learning and testing. Upside-down faces are much harder to recognize, and the size of the drop measures how much the participant relies on seeing the face as a whole.
variations.justification: Inverted face stimuli; disrupts configural processing; distinct task demand

variations.name: Cambridge Face Perception Test (CFPT)
variations.description: A companion task with no memory component. The participant sees a target face and six faces that have been morphed to resemble it to different degrees, and sorts the six by similarity to the target.
variations.justification: Morph-ordering perception task instead of recognition; different participant operation

variations.name: Short-Form CFMT
variations.description: A shortened version with fewer trials for quick screening of face recognition ability, following the same learn-then-choose procedure.
variations.justification: Abbreviated item set for screening; recognized published short-form instrument

families.rationale: Learn then recognize faces; could be filed under perceptual judgment as a face-processing measure

short_definition: Brief sample array followed after a blank delay by a probe array; participant reports whether any item changed. Yields visual working memory capacity (K).
description: The Change Detection Task, developed by Luck and Vogel (1997), is the standard paradigm for measuring visual working memory capacity. Participants briefly view a memory array of colored squares (typically 100-500 ms), followed by a blank retention interval (~900 ms), then a test array. On half the trials, one item changes color; participants report whether a change occurred. Performance is converted to a capacity estimate (K) using Cowan's formula: K = set size x (hit rate - false alarm rate). The task established that visual WM capacity is approximately 3-4 items in healthy adults and has been instrumental in research linking WM capacity to attention, intelligence, and neural oscillations.

procedure: A brief memory array of colored squares (or oriented bars) is followed by a retention interval and a test array.
Participants indicate whether a change occurred.
measurements: Accuracy converted to capacity estimate K (Cowan's K or Pashler's K)

variations.name: Standard Color Change Detection
variations.description: A few colored squares appear briefly, the screen goes blank for about a second, and the squares reappear. On half the trials one square has changed color. The participant reports whether anything changed. Accuracy at different numbers of squares gives an estimate of how many items can be held in mind.
variations.justification: Canonical flicker paradigm: colored squares change across blank; whole/partial report

variations.name: Single-Probe Change Detection
variations.description: After the blank interval only one square reappears, at one of the original locations, and the participant reports whether that one square is the same or different. This removes the need to compare the whole display.
variations.justification: Post-array probe tests one item; different response structure from whole-display report

variations.name: Orientation Change Detection
variations.description: The items are tilted bars rather than colored squares, and a change is a bar rotating to a new angle. Everything else is as in the color version.
variations.justification: Orientation feature instead of color; different perceptual dimension

variations.name: Conjunction Change Detection
variations.description: Each item has two features, such as a color and an orientation, and a change can swap features between items or alter one feature. The participant must remember which color went with which orientation, not just which features were present.
variations.justification: Conjunctions of features can change; higher-order binding demand

variations.name: Change Detection with Filtering
variations.description: The display includes items the participant is told to ignore (for example, remember only the red bars, not the blue ones). Memory for the relevant items is then compared with a display that had no distractors, measuring how well the irrelevant items were kept out.
variations.justification: Some items task-relevant, others to be ignored; adds selective attention demand

variations.name: Continuous Report / Precision Task
variations.description: Instead of a same-or-different answer, one location is probed and the participant reproduces the remembered feature exactly, for example by clicking the remembered color on a color wheel. The spread of errors measures how precise each memory is.
variations.justification: Participant reports exact remembered value on continuous wheel; different response format

variations.name: Sequential Presentation
variations.description: The items are shown one after another rather than all at the same time, and the test display follows the last item. Memory must be built up serially instead of from a single glance.
variations.justification: Items presented serially before test; different encoding structure

families.rationale: Sample array, delay, probe array

short_definition: Visual search in which some distractor configurations repeat across blocks; faster search on repeated configurations indexes implicit spatial context learning.
description: Participants perform visual search for a T-shaped target among L-shaped distractors. Critically, half the search displays repeat across blocks (with the target always in the same location within a given repeated display), while the other half are newly generated on each block. Search becomes faster for repeated displays over blocks, even though participants cannot consciously recognize which displays have been repeated. Chun and Jiang (1998) demonstrated that this contextual cueing effect reflects implicit learning and memory for spatial configurations that guide spatial attention to the likely target location. The paradigm has become a standard tool for studying the interface between attention, implicit learning, and long-term memory.

procedure: Visual search through letter arrays.
Some spatial configurations repeat across blocks while others are novel.
Participants find and respond to a target embedded in the display.
measurements: RT advantage for repeated over novel configurations (contextual cueing effect)

variations.name: Standard Visual Search CC
variations.description: The participant searches for a rotated T among rotated Ls and reports which way the T points. Unknown to the participant, half the displays repeat the same arrangement of items across blocks. Search gets faster on the repeated displays even though participants cannot tell them from new ones.
variations.justification: Canonical: repeated spatial configurations implicitly facilitate target detection

variations.name: Configuration-Based vs. Association-Based CC
variations.description: Repeated displays are built so that either the whole layout repeats, or only the pairing between the target's position and the positions of a few distractors repeats while the rest changes. Comparing the two shows what part of the context is being learned.
variations.justification: Separates global configuration from local target-distractor association; different learning conditions

variations.name: Semantic Contextual Cueing
variations.description: The search displays are photographs of real scenes with a target object placed somewhere in each. Scenes repeat across blocks, and the participant learns where the target is likely to be in a given scene.
variations.justification: Semantic scene content instead of arbitrary array; different memory system engaged

variations.name: Cross-Modal Contextual Cueing
variations.description: The repeated context is a sound or a touch pattern rather than a visual layout. A particular sound is paired with a particular target location, and search becomes faster when that sound plays.
variations.justification: Auditory context cues visual search; cross-modal learning paradigm

variations.name: Dynamic Contextual Cueing
variations.description: The items in the search display move. What repeats is the pattern of motion and the target's eventual position rather than a fixed static layout, and the participant learns to find the target from the repeated motion pattern.
variations.justification: Moving-element arrays instead of static; different perceptual and memory demands

variations.name: Transfer of Contextual Cueing
variations.description: After the usual learning blocks, the repeated displays are altered in a test phase: distractor identities are changed, distractors are added or removed, or the target is moved to a new place in a familiar layout. Whether the speed-up survives shows what was learned.
variations.justification: Tests whether learned context transfers to new target locations; different probe phase

families.rationale: Visual search with repeated layouts; the learning could argue for conditioning and implicit learning

short_definition: Extended stream of stimuli in which a rare target requires a response; omission and commission errors index sustained attention and response control.
description: The Continuous Performance Task requires participants to continuously monitor a stream of stimuli and respond selectively to infrequent target stimuli while withholding responses to non-targets over an extended period (5-15 minutes). The standard version involves responding when the letter "X" appears; the AX-CPT variant requires responding only when "A" is immediately followed by "X." Target frequency is typically 5-25% of trials. Performance measures include hit rate, false alarm rate, d' (sensitivity), and vigilance decrement over time. The task is widely used in ADHD research and clinical neuropsychology.

procedure: A rapid sequence of stimuli is presented.
Participants respond to infrequent target stimuli and withhold responses to non-targets over a prolonged session (10-20 min).

variations.name: X-CPT (Simple)
variations.description: Single letters appear one at a time for several minutes, and the participant presses a key only when the letter X appears, which is rare. Missed Xs and presses to other letters are the measures.
variations.justification: Respond to single target letter; canonical simple vigilance paradigm

variations.name: AX-CPT (Context Processing)
variations.description: Letters appear in pairs. The participant presses the target key only when an X follows an A; an X after any other letter, or any other letter after an A, gets the non-target key. The participant has to remember the previous letter to respond correctly, and A-then-X pairs are made frequent so that the A creates a strong expectation.
variations.justification: Context-dependent target requires tracking A->X sequence; different working memory demand

variations.name: Identical Pairs CPT (IP-CPT)
variations.description: A stream of digits or shapes is shown, and the participant presses a key whenever an item is identical to the one just before it. Each item must be held briefly and compared with the next.
variations.justification: Respond when consecutive stimuli match; different stimulus-response rule

variations.name: Gradual-Onset CPT (gradCPT)
variations.description: Photographs of scenes fade continuously into one another with no blank gaps, about one every 800 ms. The participant presses a key for one category (for example cities) and withholds for the rare other category (mountains). The lack of abrupt onsets makes the task depend on steady attention rather than being prompted by each new stimulus.
variations.justification: Stimuli gradually transition instead of discrete flashes; different perceptual and decision dynamics

variations.name: Auditory CPT
variations.description: The stream of items is heard rather than seen, for example spoken letters or tones through headphones, and the participant responds only to the rare target sound.
variations.justification: Auditory stimulus stream instead of visual; different sensory modality

variations.name: Conners' CPT-3
variations.description: A commercial standardized version in which the participant presses the space bar for every letter except X, which is withheld. The 14-minute task varies the pace between blocks and provides age norms used in attention-deficit assessment.
variations.justification: Standardized commercial CPT with letter stimuli and specific timing; named published instrument

variations.name: TOVA (Test of Variables of Attention)
variations.description: A commercial version using a simple geometric shape that appears at the top or bottom of the screen. The participant presses a button for the target position only. Targets are rare in the first half and frequent in the second, and timing and norms are fixed by the instrument.
variations.justification: Geometric stimuli, fixed ISI; distinct named instrument with different timing parameters

variations.name: CPT with Emotional Distractors
variations.description: Emotional pictures or faces appear in the background or between items while the participant performs the usual target detection, so sustained attention is measured in the presence of emotional distraction.
variations.justification: Emotional stimuli as distractors; retained per section 5.1 (EMOT retired)

families.rationale: Rare targets in an extended stream

short_definition: Experimenter taps a sequence on spatially arranged blocks; participant reproduces the sequence forward or backward. Indexes visuospatial short-term and working memory span.
description: The Corsi Block-Tapping Task measures visuospatial short-term and working memory. Nine blocks are arranged irregularly on a board (or screen). The examiner taps a sequence of blocks, and the participant reproduces the sequence. Sequence length increases from 2 blocks upward until the participant fails two consecutive sequences at a given length. The maximum reliably reproduced length defines the Corsi span, typically around 5-6 for healthy adults. The backward version requires reproducing sequences in reverse order, adding executive demands. The task is the spatial counterpart of Digit Span and is critical for understanding the visuospatial sketchpad component of working memory.

procedure: The experimenter (or computer) taps a sequence of blocks on a board.
The participant reproduces the sequence in the same (or reverse) order.
Sequence length increases until recall fails.

variations.name: Forward Corsi Span
variations.description: Nine identical blocks are fixed to a board in an irregular layout. The experimenter taps a sequence of blocks, and the participant taps the same blocks in the same order. Sequences get longer until the participant fails, and the longest correct length is the span.
variations.justification: Reproduce tapped sequence in same order; canonical visuospatial span

variations.name: Backward Corsi Span
variations.description: The experimenter taps a sequence and the participant taps the same blocks in reverse order, from last to first. This requires holding the sequence and reordering it before responding.
variations.justification: Reproduce sequence in reverse order; requires mental transformation

variations.name: Computerized (eCorsi)
variations.description: The blocks are squares on a touchscreen or monitor that light up in sequence, and the participant touches or clicks them in order. Timing of each touch is recorded, and the squares cannot be felt as physical objects.
variations.justification: Screen-based tapping vs. physical blocks; per section 5.6 changes spatial/motor demands

variations.name: Supra-Span Corsi
variations.description: The same sequence, longer than the participant's span, is presented repeatedly until it can be reproduced correctly. The number of attempts needed measures how quickly a spatial sequence is learned.
variations.justification: Sequences exceed span; repeated learning-to-criterion procedure

variations.name: Walking Corsi (large-scale)
variations.description: The blocks are replaced by tiles or markers on the floor of a room. The experimenter walks to a sequence of tiles, and the participant then walks the same route. Memory is tested for places reached by walking rather than by hand.
variations.justification: Full-body locomotion to large floor locations; different motor modality from finger tapping

variations.name: Sequential vs. Simultaneous Presentation
variations.description: In the simultaneous version the blocks of a set are highlighted all at once, with numbers or arrows showing the order, instead of being tapped one after another. The participant still reproduces them in order.
variations.justification: All blocks illuminated at once vs. sequentially; changes encoding demands

variations.name: Crossed/Uncrossed Paths
variations.description: Sequences are chosen so that the path from block to block either crosses over itself or does not. Sequences whose path crosses are harder to remember even when the same number of blocks is tapped.
variations.justification: Spatial crossing of sequence paths tests motor programming constraints

families.rationale: Reproduce a spatial sequence

short_definition: Repeated choices between smaller-sooner and larger-later rewards at varying delays; indifference points estimate a temporal discount function.
description: Participants make repeated choices between a smaller immediate reward and a larger delayed reward (e.g., "$10 now or $25 in 1 week"). The immediate amount or delay is systematically varied to estimate indifference points, yielding a discount rate reflecting how steeply the subjective value of rewards declines with delay. Steeper discounting reflects greater impulsivity. fMRI reveals differential activation of ventromedial PFC and nucleus accumbens (immediate preference) versus dorsolateral PFC and posterior parietal cortex (delayed preference), supporting dual-system valuation models.

procedure: Participants choose between a smaller immediate reward and a larger delayed reward across many trials with varying amounts and delays.

variations.name: Adjusting-Amount Method
variations.description: For each delay (for example one week, one month, one year) the participant repeatedly chooses between a smaller amount now and a fixed larger amount later. The immediate amount is raised or lowered after each choice until the participant is indifferent. That amount is the present value of the delayed reward.
variations.justification: Adjusts smaller-sooner amount until indifferent; adaptive titration procedure

variations.name: Adjusting-Delay Method
variations.description: The two amounts are fixed, and it is the waiting time for the larger amount that is adjusted after each choice until the participant is indifferent between the two options.
variations.justification: Adjusts delay until indifferent; different dimension titrated

variations.name: 5-Trial Adjusting Delay
variations.description: A very short version that finds the delay at which a reward loses half its value in just five choices, each halving the range of possible delays. It takes about a minute.
variations.justification: Rapid 5-trial protocol; distinct abbreviated titration method

variations.name: Fixed-Choice Discrete Trials
variations.description: The participant answers a fixed list of now-versus-later questions, such as the 27-item Monetary Choice Questionnaire, with no adjustment based on earlier answers. The pattern of choices is fitted afterwards to estimate the discount rate.
variations.justification: Fixed set of choices without adaptation; different decision structure

variations.name: Magnitude Manipulation
variations.description: The whole procedure is run separately for small, medium and large rewards (for example 10, 100 and 1000 dollars). Larger amounts are usually discounted less steeply.
variations.justification: Systematically varies reward magnitude; tests magnitude effect on discounting

variations.name: Real vs. Hypothetical Rewards
variations.description: In the real version one of the participant's choices is selected and paid for real, including the actual wait for a delayed reward. In the hypothetical version the participant imagines the choices and nothing is paid.
variations.justification: Real monetary payoff vs. hypothetical; changes incentive structure and motivation

variations.name: Experiential Discounting Task
variations.description: The delays are short (seconds to a minute) and are actually waited out during the session, with the reward delivered at the end of each wait, rather than being described in words and imagined.
variations.justification: Delays experienced in real time; different temporal structure from verbal/hypothetical

variations.name: Gain vs. Loss Framing
variations.description: Alongside the usual choices between gains, the participant chooses between paying a smaller amount now or a larger amount later. Delayed losses are usually discounted less steeply than delayed gains.
variations.justification: Loss domain discounting; different valence changes decision context

variations.name: Probabilistic Discounting
variations.description: The larger reward is uncertain rather than delayed: the participant chooses between a smaller sure amount and a larger amount with some probability. The same adjusting procedures find the probability at which the two are equal.
variations.justification: Reward probability instead of delay; tests probability rather than temporal discounting

variations.name: Cross-Commodity Discounting
variations.description: The rewards are something other than money, such as food, a drug of abuse, or time with friends, or the two options are in different commodities. Shows whether the discount rate depends on what is being delayed.
variations.justification: Non-monetary rewards (food, drugs); different commodity changes motivational basis

families.rationale: Smaller-sooner versus larger-later choices

short_definition: Sample stimulus followed by a delay and then a probe or choice array; response indicates whether the probe matches the sample. Indexes short-term memory maintenance.
description: The Delayed Match-to-Sample (DMTS) task consists of three phases: sample, delay, and choice. During the sample phase, a stimulus is presented. Following a delay period (0-30 seconds), the participant must identify which of several test stimuli matches the original sample. Memory demands are manipulated by varying delay duration or the number of choice alternatives. The task has been fundamental in primate neuroscience for identifying the neural substrates of working memory, particularly delay-period persistent activity in prefrontal cortex.

procedure: A sample stimulus is presented, followed by a retention interval (delay), then a test stimulus.
Participants indicate whether the test matches the sample.

variations.name: Standard DMTS
variations.description: A single picture or pattern (the sample) is shown, then disappears for a delay of a few seconds. Two items then appear, one identical to the sample and one new, and the participant picks the one that matches.
variations.justification: Canonical: sample presented, delay, then match from array

variations.name: Variable Delay DMTS
variations.description: The blank interval between the sample and the choice display is varied from trial to trial, from no delay up to 30 seconds or more, so that accuracy can be plotted against how long the sample had to be held in memory.
variations.justification: Systematically varies delay length; tests forgetting function

variations.name: Multi-Choice DMTS
variations.description: The choice display contains three or more items instead of two, only one of which matches the sample. More alternatives means the memory must be more exact to rule out similar distractors.
variations.justification: More than two choices at test; increases decision complexity

variations.name: DMTS with Distraction During Delay
variations.description: Other pictures, sounds or a brief secondary task are presented while the participant is holding the sample in memory. Measures how well the memory withstands interference.
variations.justification: Interfering stimuli during retention interval; changes delay period structure

variations.name: Spatial DMTS
variations.description: What must be remembered is where the sample appeared, not what it looked like. After the delay the participant indicates the sample's location or chooses between locations.
variations.justification: Location rather than identity must be matched; different memory dimension

variations.name: DMTS with Object Complexity Manipulation
variations.description: Samples range from simple colored shapes to detailed, hard-to-name patterns. Comparing accuracy across levels shows how memory depends on how much there is to encode.
variations.justification: Varies object complexity; tests encoding difficulty directly

variations.name: Delayed Non-Match-to-Sample (DNMS)
variations.description: The rule is reversed: after the delay the participant must choose the item that was not the sample, the new one. The display is the same as in the matching version.
variations.justification: Respond to non-matching item; opposite stimulus-response mapping

families.rationale: Sample, delay, match judgment

short_definition: One-shot allocation task in which a proposer unilaterally divides an endowment between self and a passive receiver; indexes altruism and social preferences.
description: One player (dictator) unilaterally decides how much of an endowment to give to an anonymous recipient, who has no power to reject. Despite having complete power, many dictators give 20-30% of their endowment, reflecting intrinsic fairness concerns. fMRI shows generous allocations activate reward regions (ventral striatum, OFC) and empathy regions (anterior insula, ACC), suggesting altruistic choices engage similar neural systems as personal reward.

procedure: Participants in the dictator role are endowed with a sum and decide how much (if any) to give to an anonymous recipient.
The recipient has no choice but to accept.

variations.name: Standard Dictator Game
variations.description: The participant is given a sum of money and decides how much of it, if any, to give to another anonymous person who has no say and cannot respond. The amount given is the measure of generosity.
variations.justification: Canonical: unilateral allocation from fixed endowment to anonymous recipient

variations.name: Take Game
variations.description: The other person starts with the money, and the participant decides how much to take from them rather than how much to give. The outcomes possible are the same, but the action is taking rather than giving.
variations.justification: Dictator can take from recipient; different action space

variations.name: Give-or-Take Game
variations.description: Both people start with money, and the participant may either give some of their own to the other person or take some of the other person's money. Any split within the combined total is possible.
variations.justification: Both giving and taking possible; combined action space

variations.name: Double Dictator
variations.description: Both participants are given money and each decides at the same time how much to give the other, without knowing the other's decision. Each person is a giver and a recipient.
variations.justification: Both players act as dictators simultaneously; distinct social structure

variations.name: Earned vs. Windfall Endowment
variations.description: Before the game, the participant either earns the money by doing a task (such as a quiz or typing job) or is simply handed it. People tend to give less when they earned the money themselves.
variations.justification: Endowment earned through effort vs. given randomly; changes perceived legitimacy

variations.name: Audience/Observation Effects
variations.description: The decision is made while the experimenter or another person can see it, or will learn of it, compared with a fully anonymous decision where nobody can link the giver to the amount.
variations.justification: Observer present or aware of allocation; changes social context

variations.name: N-Person Dictator
variations.description: The participant divides the money among several recipients rather than one, and may give different amounts to different people.
variations.justification: Multiple recipients; changes social structure and distribution decision

variations.name: Charitable Giving Dictator
variations.description: The recipient is a named charity instead of an anonymous person. The participant decides how much of the money to donate.
variations.justification: Recipient is charity; different social/moral framing

variations.name: Exit Option
variations.description: Before dividing the money, the participant may choose not to play at all and keep a slightly smaller amount, so that the recipient never learns a game existed. Taking the exit shows that giving in the standard game is partly driven by not wanting to be seen as unfair.
variations.justification: Option to leave game rather than allocate; adds outside option to choice set

families.rationale: Unilateral allocation to a passive receiver

short_definition: Auditory or visual digit sequences reproduced in forward or backward order; longest correctly reproduced length indexes verbal short-term and working memory span.
description: The Digit Span task measures verbal short-term and working memory capacity. In the Forward condition, participants listen to sequences of digits presented at a rate of one per second and immediately repeat them in the same order; sequence length increases until recall fails. In the Backward condition, participants repeat digits in reverse order, adding a manipulation component. The Sequencing condition (from WAIS-IV) requires reordering digits numerically. Digit Span is one of the oldest and most widely administered neuropsychological measures, embedded in the Wechsler intelligence and memory scales. Forward span primarily indexes the phonological loop, while backward span engages central executive processes.

procedure: Sequences of digits are presented at a rate of one per second.
Participants reproduce the sequence in forward, backward, or sequencing order.
Length increases until two consecutive failures.
measurements: Forward-backward difference as index of executive load

variations.name: Forward Digit Span
variations.description: The experimenter reads a list of digits aloud at one per second, and the participant repeats them in the same order. Lists get longer until the participant fails, and the longest list repeated correctly is the span.
variations.justification: Reproduce digits in order; canonical phonological span measure

variations.name: Backward Digit Span
variations.description: The participant repeats the digits in reverse order, last digit first. The list must be held and reversed before it can be spoken.
variations.justification: Reproduce in reverse; requires mental transformation

variations.name: Digit Span Sequencing (WAIS-IV)
variations.description: The participant repeats the digits sorted from smallest to largest, regardless of the order heard. Part of the Wechsler intelligence scales.
variations.justification: Reorder digits from smallest to largest; different transformation requirement

variations.name: Letter-Number Sequencing
variations.description: The list mixes letters and digits (for example 7-B-3-K). The participant must say the digits first in ascending order, then the letters in alphabetical order.
variations.justification: Alternating letters and numbers reordered separately; dual sequencing demand

variations.name: Auditory vs. Visual Presentation
variations.description: The digits are shown one at a time on a screen instead of being spoken. The participant then says or types them back. Compares memory for seen and heard sequences.
variations.justification: Visual digit presentation vs. auditory; different input modality

variations.name: Adaptive Staircase Versions
variations.description: A computer sets the next list length from the participant's recent accuracy, making lists longer after correct responses and shorter after errors, and estimates the span from where performance settles.
variations.justification: Adaptive difficulty tracking; different trial-generation procedure

variations.name: Spatial Digit Span
variations.description: Each digit appears at a different position on the screen, and the participant must reproduce the digits in order, sometimes also indicating where each appeared.
variations.justification: Digits at spatial locations; adds spatial component

variations.name: Running Digit Span
variations.description: Digits are read in lists of unpredictable length, and when the list stops the participant must report the last few digits (for example the last four). Because the end cannot be anticipated, the participant has to keep updating which digits to hold.
variations.justification: Recall last N digits of unknown-length list; different task structure

variations.name: Grouped/Chunked Presentation
variations.description: The digits are read with pauses that group them into clusters of two or three (like a phone number) instead of at an even pace. Grouping usually helps recall.
variations.justification: Digits presented in groups; tests chunking facilitation

variations.name: Matrix Span
variations.description: Instead of digits, a sequence of cells lights up in a grid, and the participant indicates the cells in the order shown. A spatial counterpart of digit span.
variations.justification: Spatial matrix locations instead of digits; different stimulus type

variations.name: Supra-Span Lists
variations.description: A list longer than the participant's span is repeated until it can be recalled perfectly. The number of repetitions needed measures how fast a long sequence is learned.
variations.justification: Lists exceed span; tests learning over trials

families.rationale: Reproduce a digit sequence

short_definition: Timed paper-and-pencil or computerized task: substitute digits for symbols (or vice versa) using a visible key; items completed in a fixed interval index processing speed.
description: The Digit Symbol Substitution Test (also known as Symbol Digit Modalities Test, SDMT, in its symbol-to-digit variant) is one of the most sensitive neuropsychological measures of processing speed and cognitive efficiency. Participants view a key pairing digits 1-9 with unique abstract symbols. They then fill in the corresponding symbol for each digit in a series (DSST) or write the digit for each symbol (SDMT), working as quickly and accurately as possible for 90-120 seconds. The number of correct substitutions is the primary score. The DSST/SDMT is included in the WAIS and is among the most sensitive tests for detecting cognitive impairment from neurological conditions, medication side effects, and normal aging.

procedure: A key pairs digits 1-9 with unique symbols.
Participants fill in the correct symbol below each digit in a long sequence, working as quickly as possible for 90-120 seconds.
measurements: Number of correct substitutions in the time limit

variations.name: DSST (Digit-to-Symbol; WAIS)
variations.description: A key at the top of the page pairs each digit 1 to 9 with a simple symbol. Below are rows of digits with empty boxes, and the participant writes the matching symbol under each digit as fast as possible for 90 or 120 seconds. The score is the number completed.
variations.justification: Canonical DSST: given digit, write corresponding symbol; pencil-and-paper version

variations.name: SDMT (Symbol-to-Digit; Smith)
variations.description: The direction is reversed: the rows show symbols, and the participant writes the digit that goes with each one, again using a key at the top of the page.
variations.justification: Given symbol, write digit; reverse lookup direction

variations.name: Oral SDMT
variations.description: The participant says each digit aloud instead of writing it, while the examiner records the answers. Used when writing is slow or impossible, for example with motor impairment.
variations.justification: Verbal response instead of written; different output modality

variations.name: Computerized DSST/SDMT
variations.description: Items appear one at a time on a screen and the participant presses a key or taps a symbol for each. The computer records the time taken on every item rather than just the total completed.
variations.justification: Button pressing vs. handwriting; per section 5.6, changes fine motor skill

variations.name: Paired-Associate Variant
variations.description: After the timed substitution, the key is removed and the participant is asked which symbol went with each digit. This adds an unannounced memory test for the pairings practiced during the task.
variations.justification: Symbol-digit pairs studied as paired associates; different explicit learning structure

families.rationale: Speeded symbol coding; processing speed rather than motor control is the usual reading

short_definition: Study-phase cues instruct participants to remember or forget specific items or lists; later memory tests index intentional forgetting.
description: Participants study items (typically words) under instructions that each item should either be remembered or forgotten. In the item method, a remember or forget cue follows each individual item. In the list method, a single cue midway through the study phase instructs participants to forget everything studied so far. On a subsequent memory test, recall and recognition of forget-cued items is impaired relative to remember-cued items. The paradigm provides the primary laboratory tool for studying intentional forgetting and memory control, with theoretical implications for understanding inhibitory control over memory, context change, and selective rehearsal.

procedure: Items are presented one at a time or in lists.
After each item (item method) or after a full list (list method), a cue instructs the participant to remember or forget it.
A final test probes all items.
measurements: Recall/recognition accuracy for remember-cued vs. forget-cued items

variations.name: Item-Method Directed Forgetting
variations.description: Words are shown one at a time, and each is followed by an instruction to remember it or to forget it. A later memory test, which asks for all words including the to-be-forgotten ones, shows worse memory for the forget-cued words.
variations.justification: Forget cue follows each item; individual item suppression

variations.name: List-Method Directed Forgetting
variations.description: A whole list of words is studied, and only then is the participant told either to forget that list (it was practice) or to keep remembering it. A second list is then studied. The final test covers both lists.
variations.justification: Forget cue follows entire first list; list-level suppression

variations.name: Recognition vs. Recall Test
variations.description: The final memory test is a recognition test, in which studied words are mixed with new ones and the participant picks out the old ones, rather than free recall. The forgetting effect is usually weaker with recognition.
variations.justification: Different retrieval test changes what type of access is measured

variations.name: Directed Forgetting with Source Memory
variations.description: At test the participant must also say which cue each remembered word received, or which list it came from, rather than just whether it was studied.
variations.justification: Retrieval includes source judgment; adds contextual memory component

variations.name: Emotional Directed Forgetting
variations.description: The studied items include emotional words or pictures as well as neutral ones. Tests whether emotional material can be forgotten on instruction as easily as neutral material.
variations.justification: Emotional to-be-forgotten material; retained per section 5.1 (EMOT retired)

variations.name: Directed Forgetting of Actions (SPT)
variations.description: The items are short action phrases such as 'fold the paper' that the participant physically performs during study, after which each is cued to be remembered or forgotten.
variations.justification: Subject-performed tasks as to-be-forgotten items; different encoding modality

variations.name: Cumulative Directed Forgetting
variations.description: Several lists are studied in a row, each followed by a forget or remember instruction, so that forgetting instructions accumulate across the session before the final test.
variations.justification: Multiple forget cues accumulate across list; different suppression structure

families.rationale: Remember or forget cues at study

short_definition: A pair of cues (often threat/neutral) is followed by a probe at one cue location; RT difference by cue type indexes attentional bias.
description: The Dot-Probe Task measures attentional bias toward or away from emotionally salient stimuli. On each trial, a pair of stimuli (e.g., one threatening face and one neutral face) appears briefly (typically 500 ms), followed by a probe (dot or arrow) at the location of one stimulus. Participants respond to the probe (detect or classify it). Attentional bias is inferred from faster responses to probes replacing the emotional stimulus (vigilance toward threat) versus slower responses (avoidance). The task is a cornerstone of research on anxiety-related attentional biases and has been central to Attentional Bias Modification (ABM) treatments.

procedure: Two stimuli (e.g., a threatening face and a neutral face) appear briefly on screen.
One is replaced by a probe (dot or letter) that participants locate or classify.
manipulations: Probe location (congruent with threat vs. incongruent)
measurements: RT difference between congruent and incongruent probe trials (attentional bias score)

variations.name: Standard Face Dot-Probe
variations.description: Two faces appear side by side for about half a second, one emotional (usually threatening) and one neutral. They disappear and a small probe (a dot or arrow) appears where one of them was. The participant indicates the probe's location or identity as fast as possible. Faster responses to probes behind emotional faces indicate attention was drawn there.
variations.justification: Canonical: face pair followed by probe; measures attentional bias to faces

variations.name: Word Dot-Probe
variations.description: The pair consists of a threat-related word and a neutral word, one above the other or side by side, followed by the probe at one of the word locations.
variations.justification: Word stimuli instead of faces; different stimulus type

variations.name: Pictorial Dot-Probe
variations.description: The pair consists of emotional and neutral photographs of scenes or objects, such as pictures from the International Affective Picture System, rather than faces or words.
variations.justification: Scene/object pictures; different stimulus class

variations.name: Detection vs. Classification Probe
variations.description: In the detection version the participant presses a single key as soon as the probe appears. In the classification version the probe has two possible forms (for example one or two dots, or an arrow pointing up or down) and the participant reports which it was.
variations.justification: Probe identity discrimination vs. simple detection; different response task

variations.name: Subliminal/Masked Dot-Probe
variations.description: The face or word pair is shown for only about 15 to 20 ms and immediately covered by a mask, so the participant cannot consciously see which side the emotional item was on, before the probe appears.
variations.justification: Primes below threshold; changes conscious awareness of cue

variations.name: Positive Dot-Probe
variations.description: The emotional item in each pair is positive, such as a happy face or a pleasant picture, paired with a neutral item, to measure attention toward pleasant rather than threatening content.
variations.justification: Positive stimuli as cues; different emotional valence of attention capture stimuli

families.rationale: Probe appears at one of two cue locations
