short_definition: View affective images under instructions to reappraise or passively view; self-reported affect, physiological responses, and neural activity index emotion regulation ability.
description: Participants view emotionally evocative stimuli (typically IAPS images) and are instructed to either passively view them ("look" condition) or regulate their emotional response using cognitive reappraisal (e.g., reinterpreting a car accident as a movie scene). After each trial, participants rate their emotional experience. Reappraisal successfully reduces subjective negative affect and modulates neural activity: it increases dorsolateral and ventrolateral PFC activation while decreasing amygdala activation, demonstrating top-down prefrontal regulation of emotion generation systems.

procedure: Participants view emotionally evocative images and are instructed to regulate their emotional response using a specified strategy (e.g., cognitive reappraisal, suppression, or distraction) or to simply attend.

variations.name: Reinterpretation/Reappraisal
variations.description: Before an unpleasant picture, the participant is instructed to change what the picture means to them, for example by imagining that the injured person will recover or that the scene is staged. On other trials they simply watch. Ratings or physiological responses on reappraise trials are compared with watch trials.
variations.justification: Participant cognitively reframes stimulus meaning; changes cognitive strategy instructions

variations.name: Distancing/Detachment
variations.description: The participant is instructed to view the picture as a detached observer, for example as a scientist or from far away, without changing what the picture shows. The feeling is reduced by stepping back from it rather than by reinterpreting it.
variations.justification: Third-person perspective taking; distinct cognitive strategy

variations.name: Distraction/Attentional Deployment
variations.description: While the emotional picture is on screen, the participant is given something else to attend to, such as a mental arithmetic problem or a letter-memory task, so that attention is pulled away from the emotional content.
variations.justification: Attention redirected away from stimulus; different regulatory mechanism

variations.name: Expressive Suppression
variations.description: The participant is instructed to keep their face and body completely still so that an observer could not tell what they are feeling, while watching the emotional picture or film clip. The feeling itself is not targeted, only its outward expression.
variations.justification: Inhibit visible emotional response; behavioral output regulation

variations.name: Acceptance/Mindful Awareness
variations.description: The participant is instructed to notice whatever feelings the picture produces and let them be, without trying to change, avoid or judge them.
variations.justification: Non-judgmental observation; different regulatory stance

variations.name: Situation Selection/Modification
variations.description: Rather than regulating a response to a picture already on screen, the participant chooses which of several pictures or situations to be exposed to, or can act to change the situation, for example by ending a clip early. Regulation happens through the choice.
variations.justification: Choice between stimuli or contexts; different task structure with decision component

variations.name: Up-Regulation
variations.description: The participant is instructed to make the feeling stronger, for example by imagining the pictured event happening to a loved one or by immersing themselves in the scene, instead of weaker.
variations.justification: Amplify rather than down-regulate emotional response; opposite regulatory direction

variations.name: Regulation of Positive vs. Negative Emotions
variations.description: The pictures are pleasant rather than unpleasant, and the participant is instructed to increase (savor) or decrease (dampen) the positive feeling. Tests whether regulating pleasant emotion works like regulating unpleasant emotion.
variations.justification: Valence manipulation changes emotional context of regulation

variations.name: Implicit Emotion Regulation
variations.description: No regulation instruction is given. Regulation is measured indirectly, for example from how responses to emotional pictures change after a task that primes the idea of self-control, or from spontaneous recovery after an emotional event.
variations.justification: No explicit instruction to regulate; tests implicit regulatory processes

families.rationale: Reappraise or passively view affective images

short_definition: Color-naming of emotionally valenced words; RT slowing on threat-related words indexes attentional bias to affective content.
description: A variant of the classic Stroop in which participants name the ink color of words that vary in emotional valence (threat-related, positive, neutral). Emotional interference is measured as the slowing of color naming for emotional relative to neutral words, indexing the degree to which emotional content captures attentional resources. The task is widely used in anxiety and PTSD research, where threat-related words produce disproportionate interference. The emotional interference effect reflects automatic processing of affectively significant information.

procedure: Color words are replaced by emotionally valenced or threat-related words.
Participants name the ink color while ignoring word meaning.
manipulations: Word valence/threat relevance (disorder-specific, general threat, neutral)
measurements: RT slowing for threat/emotional words relative to neutral (emotional Stroop interference)

variations.name: Threat-Related Emotional Stroop
variations.description: Words printed in different ink colors are shown one at a time, and the participant names the ink color while ignoring the word. Some words are threatening (such as death, attack, failure) and others neutral. Slower color naming for threat words indicates the word's meaning captured attention.
variations.justification: Threat words produce interference; canonical emotional Stroop design

variations.name: Disorder-Specific Variants
variations.description: The emotional words are chosen to match a particular clinical concern, for example trauma words for post-traumatic stress disorder, body and food words for eating disorders, or alcohol words for drinking problems. The participant still names ink colors.
variations.justification: Stimulus set tailored to specific disorder (e.g., spider phobia words); different content domain

variations.name: Positive vs. Negative Emotional Stroop
variations.description: Pleasant words are included alongside unpleasant and neutral words, so that slowing can be compared for positive and negative content.
variations.justification: Positive stimuli alongside negative; tests valence symmetry of interference

variations.name: Pictorial Emotional Stroop
variations.description: Emotional and neutral pictures are shown with a colored border, tint or overlay, and the participant names the color while ignoring the picture.
variations.justification: Emotional pictures instead of words; different stimulus modality

variations.name: Subliminal Emotional Stroop
variations.description: Each emotional or neutral word is flashed very briefly and then covered by a colored mask or letter string, and the participant names the color of the mask. The participant cannot consciously read the word.
variations.justification: Masked words below awareness; changes conscious access to emotional stimuli

variations.name: Face-Word Emotional Stroop
variations.description: A face with an emotional expression is shown with an emotion word (such as HAPPY or ANGRY) written across it. The participant names the face's expression while ignoring the word, or reads the word while ignoring the face, and conflict between the two slows responses.
variations.justification: Emotional faces paired with color words; cross-domain emotional conflict

families.rationale: Stroop procedure with emotional words

short_definition: A central target flanked by congruent or incongruent distractors; RT and error differences index selective attention and conflict resolution.
description: The Eriksen Flanker Task measures selective attention and the ability to inhibit responses to irrelevant flanking stimuli. Participants view a brief display of five items arranged horizontally, with a central target flanked by two non-target items on each side. The central target requires a specific response, while flanking items may be congruent (same response), incongruent (opposite response), or neutral. Participants respond via speeded button press while ignoring flankers. The flanker compatibility effect (slowed RT and increased errors on incongruent trials) indexes the degree of response competition and the efficiency of attentional filtering.

procedure: Participants identify a central target (arrow or letter) flanked by congruent, incongruent, or neutral distractors.

variations.name: Arrow Flanker (Standard)
variations.description: Five arrows appear in a row. The participant presses a left or right key for the direction of the middle arrow. The outer arrows point the same way (congruent) or the opposite way (incongruent), and responses are slower and less accurate when they conflict.
variations.justification: Canonical flanker: central arrow surrounded by congruent/incongruent arrows

variations.name: Letter Flanker
variations.description: The row consists of letters, and the participant presses one key for a central H and another for a central S (for example). The flanking letters belong to the same response as the center or to the other one. This is the original 1974 form of the task.
variations.justification: Letter stimuli instead of arrows; different S-R mapping and stimulus class

variations.name: Color Flanker
variations.description: The participant responds to the color of a central patch or item while the flanking items are the same or a different color linked to the other response.
variations.justification: Color response with flanking distractors; different response dimension

variations.name: Emotional Flanker
variations.description: The central item and the flankers are faces or pictures with emotional expressions. The participant classifies the central item's emotion while the flanking items show the same or a different emotion.
variations.justification: Emotional face flankers; retained per section 5.1 (EMOT retired)

variations.name: Numerical Flanker
variations.description: The items are digits, and the participant judges the central digit, for example whether it is larger or smaller than 5, while flanking digits fall on the same or the other side of 5.
variations.justification: Number stimuli with magnitude response; different S-R domain

variations.name: Proportion-Congruent Flanker
variations.description: The share of conflicting trials is changed between blocks, for example 80 percent congruent in one block and 20 percent in another. Conflict effects shrink when conflict is common, because the participant learns to focus more narrowly.
variations.justification: Varies ratio of congruent to incongruent trials; changes conflict adaptation context per section 5.2

variations.name: Combined Flanker + Go/No-Go
variations.description: On most trials the participant responds to the central item as usual, but on some trials a feature of the display (for example a particular color) signals that no response should be made. The task measures withholding a response under flanker conflict.
variations.justification: Integrated flanker-GNG design; targets response inhibition under conflict

families.rationale: Target with congruent or incongruent flankers

short_definition: Blocked or event-related presentation of faces vs. objects (or scrambled faces) to localize face-selective cortical regions (FFA, OFA, pSTS).
description: The FFA Localizer presents alternating blocks of faces and non-face objects (houses, cars, scrambled images) while participants perform passive viewing or a simple task (one-back matching, gender judgment). The contrast of faces > objects identifies face-selective regions, particularly the fusiform face area (FFA) in ventral temporal cortex. The task provides an individually-defined localizer for face-selective cortex and has been fundamental to understanding the neural basis of face perception and the question of domain-specific processing modules.

procedure: Blocks of faces alternate with blocks of non-face objects (houses, scrambled images) while participants perform a simple repetition-detection task.
The contrast localizes face-selective cortex.
manipulations: Stimulus category (faces vs. objects vs. scrambled vs. scenes)
measurements: fMRI contrast (faces > objects) identifying FFA, OFA, STS
Extent and magnitude of face-selective activation

variations.name: Faces vs. Objects Block Design
variations.description: Pictures of faces and pictures of everyday objects are shown in alternating blocks of about 15 to 20 seconds each while brain activity is recorded. The participant usually just watches, or presses a key when a picture repeats to stay alert. Comparing face blocks with object blocks locates face-selective brain areas.
variations.justification: Localizer with objects as contrast; category-selective activation paradigm

variations.name: Faces vs. Scrambled Faces
variations.description: The comparison pictures are the same face images cut into pieces and rearranged so they no longer look like faces. This keeps the colors and contrast identical, so any difference is due to seeing a face rather than to low-level image properties.
variations.justification: Scrambled faces as control; tests configural vs. feature processing

variations.name: Faces vs. Houses
variations.description: The comparison blocks show pictures of houses or buildings, another category with its own specialized brain response, giving a clean contrast for locating face areas.
variations.justification: Houses as non-face object category; standard FFA localizer contrast

variations.name: Dynamic Face Localizer
variations.description: Short video clips of moving faces (talking, changing expression) are used instead of still photographs, with moving objects as the comparison. Video gives stronger and more reliable responses in face areas.
variations.justification: Moving/dynamic faces; different temporal and motion processing demands

variations.name: Upright vs. Inverted Faces
variations.description: Faces are shown upright in some blocks and upside down in others. Inverted faces are harder to process as a whole, and the difference between the two isolates whole-face processing.
variations.justification: Face inversion disrupts configural processing; different perceptual experience

variations.name: Identity Adaptation
variations.description: Faces are shown in pairs or short runs. Sometimes the same person's face repeats, sometimes a different person follows. The brain response is weaker to a repeated identity, so the drop measures sensitivity to who the face belongs to.
variations.justification: Adaptation paradigm with identity pairs; different temporal structure

variations.name: Face Parts (Eyes, Mouth)
variations.description: Only parts of faces are shown, such as the eyes alone or the mouth alone, in separate blocks from whole faces, to see whether face areas respond to features or need the whole face.
variations.justification: Isolated face regions; participant views different spatial configuration

variations.name: Familiar vs. Unfamiliar Faces
variations.description: Some faces are of people the participant knows personally or famous people, and others are strangers. The participant views them (or judges familiarity), and responses to known and unknown faces are compared.
variations.justification: Familiarity manipulation changes recognition demand

families.rationale: Passive presentation of faces versus objects to isolate a perceptual response

short_definition: Identification of an emotion category from a face image; accuracy and RT per emotion index emotion decoding ability.
description: Participants view photographs of facial expressions (typically from the Ekman and Friesen Pictures of Facial Affect or similar validated sets) and identify the emotion portrayed. The standard set includes six basic emotions (anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise) plus neutral. Accuracy and RT are measured across emotion categories. The task engages a network including the amygdala (particularly for fear), fusiform face area, superior temporal sulcus, and prefrontal cortex. It is widely used in clinical research on schizophrenia, autism, and mood disorders.

procedure: Participants view face photographs displaying basic emotions and identify the expressed emotion from a fixed set (happy, sad, angry, fearful, disgusted, surprised, neutral).

variations.name: Static Ekman Faces (6 basic emotions)
variations.description: Photographs of posed facial expressions are shown one at a time, and the participant chooses which of six labels fits: anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness or surprise (sometimes also neutral). Accuracy and response time are recorded for each emotion.
variations.justification: Canonical categorical recognition with posed expressions

variations.name: Morphed Intensity
variations.description: Each expression is blended with a neutral face to produce a range of intensities, from faint to full. The participant labels each face, and the intensity at which the emotion is first recognized is the measure.
variations.justification: Continuous emotion intensity gradient; participant categorizes or rates on morph scale

variations.name: Dynamic Expressions
variations.description: Short video clips show a face moving from neutral to a full expression, rather than a still photograph. The participant names the emotion, often as soon as it can be identified.
variations.justification: Temporally unfolding expressions; different stimulus type with motion information

variations.name: Microexpression Detection
variations.description: A neutral face is shown, an expression is flashed for only 40 to 200 ms, and the neutral face returns. The participant names the brief expression. Tests recognition of expressions too fast to study.
variations.justification: Very brief (~40 ms) expressions; different detection difficulty and timing

variations.name: Emotion-in-Context
variations.description: The face is shown together with a body posture or a background scene that fits or contradicts the expression. The participant labels the face's emotion, and the context's influence on the label is measured.
variations.justification: Body or scene context accompanies face; changes integration demands

variations.name: Expression Matching
variations.description: Instead of naming an emotion, the participant decides whether two faces show the same expression, or picks the face that matches a target expression from a set.
variations.justification: Match-to-sample format; different response structure from labeling

variations.name: Compound Expressions
variations.description: The faces show two emotions at once, such as happily surprised or angrily disgusted, and the participant must identify the blend or its components.
variations.justification: Blended or simultaneous multi-emotion displays; different stimulus category

variations.name: Dimensional Ratings
variations.description: Rather than picking a category, the participant rates each face on scales such as how pleasant it looks and how aroused or intense it is.
variations.justification: Continuous valence/arousal ratings instead of categorical labels; different response type and scale

families.rationale: Identify the emotion category of a face

short_definition: Wimmer & Perner-style narrative in which a protagonist holds a belief the participant knows to be false; correct prediction of the protagonist's action indexes mentalizing.
description: The False Belief Task assesses the ability to attribute mental states to others that differ from reality. In the classic Sally-Anne version, Sally places an object in location A and leaves; Anne moves the object to location B. Participants are asked where Sally will look for the object. Correct performance (location A) requires representing Sally's false belief rather than the true state of the world. Adult neuroimaging versions use animated vignettes requiring belief reasoning. fMRI consistently activates medial prefrontal cortex, precuneus, and right temporoparietal junction.

procedure: Participants hear or read vignettes in which a character holds a belief that conflicts with reality (e.g., Sally-Anne scenario), then predict the character's behavior.
manipulations: True belief vs. false belief conditions
measurements: Accuracy on false-belief vs. true-belief questions

variations.name: Sally-Anne / Change-of-Location
variations.description: A story, usually acted with dolls or pictures: Sally puts a marble in her basket and leaves. Anne moves it to a box. Sally returns, and the child is asked where Sally will look for the marble. The correct answer is the basket, because Sally does not know it was moved.
variations.justification: Classic change-of-location false belief; canonical ToM paradigm

variations.name: Unexpected Contents (Smarties/Crayon Box)
variations.description: The child is shown a familiar candy box and asked what is inside, then shown it actually contains pencils. The child is asked what a friend who has not looked inside will think it contains, and sometimes what they themselves first thought.
variations.justification: Container with unexpected content; different scenario structure

variations.name: Second-Order False Belief
variations.description: The story involves one character's belief about another character's belief, for example 'Where does John think Mary will look for the ice-cream van?'. The participant must track a belief about a belief.
variations.justification: Belief about another's belief; higher-order recursive ToM

variations.name: Diverse Beliefs Task
variations.description: A simpler task from the same series: two characters believe different things about the same object (for example where a cat is hiding), neither known to be true, and the child predicts how a character will act on their own belief.
variations.justification: Two agents with different beliefs about same object; tests belief diversity understanding

variations.name: Implicit False Belief (Looking Time)
variations.description: For infants who cannot answer questions. The infant watches a scene in which an actor searches either where they should believe an object is or where it really is, and looking time is recorded. Longer looking at the action inconsistent with the actor's belief indicates surprise.
variations.justification: Looking time measure of anticipation; no verbal response required

variations.name: Anticipatory Looking
variations.description: An eye tracker records where the participant looks just before a character acts. Looking toward the place where the character wrongly believes the object to be shows that the participant has predicted the character's belief, without any verbal answer.
variations.justification: Eye-tracking where agent will look; different response modality

variations.name: Animated Triangles (Heider-Simmel)
variations.description: Short animations of simple geometric shapes moving in ways that suggest intentions, such as one shape coaxing or chasing another. The participant describes what happened, and the description is scored for how much it attributes mental states to the shapes.
variations.justification: Geometric shapes with attributed mental states; different stimulus and attribution task

variations.name: Cartoon/Story Vignette Tasks
variations.description: False-belief situations are presented as written or spoken stories or cartoon strips rather than acted out with props, and the participant answers questions about what a character thinks or will do.
variations.justification: Story-based false belief; different presentation format

variations.name: Belief-Desire Reasoning
variations.description: The character has both a false belief and a particular desire, for example wanting to avoid something they wrongly think is in a certain place. The participant must combine what the character wants with what the character believes to predict the action.
variations.justification: Combines belief and desire attribution; more complex ToM reasoning

variations.name: Adult False Belief with Reaction Time
variations.description: Adults read or watch many short false-belief scenarios and answer quickly by key press. Because adults are at ceiling on accuracy, response time is the measure, often compared with matched scenarios that need no belief reasoning.
variations.justification: RT version for adults; measures implicit processing speed alongside accuracy

variations.name: Competitive False Belief (Deception)
variations.description: The participant plays against another person and can win by creating a false belief in them, for example by pointing to the wrong hiding place. Success requires using the other person's belief rather than just reporting it.
variations.justification: Strategic deception context; tests belief reasoning under competitive motivation

families.rationale: Predict behavior from a protagonist's false belief

short_definition: Repetitive single-finger or sequence tapping at fastest or paced rates; taps-per-interval and tap-timing variability index motor speed and rhythm control.
description: Participants tap their fingers (typically index finger) in a repetitive manner at a self-paced or externally paced rate. Self-paced tapping is typically at 2-3 Hz; externally paced versions use an auditory or visual metronome. The task consists of tapping blocks (20-40 seconds) alternating with rest periods. Performance metrics include tapping frequency, inter-tap interval variability, and accuracy. It is the most commonly used simple motor paradigm for motor cortex mapping, clinical motor assessment, and studying motor control. Contralateral primary motor cortex and supplementary motor area are consistently activated.

procedure: Participants tap a key or button with a single finger as rapidly as possible (maximum rate) or in synchrony with a metronome (paced tapping).
measurements: Synchronization error and drift in paced conditions

variations.name: Self-Paced Tapping
variations.description: The participant taps a key or pad repeatedly with one finger at a steady rate of their own choosing, with no external timing signal. The chosen tempo and its regularity are measured.
variations.justification: Participant taps at preferred rate; measures preferred motor tempo

variations.name: Auditorily-Paced Tapping
variations.description: A metronome click is played at a fixed rate, and the participant taps in time with it. The offset between each tap and the click, and the variability of that offset, are measured.
variations.justification: Synchronize to auditory metronome; different sensorimotor integration

variations.name: Visually-Paced Tapping
variations.description: The pacing signal is a flashing shape on a screen rather than a sound, and the participant taps in time with the flashes.
variations.justification: Synchronize to visual metronome; different sensory modality for pacing

variations.name: Unimanual vs. Bimanual
variations.description: Tapping with both hands at once, either in unison or alternating, is compared with tapping with one hand. Coordinating the two hands adds its own difficulty.
variations.justification: One vs. two hands; bimanual coordination introduces interlimb constraints

variations.name: Sequential Multi-Finger
variations.description: Rather than one finger repeating, the participant taps a fixed order of fingers (for example index, middle, ring, little) over and over, as fast or as regularly as possible.
variations.justification: Specific finger sequence rather than single finger; different motor programming

variations.name: Complex Rhythmic Patterns
variations.description: The participant reproduces a rhythm with uneven gaps between taps, such as long-short-short, rather than tapping at an even beat.
variations.justification: Non-isochronous rhythm; changes temporal structure of tapping

variations.name: Continuation Paradigm
variations.description: The participant first taps along with a metronome, then the metronome stops and they must keep tapping at the same rate without it. Drift and variability after the metronome stops show how well the rate is kept internally.
variations.justification: External pacing withdrawn mid-task; isolates internal vs. externally guided timing

families.rationale: Tapping rate and timing

short_definition: Study of a list of items followed by unaided recall in any order; serial-position curves dissociate primacy and recency.
description: Participants study a list of items (typically words) presented sequentially, then attempt to recall all items in any order during an extended recall period. Performance is analyzed via serial position curves showing primacy effects (enhanced recall of early items, attributed to long-term memory consolidation) and recency effects (enhanced recall of recent items, attributed to short-term memory). Clustering analyses examine whether semantically or contextually related items are recalled together, revealing the organization of memory search. The task engages prefrontal, parietal, and temporal memory networks.

procedure: Participants study a list of items (words, pictures) presented one at a time, then recall as many as possible in any order after the last item.

variations.name: Immediate Free Recall (IFR)
variations.description: A list of words is presented one at a time, and as soon as it ends the participant writes or says as many as they can in any order. The first and last few words are recalled best.
variations.justification: Recall tested immediately after list; canonical free recall

variations.name: Delayed Free Recall (DFR)
variations.description: After the list ends, the participant does an unrelated task such as mental arithmetic for 15 to 30 seconds before recalling. The delay removes the advantage for the last few words.
variations.justification: Filled delay before recall; tests long-term retention

variations.name: Continual Distractor Free Recall (CDFR)
variations.description: A short arithmetic task is inserted after every word in the list as well as after the last one. The last words regain their recall advantage despite the delay, which shows that the advantage is not simply due to a short-term store.
variations.justification: Distractors between each item and at end; eliminates recency via distractor

variations.name: Final Free Recall
variations.description: At the end of a session with many lists, the participant is unexpectedly asked to recall every word from every list. Measures long-term retention and how words from different lists are organized in memory.
variations.justification: Recall all lists at end of session; tests long-term retention and inter-list organization

variations.name: Categorized Free Recall
variations.description: The list is built from several categories (such as animals, tools and fruits) presented in mixed order. Participants tend to recall items from the same category together, which measures how memory is organized.
variations.justification: Semantically categorized lists; tests organizational clustering

variations.name: Repeated Free Recall
variations.description: The same list is recalled several times in a row without being studied again. Recall usually improves across attempts, and items recalled on one attempt but not another can be tracked.
variations.justification: Same list recalled multiple times; tests learning across trials

variations.name: Directed Forgetting in Free Recall
variations.description: Partway through, or after a list, the participant is told to forget some of the words. The final recall test asks for all of them, and recall of the forget-cued words is compared with the others.
variations.justification: Forget instructions after list learning; suppression measured in free recall

variations.name: Externalized Free Recall
variations.description: The participant is asked to say every word that comes to mind during recall, including ones they think may be wrong, and to flag the ones they reject. This reveals words that were retrieved but would normally be withheld.
variations.justification: Participants report all retrievals including partial/uncertain; different response protocol

families.rationale: Study a list, recall in any order

short_definition: Responses required to frequent "go" stimuli must be withheld on rare "no-go" stimuli; commission errors and N2/P3 ERPs index response inhibition.
description: The Go/No-Go Task measures response inhibition by requiring participants to respond quickly to frequent "go" stimuli while withholding responses to infrequent "no-go" stimuli. The typical ratio is 70-80% go and 20-30% no-go trials, creating a strong prepotent tendency to respond. Performance is measured by go-trial RT (engagement), go-trial accuracy (compliance), and no-go accuracy / false alarm rate (inhibitory control). The task is simpler than the Stop-Signal task as it measures the ability to withhold (rather than cancel) a response.

procedure: Stimuli appear one at a time.
Participants respond (Go) to frequent targets and withhold (No-Go) responses to infrequent non-targets.
measurements: No-Go N2 and P3 ERP components

variations.name: Standard Go/No-Go
variations.description: Stimuli appear one at a time. The participant presses a key for the common type (go, about 75 to 80 percent of trials) and makes no response to the rare type (no-go). Pressing on a no-go trial is the main error measure.
variations.justification: Canonical: respond to go, withhold to no-go; measures response inhibition

variations.name: Emotional Go/No-Go
variations.description: The go and no-go stimuli are faces with different expressions or emotional words, for example respond to happy faces and withhold to fearful ones, with the assignment switched in other blocks.
variations.justification: Emotional stimuli as go/no-go signals; retained per section 5.1 (EMOT retired)

variations.name: Reward/Punishment Go/No-Go
variations.description: Each stimulus signals whether responding or withholding will be rewarded or will avoid a loss. The four combinations (go to win, no-go to win, go to avoid losing, no-go to avoid losing) reveal that people find it easier to act for reward and to hold back to avoid punishment.
variations.justification: Monetary outcomes for correct responses; motivation manipulation changes decision context

variations.name: Probabilistic Go/No-Go
variations.description: The proportion of go trials is varied between blocks, from 50 percent up to 90 percent. The more often the participant has to respond, the stronger the urge to respond becomes and the harder it is to withhold.
variations.justification: Probabilistic rather than deterministic stimulus-response rules; different learning structure

variations.name: Cued Go/No-Go
variations.description: A cue before each stimulus indicates whether a go or a no-go stimulus is likely to follow. The participant can prepare to respond or to hold back, and errors are compared for correctly and incorrectly cued trials.
variations.justification: Preparatory cue precedes imperative signal; different temporal structure

variations.name: Flanked Go/No-Go
variations.description: The go or no-go stimulus is surrounded by distractor items that match or conflict with it, combining the need to withhold responses with the need to ignore the flankers.
variations.justification: Go/no-go signal surrounded by flanking distractors; adds conflict component

variations.name: Reversal Go/No-Go
variations.description: Partway through the task, the stimuli switch roles: what was go becomes no-go and vice versa, with or without warning. The participant must unlearn the old mapping.
variations.justification: Go/no-go assignments reverse mid-task; tests reversal of inhibitory mappings

variations.name: Saccadic Go/No-Go
variations.description: The response is an eye movement to a target rather than a key press, and on no-go trials the participant must keep looking at the center. Eye position is tracked.
variations.justification: Eye movement response instead of button press; different response effector

variations.name: Multi-Stimulus Go/No-Go
variations.description: Several different stimuli are go signals and several others are no-go signals, so the participant must remember a larger set of rules rather than a single go stimulus and a single no-go stimulus.
variations.justification: Multiple stimulus categories with different go/no-go rules; more complex rule set

families.rationale: Withhold on rare no-go stimuli

short_definition: Speeded categorization of stimuli belonging to two target concepts and two evaluative attributes using shared response keys; congruence-condition RT difference indexes implicit association.
description: Participants rapidly classify stimuli from four categories using two response keys. Two categories are target concepts (e.g., "flowers" vs. "insects") and two are evaluative attributes (e.g., "pleasant" vs. "unpleasant"). In the critical comparison, one block pairs congruent categories on the same key (flowers + pleasant) and another pairs incongruent categories (flowers + unpleasant). The IAT effect - faster responding in the congruent block - is interpreted as reflecting the strength of automatic associations between the concepts and attributes. Greenwald et al. (1998) introduced the IAT as a measure of implicit attitudes, and it has become one of the most widely administered psychological tests, with applications spanning racial bias, self-esteem, clinical anxiety, consumer preferences, and political attitudes.

procedure: Participants sort stimuli from two target categories (e.g., Black/White faces) and two attribute categories (e.g., pleasant/unpleasant words) using two response keys.
Critical comparison is between compatible and incompatible pairings.
manipulations: Number of practice and test trials
measurements: IAT D-score (standardized RT difference between incompatible and compatible blocks)

variations.name: Race IAT
variations.description: Faces of Black and White people and pleasant and unpleasant words appear one at a time, and the participant sorts each with a left or right key. In one block Black faces and pleasant words share a key; in another, White faces and pleasant words share a key. Faster sorting in one pairing than the other is taken as an implicit association.
variations.justification: Canonical IAT measuring race-valence associations

variations.name: Gender-Science IAT
variations.description: The categories are male and female names or faces paired with science words and liberal arts words. The participant sorts with shared keys as in the race version, and the speed difference between pairings measures the gender-science stereotype.
variations.justification: Gender-career associations; different conceptual domain

variations.name: Self-Esteem IAT
variations.description: The categories are self words (I, me, mine) versus other words (they, them) paired with pleasant and unpleasant words, so that the speed difference measures how strongly the self is linked with positive evaluation.
variations.justification: Self-related vs. other category; different self-referential structure

variations.name: Single-Category IAT (SC-IAT)
variations.description: Only one target category is used (for example, just Black faces) along with pleasant and unpleasant words. One block pairs the category with pleasant, another with unpleasant. Gives an association for that category alone rather than relative to a contrasting category.
variations.justification: One target category instead of two; different design structure

variations.name: Brief IAT (BIAT)
variations.description: A shorter version with fewer blocks and trials in which the participant focuses on only two of the four categories in each block, pressing one key for them and the other key for everything else.
variations.justification: Shorter version with different block structure; distinct published instrument

variations.name: Go/No-Go Association Task (GNAT)
variations.description: The participant presses a key for items that belong to a target pairing (for example Black faces or pleasant words) and makes no response to everything else. Sensitivity in detecting the pairing replaces the key-sharing design.
variations.justification: Detection response instead of categorization; different response structure

variations.name: Recoding-Free IAT (IAT-RF)
variations.description: Four response keys are used, one per category, so no two categories ever share a key. The critical pairings are created by instructions about which keys are relevant on each trial, which prevents participants from simply recoding the task as one two-way sort.
variations.justification: Response keys don't change across blocks; removes recoding confound

variations.name: Personalized IAT (P-IAT)
variations.description: The attribute categories are labeled 'I like' and 'I don't like' rather than 'pleasant' and 'unpleasant', and the words are chosen to reflect personal preferences, so that the measure reflects the participant's own attitudes rather than knowledge of cultural stereotypes.
variations.justification: Self-relevant exemplars; different stimulus set and personal relevance

variations.name: Developmental / Child IAT
variations.description: A version for children in which all categories are pictures rather than words, instructions are spoken, there are fewer trials, and the sorting keys are large buttons or a touch screen.
variations.justification: Picture-based categories for children; procedure adapted per section 5.3

families.rationale: Response-key compatibility effect between paired categories

short_definition: Actions are reinforced by contingent outcomes under defined schedules; response rate and choice probability across schedules index instrumental learning. Specific human instantiations include lever/button-press reward paradigms and free-operant tasks.
description: In instrumental conditioning, voluntary actions are associated with rewarding or punishing consequences through repeated experience. Laboratory implementations present discrete choice options where specific responses are followed by desirable outcomes (food, money, points) or undesirable outcomes (loss, punishment). Common schedules include fixed-ratio, variable-ratio, fixed-interval, and variable-interval. Performance measures include response rates, choice patterns, and reaction times. The ventral striatum, dopamine system, and orbitofrontal cortex are critical for representing value predictions and learning from outcomes.

procedure: Participants perform actions (button presses, lever responses) that produce contingent outcomes (rewards or punishments) according to defined reinforcement schedules.
manipulations: Reinforcement schedule (fixed ratio, variable ratio, fixed interval, variable interval)
measurements: Sensitivity to contingency and outcome devaluation
Transfer effects between Pavlovian cues and instrumental actions

variations.name: Fixed Ratio (FR)
variations.description: A reward (points, money or food) is delivered after every fixed number of responses, for example every tenth press. The participant learns how many presses each reward costs.
variations.justification: Reward after fixed number of responses; canonical ratio schedule

variations.name: Variable Ratio (VR)
variations.description: A reward is delivered after an unpredictable number of responses that average a set value, like a slot machine. Produces high steady rates of responding.
variations.justification: Reward after variable number of responses; different reinforcement statistics

variations.name: Fixed Interval (FI)
variations.description: A reward is available only after a fixed time has passed since the last reward, and the first response after that time earns it. Responses before the interval ends do nothing.
variations.justification: First response after fixed time rewarded; different temporal reinforcement structure

variations.name: Variable Interval (VI)
variations.description: Like the fixed interval schedule, but the waiting time before a reward becomes available varies unpredictably around an average.
variations.justification: Variable time intervals; different temporal unpredictability

variations.name: Progressive Ratio
variations.description: The number of responses needed for each successive reward increases, for example 5, then 10, then 20. The point at which the participant stops responding (the breakpoint) measures how hard they are willing to work for the reward.
variations.justification: Ratio requirement escalates; measures motivational breakpoint

variations.name: Concurrent Choice
variations.description: Two or more response options are available at the same time, each paying off on its own schedule. How the participant divides responses between them is compared with the relative rates of reward.
variations.justification: Two simultaneously available schedules; choice behavior reveals preference

variations.name: Two-Stage Decision Task (Daw)
variations.description: A choice between two options leads, with set probabilities, to one of two second-stage states, where another choice yields a reward with slowly changing probability. Whether a participant's choices reflect knowledge of the transition structure separates planning from habit. Cataloged in its own right as the Two-Stage Decision Task.
variations.justification: Two-step Markov decision; measures model-based vs. model-free learning

variations.name: Devaluation Paradigm
variations.description: After learning that a response earns a particular reward, the reward is made less desirable, for example by feeding the participant that food to satiety or by telling them it is no longer worth points. A test follows without rewards. Responding that drops shows goal-directed control; responding that persists shows habit.
variations.justification: Outcome devaluation tests goal-directed vs. habitual control; different post-training procedure

variations.name: Contingency Degradation
variations.description: After learning, the reward begins to appear whether or not the participant responds, so the response no longer makes a difference. A drop in responding shows that the participant is tracking what their actions cause.
variations.justification: Action-outcome contingency degraded; tests action sensitivity

variations.name: Outcome-Specific Pavlovian-Instrumental Transfer (PIT)
variations.description: In separate phases the participant learns that certain cues predict certain rewards and that certain responses earn those same rewards. In a final test the cues are presented while the participant can respond freely, and a cue increases responding for the reward it predicts.
variations.justification: Pavlovian CS influences instrumental responding; different multi-phase design

variations.name: Avoidance Learning
variations.description: Instead of earning a reward, a response prevents an unpleasant outcome such as a shock, loud noise or loss of money. The participant learns which response, or which response to which warning signal, keeps the outcome away.
variations.justification: Response prevents aversive outcome; different valence and contingency structure

families.rationale: Actions reinforced under a schedule

short_definition: Repeated choices among four decks with hidden reward and loss distributions; preference shift toward advantageous decks indexes affective decision making.
description: Participants choose cards from four decks to maximize winnings. Two decks (A, B) have high wins but higher losses (net loss); two decks (C, D) have smaller wins but minimal losses (net gain). Over 100 trials, healthy participants gradually learn to prefer advantageous decks. The IGT is particularly sensitive to ventromedial prefrontal cortex damage; vmPFC patients fail to develop a preference for advantageous decks despite normal intellectual functioning. The task operationalizes the Somatic Marker Hypothesis.

procedure: Four decks of cards are presented.
Participants draw one card at a time from any deck.
Each draw yields a reward and sometimes a penalty.
Two decks are advantageous (smaller rewards, smaller penalties, net positive) and two are disadvantageous (larger rewards, larger penalties, net negative).

variations.name: Standard IGT
variations.description: Four decks of cards are on screen. Each card drawn wins play money and sometimes also loses some. Two decks give big wins but bigger occasional losses and are bad in the long run; two give smaller wins and smaller losses and come out ahead. The participant draws 100 cards from any decks and must discover which decks are good.
variations.justification: Canonical four-deck IGT with covert payoff structure

variations.name: Soochow Gambling Task (SGT)
variations.description: A redesign in which the decks that lose money overall deliver frequent small gains and rare large losses, while the decks that win overall deliver frequent small losses and rare large gains. Participants who follow how often they win end up choosing the bad decks, which separates sensitivity to frequency from sensitivity to amount.
variations.justification: Reversed long-run structure; tests frequency vs. magnitude sensitivity

variations.name: Child Versions
variations.description: Versions such as the Hungry Donkey Task and the Children's Gambling Task, in which a cartoon character collects apples or candies from doors or decks with the same good and bad payoff structure, with fewer trials and simpler feedback.
variations.justification: Simplified decks and stimuli for children; procedure adapted per section 5.3

variations.name: Extended IGT (150-200 trials)
variations.description: The same four decks played for 150 to 200 draws instead of 100, to see whether deck preferences continue to change once the usual task would have ended.
variations.justification: Extended trial count; tests learning at longer timescales

variations.name: IGT with Explicit Probabilities
variations.description: The participant is told the win and loss amounts and probabilities of each deck before playing instead of having to discover them by experience. Removes the learning component and tests choice with full information.
variations.justification: Payoff probabilities stated explicitly; changes information structure

variations.name: Modified Payoff Variants
variations.description: The payoff schedules are altered, for example so that all decks lose equally often, or so that the deck that was best becomes worst, to test which features of the payoffs drive deck choice.
variations.justification: Different win/loss schedules; tests sensitivity to schedule structure

families.rationale: Deck choices with hidden gain and loss distributions

short_definition: Speeded word/nonword judgment; RT and accuracy index lexical access and are sensitive to frequency, priming, and context.
description: Participants view letter strings and must rapidly determine whether each string is a valid word or a nonword by pressing designated response buttons. Stimuli include high- and low-frequency words and pronounceable nonwords. RT and accuracy to words versus nonwords indexes lexical access efficiency. The task is often combined with priming manipulations to examine semantic, phonological, or morphological processing. It is one of the most fundamental paradigms in psycholinguistics.

procedure: Letter strings are presented one at a time.
Participants classify each as a real word or a nonword as quickly and accurately as possible.

variations.name: Standard Visual LDT
variations.description: Strings of letters appear one at a time on a screen. The participant presses one key if the string is a real word (such as TABLE) and another if it is not (such as TOBLE), as quickly as possible.
variations.justification: Canonical: word/nonword judgment to visually presented strings

variations.name: Auditory LDT
variations.description: The items are spoken through headphones rather than shown, and the participant decides whether what they heard was a real word.
variations.justification: Auditory presentation; different sensory modality

variations.name: Masked Priming LDT
variations.description: Immediately before each target, a prime word is flashed for about 50 ms between masking patterns so the participant does not consciously see it. The word decision on the target is faster when the hidden prime is related to it.
variations.justification: Brief masked prime before target; changes prime awareness

variations.name: Cross-Modal LDT
variations.description: A prime is heard and the target is seen (or the reverse). The participant decides whether the visible target is a word while a spoken word or sentence is played just before or during it.
variations.justification: Prime in one modality, target in another; cross-modal priming structure

variations.name: LDT with Different Nonword Types
variations.description: The non-words are chosen to be more or less word-like: strings that sound like real words when read aloud (BRANE), strings with two letters swapped (JUGDE), or unpronounceable consonant strings (TBLK). More word-like non-words make the decision harder.
variations.justification: Pseudowords, random letter strings, pseudohomophones; nonword type changes task difficulty

variations.name: Bilingual LDT
variations.description: Words from two languages the participant speaks are mixed in the same list, sometimes with words that exist in both languages, and the participant decides whether each is a word in either language or in a specified one.
variations.justification: Targets in two languages; different language switching demand

variations.name: LDT Megastudies
variations.description: Each participant responds to thousands of words over many sessions, as in the English Lexicon Project, so that response times are available for every word rather than for small chosen sets.
variations.justification: Large-scale normed stimulus sets enabling item-level analyses; different methodological scope

variations.name: Go/No-Go LDT
variations.description: The participant presses a key only for words and makes no response to non-words (or the reverse), instead of having a separate key for each.
variations.justification: Respond to one word class, withhold to another; different response structure

families.rationale: Word versus nonword judgment

short_definition: Judgment of whether two rotated objects are identical or mirror images; RT scales linearly with angular disparity, indexing mental rotation.
description: Participants view pairs of 3D objects (block figures, letters, or geometric forms) and determine whether they are identical (one is a rotated version of the other) or mirror images. Objects are rotated at angles ranging from 0 to 180 degrees relative to each other. The well-established finding is that RT increases linearly with angular disparity, suggesting an analog mental rotation process. The task measures spatial visualization ability, mental imagery, and visuospatial working memory. Sex differences in mental rotation are among the most reliable cognitive sex differences.

procedure: Two figures (3-D block shapes, letters, or hands) are presented at different orientations.
Participants judge whether they are the same or mirror-reversed.
manipulations: Angular disparity between the two figures (0-180 degrees)
measurements: RT as a function of angular disparity (linear slope = rotation rate)

variations.name: Shepard-Metzler 3D Block Figures
variations.description: Two drawings of a three-dimensional object made of cubes are shown side by side, one rotated relative to the other. The participant decides whether they are the same object or mirror images. Response time grows with the angle of rotation.
variations.justification: Canonical 3D block figure rotation; depth and perspective rotation

variations.name: 2D Shape Rotation
variations.description: The items are flat shapes such as letters, digits or polygons, rotated in the picture plane. The participant decides whether a rotated item is normal or mirror-reversed.
variations.justification: Flat 2D figures; different stimulus complexity and dimensionality

variations.name: Body Part Rotation (Hand Laterality)
variations.description: Pictures of a hand in various orientations are shown, and the participant decides whether each is a left or right hand. People tend to solve this by imagining moving their own hand into the position.
variations.justification: Hands judged as left/right; embodied rotation via motor imagery

variations.name: Mirror vs. Identical Discrimination
variations.description: Each trial presents a rotated figure and the participant decides whether it is the standard figure or its mirror image, rather than comparing two figures shown together.
variations.justification: Distinguish mirrored from same-orientation figure; different judgment type

variations.name: Embodied/Motor-Assisted Rotation
variations.description: While judging the rotated figures, the participant turns a handle or makes a rotating gesture with the hand, in the same or the opposite direction as the mental rotation. Compatible movements speed the judgment.
variations.justification: Physical hand rotation accompanies mental rotation; different embodiment condition

variations.name: Virtual Reality Mental Rotation
variations.description: The objects are shown in stereoscopic 3D through a head-mounted display and can sometimes be walked around or handled with controllers, instead of being flat drawings on a screen.
variations.justification: Immersive VR environment; full-body spatial context changes processing

variations.name: Egocentric vs. Allocentric Rotation
variations.description: In one condition the participant imagines turning themselves to a new viewpoint and reports what they would see; in the other they imagine the object turning while they stay still. The two kinds of imagined rotation behave differently.
variations.justification: Participant perspective vs. object-centered rotation; different reference frame

families.rationale: Rotate objects mentally; could be filed under perceptual judgment

short_definition: Tracing of a figure viewed only in a mirror; error and completion time across trials index visuomotor adaptation and procedural learning.
description: The Mirror Tracing Task measures procedural motor learning and sensorimotor adaptation. Participants trace a shape (typically a star outline) while viewing their hand only through a mirror, which reverses the visual feedback left-right. This creates a conflict between visual and proprioceptive information that must be resolved through practice. Performance improves across trials as participants learn to adapt their motor commands to the reversed visual input. Measures include tracing time, number of errors (deviations from the path), and the rate of improvement across trials. The task is a classic demonstration that procedural/implicit memory is preserved in amnesia (H.M. could learn this task despite profound declarative memory loss).

procedure: Participants trace a path (star, maze) while viewing their hand only through a mirror, which reverses visual-motor mapping.
They must stay within path boundaries.

variations.name: Star Tracing (Standard)
variations.description: A six-pointed star outline is placed behind a screen so the participant can see it only in a mirror. They trace between the double lines of the star with a pencil, and the number of times the pencil leaves the track and the time to finish are recorded over repeated attempts.
variations.justification: Canonical mirror tracing of star with visuomotor reversal

variations.name: Circle/Diamond/Complex Shapes
variations.description: The figure to be traced is a circle, diamond, spiral or other shape instead of a star. Shapes with more corners and direction changes are harder to trace in the mirror.
variations.justification: Different shape complexity and curvature demands

variations.name: Computerized Mirror Tracing
variations.description: The participant moves a mouse or stylus while the cursor on screen moves in the mirror-reversed direction. No physical mirror is used, and the cursor cannot be felt bumping the edge of the track.
variations.justification: Screen/stylus instead of physical mirror/pencil; per section 5.6, loses haptic edge feedback

variations.name: Left-Right vs. Up-Down Reversal
variations.description: The mirror or software reverses only the left-right axis, only the up-down axis, or both. Each reversal is a different remapping between what the hand does and what the eye sees.
variations.justification: Different mirror axis changes visuomotor mapping

variations.name: Rotation (Non-Mirror) Variants
variations.description: Instead of a mirror reversal, the seen cursor direction is rotated by a chosen angle (such as 30 or 90 degrees) from the hand's actual direction. The size of the rotation sets the difficulty.
variations.justification: Rotation rather than mirror reversal; different visuomotor transformation

variations.name: Prism Adaptation Analog
variations.description: The participant wears goggles with prisms that shift the visual scene sideways and reaches or points at targets. Pointing errors shrink with practice and reappear in the opposite direction when the goggles are removed.
variations.justification: Prismatic displacement of visual field; different mechanism from mirror reversal

variations.name: Dual-Hand Mirror Tracing
variations.description: Both hands trace at the same time, each with mirror-reversed feedback, either on two figures or on mirror-image halves of one figure.
variations.justification: Both hands trace simultaneously with mirrored feedback; bimanual coordination variant

variations.name: Mirror Tracing with Delay
variations.description: Tracing is practiced in one session and tested again after a delay of hours or days, with no practice in between, to see how much of the adaptation is kept.
variations.justification: Delay between practice and test; tests retention of visuomotor adaptation

families.rationale: Visuomotor adaptation to mirrored feedback

short_definition: Passive auditory oddball in which rare deviant sounds elicit a negative ERP around 150-250 ms, indexing pre-attentive auditory change detection.
description: Participants are passively exposed to repetitive acoustic stimuli (standard tones, 80%) occasionally interrupted by deviant tones (20%) differing in pitch, duration, or location. The MMN can be elicited without active attention. Recorded via EEG, the MMN appears as a negative deflection peaking at 100-250 ms after deviance onset at frontocentral sites. It reflects automatic, pre-attentive comparison between incoming input and a neural representation of the standard stimulus stored in sensory (echoic) memory. MMN is used as a biomarker of auditory processing capacity and has clinical applications in schizophrenia, coma prognosis, and language development research.

procedure: A repetitive standard tone is occasionally replaced by a deviant tone differing in frequency, duration, or intensity.
Participants typically ignore the sounds while reading or watching a silent video.
measurements: MMN amplitude and latency (deviant-minus-standard difference wave, peaking 100-250 ms)

variations.name: Frequency MMN
variations.description: A repeating tone is played about once a second while the participant reads or watches a silent film. Occasionally a tone of a different pitch is inserted. The brain response to the odd tone, minus the response to the common tone, is the mismatch negativity.
variations.justification: Frequency deviant in auditory stream; canonical MMN stimulus type

variations.name: Duration MMN
variations.description: The odd tones are the same pitch as the common tone but longer or shorter in duration.
variations.justification: Duration deviant; different acoustic dimension

variations.name: Intensity MMN
variations.description: The odd tones are louder or quieter than the common tone but otherwise identical.
variations.justification: Intensity deviant; tests loudness change detection

variations.name: Location/Spatial MMN
variations.description: The odd tones come from a different direction, for example the other ear or a different loudspeaker, while pitch, loudness and duration stay the same.
variations.justification: Spatial location change; different perceptual dimension

variations.name: Complex Pattern MMN
variations.description: The regularity is a pattern rather than a single repeating tone, for example alternating high and low tones or a rising pair. The odd event breaks the pattern (two high tones in a row) even though each individual tone is familiar.
variations.justification: Pattern-level violation; higher-order regularity processing

variations.name: Multi-Feature MMN (Optimum)
variations.description: Several kinds of odd tones (pitch, duration, loudness, location, gap) are mixed into one sequence, alternating with the common tone, so that responses to all of them are collected in about 15 minutes.
variations.justification: Multiple deviants in single paradigm; different stimulus sequence

variations.name: Phoneme/Speech MMN
variations.description: The sounds are speech syllables or vowels, for example a repeating 'ba' with an occasional 'da'. The response reflects the listener's language experience as well as the acoustic difference.
variations.justification: Phonemic contrast as deviant; linguistic processing

variations.name: Visual MMN (vMMN)
variations.description: The repeating stream is visual, such as shapes, colors or faces shown at the edge of the screen while the participant does an unrelated task in the center, and the odd item differs in some visual feature.
variations.justification: Visual change detection; different sensory modality

variations.name: Roving Standard MMN
variations.description: A tone repeats several times and then changes to a new tone, which itself repeats and becomes the new standard. Every tone is the odd one when it first appears and a standard after it has repeated, so the response can be tracked as a function of how many repeats preceded the change.
variations.justification: Standard changes after each sequence; different stimulus history structure

families.rationale: Passive auditory oddball

short_definition: Incidental encoding of images followed by a test with old, new, and lure items; discrimination of lures from repetitions indexes pattern separation.
description: The Mnemonic Similarity Task measures hippocampal pattern separation - the ability to distinguish similar but not identical memory representations. During encoding, participants view a series of everyday object images. At test, they classify each image as "old" (previously seen), "similar" (a different exemplar of a studied object with slight visual changes), or "new" (novel). The critical measure is the ability to correctly identify "similar" lures as similar rather than incorrectly endorsing them as old. This discrimination (lure discrimination index) is thought to rely on dentate gyrus/CA3 pattern separation processes and is impaired in early-stage Alzheimer's disease and normal aging.

procedure: Participants study a set of images, then view old items, new items, and similar lures (items resembling studied items).
They classify each as old, new, or similar.

variations.name: Standard Object MST
variations.description: The participant sees a series of pictures of everyday objects and judges each as indoor or outdoor. In a later test they see the same objects, new objects, and objects that are similar but not identical to studied ones, and label each as old, similar or new. Calling a similar item 'similar' rather than 'old' is the measure.
variations.justification: Canonical everyday objects with lure pairs for pattern separation

variations.name: Scene MST
variations.description: The pictures are indoor and outdoor scenes rather than single objects, with similar lures being slightly different views or versions of the studied scenes.
variations.justification: Scene stimuli instead of objects; different stimulus class

variations.name: Continuous MST
variations.description: There are no separate study and test phases. Pictures appear in one long stream, and the participant judges each as old, similar or new as it appears, with repeats and lures occurring a few items after their first appearance.
variations.justification: Study and test interleaved; different trial structure

variations.name: Parametric Similarity Manipulation
variations.description: The lure items are graded by how closely they resemble the studied object, from nearly identical to clearly different, so that discrimination can be plotted against similarity.
variations.justification: Graded lure similarity levels; tests pattern separation threshold

variations.name: MST for Faces
variations.description: The items are faces, with lures being similar faces or the same person with a changed feature, so that memory discrimination is measured for faces rather than objects.
variations.justification: Face stimuli; different recognition domain

variations.name: Spatial MST
variations.description: Objects are shown at particular locations, and at test the same object appears at the same place, a slightly shifted place, or a clearly different place. The participant judges whether the location is the same, similar or new.
variations.justification: Location-based similarity; tests spatial pattern separation

variations.name: Short-Delay vs. Long-Delay MST
variations.description: The test is given immediately after study in one condition and after a delay of hours or a day in another, to see whether discrimination of similar items fades faster than recognition of repeats.
variations.justification: Retention interval manipulation tests forgetting of pattern separation

families.rationale: Recognition with similar lures

short_definition: Cue predicts potential monetary gain or loss; speeded target response determines outcome. Striatal activity to cues indexes reward anticipation.
description: The Monetary Incentive Delay Task is the dominant paradigm for neuroimaging studies of reward anticipation and consumption. On each trial, a cue signals the potential outcome: reward (gain), loss avoidance, or neutral. After a variable delay period, participants respond to a briefly presented target; successful responses earn the reward (or avoid the loss). The critical contrast is neural activity during the anticipation period (cue-to-target), which robustly activates the ventral striatum/nucleus accumbens, versus the outcome period (after response), which more strongly engages ventromedial prefrontal cortex. The MID has been widely adopted in clinical neuroimaging of addiction, depression, and schizophrenia.

procedure: A cue signals potential reward, loss, or neutral outcome.
After a delay, a target appears and participants make a speeded response.
Outcome depends on response speed.
manipulations: Cue type (reward magnitude, loss magnitude, neutral)
measurements: fMRI activation in ventral striatum (anticipation) and medial PFC (outcome)

variations.name: Standard MID (Knutson)
variations.description: A cue shows whether the coming trial can win money, can lose money, or is neutral. After a short wait a target flashes briefly and the participant must press a button before it disappears. Fast enough presses win or avoid losing the money; the target duration is adjusted so this succeeds about two thirds of the time. Feedback follows each trial.
variations.justification: Canonical cue-anticipation-response structure with monetary reward/punishment

variations.name: Graded Reward MID
variations.description: The cues signal several different amounts, for example 20 cents, 1 dollar or 5 dollars, so that the response to anticipating reward can be compared across amounts.
variations.justification: Multiple reward magnitude levels; tests reward sensitivity parametrically

variations.name: MID with Social Rewards
variations.description: A fast response earns a smiling face or words of approval instead of money, with a neutral image for missed trials. This is the Social Incentive Delay Task, which the Catalog lists separately.
variations.justification: Social stimuli (faces) as rewards instead of money; different incentive type

variations.name: MID with Drug Cues
variations.description: The cues or rewards are related to a substance such as alcohol, cigarettes or cocaine, for example a picture of the drug signaling the trial, used with people who use that substance.
variations.justification: Drug-associated cues as incentive stimuli; different cue content

variations.name: Passive MID
variations.description: The cue and outcome are shown but the participant does not press anything; wins and losses are delivered according to a preset schedule. The brain response to anticipating gain or loss is measured without any motor preparation.
variations.justification: No response required; isolates anticipatory processing from motor preparation

variations.name: MID with Effort Component
variations.description: Instead of a quick button press, the participant must squeeze a hand grip hard enough or press a key many times to earn the cued reward, so that willingness to work for money is measured alongside anticipation.
variations.justification: Effort required to obtain reward; adds effort-discounting to incentive structure

families.rationale: Cue announces a potential monetary outcome before a speeded response

short_definition: Repeated execution of a fixed finger sequence; within- and across-session speed and accuracy changes index motor skill learning.
description: Participants are trained to execute finger sequences (e.g., pressing buttons in a specific order: 4-1-3-2-4) either continuously or in discrete blocks. Learning is indexed by decreasing RT, reduced movement duration, and decreased errors. Neuroimaging shows early learning engages cerebellum and prefrontal cortex, while consolidated sequences show greater striatal and reduced cerebellar engagement, reflecting a shift from explicit, attention-demanding processes to implicit, automatic execution. Sleep promotes offline consolidation of motor sequences.

procedure: Participants repeatedly perform a fixed sequence of finger movements (e.g., 4-1-3-2-4) in response to spatial cues.
Over practice, performance speeds up and becomes more automatic.

variations.name: Discrete Sequence Production (DSP)
variations.description: The participant is shown a short sequence of key presses (such as 4-1-3-2-4), memorizes it, and then types it from memory over and over as fast and accurately as possible. Improvement in speed across trials and sessions is the learning measure.
variations.justification: Canonical pre-learned sequence executed rapidly; measures chunking

variations.name: Serial Reaction Time Task variant
variations.description: Each key press is cued by a stimulus appearing at one of several positions, and unknown to the participant the positions follow a repeating sequence. Learning shows up as faster responses that slow again when the sequence is replaced by random positions. Cataloged in its own right as the Serial Reaction Time Task.
variations.justification: Implicit learning via RT advantages for repeating sequences

variations.name: Finger Opposition Task
variations.description: The participant touches the thumb to the other fingers of the same hand in a fixed order (for example index, ring, middle, little) repeatedly, without keys. Often used in brain imaging because it needs no equipment.
variations.justification: Thumb-to-finger opposition sequences; different finger movement type

variations.name: Bimanual Coordination
variations.description: Both hands perform sequences at the same time, either the same sequence in mirror fashion or two different sequences, so that learning includes coordinating the hands.
variations.justification: Both hands performing sequences; interlimb coordination demands

variations.name: Explicit vs. Implicit Sequence Learning
variations.description: One group is shown the sequence and told to learn it; the other performs the same key presses without being told there is a sequence. Compares deliberate learning with learning that happens without awareness.
variations.justification: Aware vs. unaware of sequence structure; different instruction and learning mechanism

variations.name: Sequence Complexity Manipulation
variations.description: Sequences of different lengths or structures are learned, from four elements up to twelve or more, to see how learning rate and the way the sequence is broken into chunks depend on complexity.
variations.justification: Varies sequence length and structure; tests learning as function of complexity

variations.name: Transfer Tests
variations.description: After practice, the learned sequence is performed with the other hand, with different fingers, or in a mirror-reversed form. How much of the speed-up carries over shows whether what was learned is the order of the movements or the movements themselves.
variations.justification: Probe what was learned by testing with modified sequence; different test phase structure

variations.name: Continuous Tracking + Sequence
variations.description: The participant continuously follows a moving target with a joystick or mouse. Part of the target's path repeats on every trial without the participant being told, and tracking becomes more accurate on the repeated segment.
variations.justification: Sequence embedded in continuous tracking; tests incidental learning during ongoing task

families.rationale: Explicit practice of a finger sequence
