short_definition: Repeated choice among options with unknown or changing reward distributions; choice sequences dissociate exploration from exploitation.
description: Participants choose among multiple options (the "arms" of a slot machine), each yielding rewards with unknown and often changing probabilities. The central challenge is the explore-exploit dilemma: whether to exploit the currently best-known option or explore alternatives that might yield higher returns. Reward probabilities may be stationary or volatile (drifting over time), with the volatile version (restless bandit) requiring continuous updating of value estimates. This paradigm is the dominant tool in computational psychiatry for studying reinforcement learning, and its computational tractability - fitting with Bayesian, Kalman-filter, or upper-confidence-bound models - has made it central to understanding decision-making deficits in addiction, schizophrenia, depression, and anxiety.

procedure: Participants choose repeatedly among multiple options (arms) that deliver stochastic rewards drawn from different distributions.
They must balance exploring unknown options with exploiting known good ones.
measurements: Fit to reinforcement learning models (learning rate, inverse temperature)

variations.name: Two-Armed Stationary Bandit
variations.description: On each trial the participant chooses one of two options (often shown as slot machines or colored boxes) and receives a reward with a fixed probability for that option. The probabilities do not change, so the participant can learn the better option and stick with it.
variations.justification: Canonical two-option stationary reward structure; stable payoff distributions

variations.name: Restless (Volatile) Bandit
variations.description: The reward probability or amount for each option drifts slowly and randomly over the session, so the best option changes. The participant must keep sampling options that seem worse to notice when they improve.
variations.justification: Reward probabilities drift over time; tests tracking of non-stationary environments

variations.name: Contextual Bandit
variations.description: A cue shown on each trial, such as a background color or a feature of the options, predicts which option is better. The participant must learn the rule linking the cue to the right choice.
variations.justification: Context features predict optimal choice; adds feature-based learning

variations.name: Horizon Task (Wilson et al.)
variations.description: The participant is told how many choices remain in the current game, either one or several. After some forced choices that show outcomes, the free choices reveal how much more people explore when there are many choices left to benefit from the information.
variations.justification: Fixed horizon with exploration vs. exploitation trade-off manipulation

variations.name: Four-Armed Bandit with Reversal
variations.description: Four options are available and, at unannounced points, their reward probabilities swap so the previously best option becomes worse. The participant must notice and switch.
variations.justification: Four arms with explicit reversal phase; tests reversal learning in bandit

variations.name: Informative vs. Non-Informative Exploration
variations.description: The design controls whether choosing an untried option actually teaches the participant something, for example by sometimes showing the outcomes of unchosen options, so that choices made for information can be separated from choices made at random.
variations.justification: Exploration choices yield differential information; changes exploration value

variations.name: Social Bandit
variations.description: Before or alongside their own choices, the participant sees the choices or outcomes of another player, and can use that player's experience to guide their own picks.
variations.justification: Observe another's choices; social learning component

variations.name: Bandit with Effort Cost
variations.description: Choosing or sampling an option costs physical or mental effort, for example several key presses or a difficult task, so the participant must weigh the cost of exploring against the value of what might be learned.
variations.justification: Effort cost added to choices; combines effort discounting with learning

variations.name: Bandit with Partial Observability
variations.description: In the usual task only the chosen option's outcome is shown. Here, in some conditions, the outcomes of all options are shown after each choice, so the participant can learn about options without choosing them and exploration is no longer needed for information.
variations.justification: Outcomes sometimes hidden; different information structure

families.rationale: Repeated choice among options with unknown payoffs

short_definition: Participants track a subset of identical moving objects among distractors for several seconds; tracking accuracy indexes sustained multifocal attention.
description: In the Multiple Object Tracking task, participants view a set of identical objects (typically 8-16 circles), a subset of which are briefly designated as targets (by flashing or color). All objects then move independently and randomly for several seconds, and participants must track the targets among distractors. After movement stops, participants identify which objects were the original targets. Performance is measured as tracking accuracy as a function of target load (typically 1-5 targets). The task provides a direct index of how many individual objects can be simultaneously tracked - a measure of visual attention capacity, estimated at approximately 4 objects.

procedure: A set of identical objects (dots) move randomly.
a subset is designated as targets.
After the targets are highlighted, all dots move for several seconds, then participants identify which dots were targets.

variations.name: Standard MOT
variations.description: Eight or more identical dots appear and a few of them flash to mark them as targets. All dots then move around randomly for several seconds, and when they stop the participant indicates which ones were the targets. Accuracy is measured for different numbers of targets.
variations.justification: Canonical: track subset of identical moving dots

variations.name: Identity-MOT (MIT)
variations.description: Each moving object has its own identity, such as a different letter, picture or color, which is hidden during movement. At the end the participant must report not just where the targets are but which identity is at each position.
variations.justification: Track identity features of moving objects; adds identity memory demand

variations.name: 3D MOT (NeuroTracker)
variations.description: The spheres move within a simulated three-dimensional volume shown with stereoscopic glasses or a 3D display, so they move in depth as well as across the screen. The speed is adjusted to find the fastest speed at which the participant can still track.
variations.justification: Three-dimensional display with depth; different spatial processing

variations.name: MOT with Occlusion
variations.description: Objects briefly pass behind visible barriers or disappear and reappear during movement, so the participant must keep track of them while they cannot be seen.
variations.justification: Objects temporarily hidden; requires inference of hidden trajectories

variations.name: Probe-Based MOT
variations.description: Rather than selecting all targets at the end, a single object is highlighted during or after movement and the participant says whether it is a target or not.
variations.justification: Probe object after tracking to test spatial knowledge; different response method

variations.name: Hierarchical MOT
variations.description: Objects move in groups, such as clusters that move together, and the targets may be whole groups or members within groups. Tests whether tracking can operate at more than one level at once.
variations.justification: Nested groups of objects tracked at multiple levels; different attentional structure

variations.name: Auditory MOT Analogs
variations.description: The moving items are sounds that move around the listener in virtual auditory space, and the participant must keep track of the target sounds by ear.
variations.justification: Tracking moving sounds; different sensory modality

families.rationale: Track moving targets among identical distractors

short_definition: Continuous stream in which each item must be compared to the one n items back; accuracy and RT index working memory updating and monitoring.
description: The N-Back task is a continuous performance paradigm in which participants view a sequence of stimuli (letters, numbers, or spatial locations) and judge whether each current stimulus matches the one presented n trials earlier. Difficulty scales parametrically with n (1-back, 2-back, 3-back). The task engages working memory maintenance, updating, and comparison processes. Performance typically shows decreased accuracy and increased RT with higher n values. The N-back is the most widely used working memory paradigm in neuroimaging, consistently activating dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and parietal regions.

procedure: A continuous stream of stimuli is presented.
Participants indicate when the current item matches the one presented N items back.

variations.name: Verbal N-Back
variations.description: Letters appear one at a time, about one every two seconds. The participant presses a key whenever the current letter is the same as the one shown n items earlier (for example two back). The level n sets the difficulty.
variations.justification: Letters or words; phonological working memory

variations.name: Spatial N-Back
variations.description: A square appears at one of several positions in a grid, and the participant responds when the current position matches the position n items earlier. The identity of the stimulus does not matter, only where it was.
variations.justification: Locations instead of letters; visuospatial working memory

variations.name: Emotional N-Back
variations.description: The items are faces with emotional expressions or emotional words, and the participant matches on identity or expression n items back, so that memory updating is measured with emotional content.
variations.justification: Emotional stimuli; retained per section 5.1 (EMOT retired)

variations.name: Dual N-Back
variations.description: Two streams run at once: a square moving among grid positions and a spoken letter on each trial. The participant responds separately when the position matches n back and when the letter matches n back. Used mainly in working memory training studies.
variations.justification: Simultaneous visual and auditory streams; recognized named paradigm (Jaeggi et al., 2008)

variations.name: Fractal/Object N-Back
variations.description: The items are abstract patterns, fractals or unfamiliar shapes that have no easy name, so the participant cannot rehearse them verbally and must hold them as images.
variations.justification: Complex visual objects; different stimulus type

variations.name: Adaptive N-Back
variations.description: The level n goes up after a block done well and down after a block done poorly, so each participant works at a level that keeps accuracy near a set target, typically around 80 percent.
variations.justification: N-level adjusts with performance; changes task difficulty trajectory

variations.name: N-Back with Lures
variations.description: The sequence is built to include items that match the one shown n-1 or n+1 items earlier, which feel familiar but are not targets. Rejecting these requires knowing exactly where in the sequence each item was.
variations.justification: Near-miss stimuli create high interference; changes task demand

variations.name: Auditory N-Back
variations.description: The items are heard rather than seen, for example tones of different pitch or spoken letters, and the participant responds when the current sound matches the one n items earlier.
variations.justification: Auditory tones or words; different sensory modality

families.rationale: Compare each item with the one n back

short_definition: Hierarchical letters in which large letters are composed of small ones; RT differences between global and local identification index attentional scope.
description: The Navon Task investigates hierarchical processing in vision using compound stimuli - large (global) letters composed of smaller (local) letters (e.g., a large "H" made of small "S" letters). Participants identify either the global or local letter depending on instruction. The robust finding of global precedence shows faster identification of global than local forms, with global-to-local interference exceeding local-to-global interference. The task dissociates dorsal/ventral visual stream contributions and is sensitive to hemispheric specialization (left hemisphere for local, right for global processing).

procedure: A large letter (global) composed of small letters (local) is presented.
Participants identify the letter at the designated level (global or local).
manipulations: Congruency (same vs. different letter at two levels)
measurements: Asymmetric interference (global disrupts local more than reverse)

variations.name: Standard Navon (Blocked)
variations.description: A large letter made up of small letters is shown, for example a big H built from small Ss. In some blocks the participant identifies the big letter, in others the small letters. People are usually faster with the big letter and are slowed when the two levels disagree.
variations.justification: Canonical blocked global/local judgment of hierarchical figures

variations.name: Mixed/Cued Navon
variations.description: Whether to report the big or the small letter is signaled by a cue on each trial rather than fixed for a block, so the participant must switch between levels from trial to trial.
variations.justification: Trial-by-trial cue indicates level; task-switching demand added

variations.name: Divided Attention Navon
variations.description: The participant looks for a target letter that may appear at either level, or must report both the big and the small letter, so attention cannot be set to one level in advance.
variations.justification: Respond to both levels simultaneously; different attentional demand

variations.name: Consistent vs. Inconsistent Stimuli
variations.description: Trials in which the big and small letters are the same (a big H made of small Hs) are compared with trials where they differ (a big H made of small Ss). The slowdown on different-letter trials measures interference between levels.
variations.justification: Local and global levels same vs. different; conflict manipulation

variations.name: Sparse vs. Dense Local Elements
variations.description: The number and spacing of the small letters making up the big letter is varied. With fewer, more widely spaced elements the big letter is harder to see and the usual advantage for the big letter shrinks.
variations.justification: Number of local elements varies; tests density effect on global processing

variations.name: Emotional Navon
variations.description: The compound figure is built from faces or emotional pictures, for example a large happy face made of small sad faces, and the participant reports the emotion at the cued level.
variations.justification: Emotional faces at global/local level; retained per section 5.1 (EMOT retired)

variations.name: Auditory Navon Analogs
variations.description: The hierarchy is in sound: a short melody (the global level) is made up of smaller note patterns (the local level), and the participant judges either the overall contour or the local pattern.
variations.justification: Hierarchical auditory stimuli; different sensory modality

variations.name: Navon with Priming
variations.description: A task that requires attending to the big or the small level is performed first, and its effect on a following task is measured. Attending to one level carries over and biases later processing toward that level.
variations.justification: Preceding prime influences level processing; temporal context manipulation

variations.name: Lateralized Presentation
variations.description: The compound letter is flashed briefly to the left or right of fixation, so that it reaches one hemisphere of the brain first. The right hemisphere tends to favor the big letter and the left the small letters.
variations.justification: Stimuli presented to one visual field; tests hemispheric contributions

variations.name: Navon Figures with Shapes
variations.description: The compound figures are geometric shapes, such as a large square made of small triangles, rather than letters, so that reading is not involved.
variations.justification: Non-letter shapes at global/local level; different stimulus class

variations.name: Temporal Precedence (Brief Exposure)
variations.description: The compound figure is flashed for only 50 to 100 ms and sometimes masked. At such short exposures the big letter is usually identified more often than the small ones, which shows which level is available first.
variations.justification: Brief exposure tests which level is processed first

families.rationale: Global-local interference; could be filed under perceptual judgment

short_definition: Sequence of standards with rare deviants or targets; deviants elicit a large positive ERP around 300 ms (P3a/P3b), indexing attention and context updating.
description: Participants are presented with a stimulus stream containing frequent standard stimuli (80% of trials) and infrequent target (oddball) stimuli (20%) that differ in some dimension (pitch, color, shape). Participants respond (button press) to targets. Target detection elicits the P3b ERP component (300-600 ms, parietal maximum), reflecting stimulus evaluation and working memory updating. Novel or unexpected stimuli also elicit the P3a component (frontocentral), reflecting automatic attention capture. The paradigm is widely used as a biomarker of cognitive function and has clinical applications in ADHD, schizophrenia, and traumatic brain injury.

procedure: A sequence of frequent standard stimuli is occasionally interrupted by rare target (and sometimes novel) stimuli.
Participants count or respond to targets.
measurements: P3b amplitude and latency to targets

variations.name: Two-Stimulus Auditory Oddball
variations.description: Two tones of different pitch are played in random order, one common (about 80 percent) and one rare. The participant presses a key or counts whenever the rare tone occurs. The rare tone produces a large positive brain wave about 300 ms after it sounds.
variations.justification: Canonical: standard + deviant tones; P300 or MMN elicitation

variations.name: Three-Stimulus Novelty Oddball
variations.description: A third kind of event is added: rare, unexpected and varied sounds such as a dog bark or a door slam that the participant should ignore. The rare target still gets a response. The novel sounds produce an earlier, more frontal brain response than the targets.
variations.justification: Novel distractors added to standard+deviant; different stimulus structure

variations.name: Visual Oddball
variations.description: The common and rare events are visual, such as a circle versus a square, or one letter versus another, shown one at a time on a screen.
variations.justification: Visual stimuli; different sensory modality

variations.name: Passive Oddball
variations.description: The participant is not asked to respond or count, and may be reading or watching something else while the sounds play. The rare sound still produces a brain response, though a smaller one.
variations.justification: No response required; isolates automatic change detection

variations.name: Active Counting vs. Button-Press Response
variations.description: The participant keeps a silent running count of the rare events and reports the total at the end, instead of pressing a key to each one. Counting avoids movement during recording.
variations.justification: Silent count vs. button press; different response modality

variations.name: Duration Deviance Oddball
variations.description: The rare tone is the same pitch as the common tone but longer or shorter, so the difference is in duration rather than pitch.
variations.justification: Duration-based deviant; different acoustic dimension from frequency

variations.name: Cross-Modal Oddball
variations.description: Common and rare events come in different senses, for example a stream of tones with an occasional light flash, or a mixed stream in which the participant responds to rare events in either sense.
variations.justification: Deviant crosses sensory modality; different cross-modal attention

variations.name: Emotional Oddball
variations.description: The rare events are emotional pictures or faces inserted into a stream of neutral ones, so that the response to rare events is measured for emotional content.
variations.justification: Emotional stimuli as deviants; retained per section 5.1 (EMOT retired)

variations.name: Roving Paradigm
variations.description: A tone repeats several times and is then replaced by a new tone, which repeats and becomes the new standard, and so on. Every tone starts as a rare event and becomes common, so the brain response can be tracked as it builds up over repetitions.
variations.justification: Standard changes after each presentation; different stimulus history structure

families.rationale: Rare deviants in a stream of standards

short_definition: Studied items mixed with new lures at test; hit and false-alarm rates yield d' and can be decomposed into recollection and familiarity via ROC or remember/know.
description: Participants study a list of stimuli (words, pictures, or faces) during an encoding phase. In the test phase, they view a mixture of studied (old) and unstudied (new) items and make binary old/new recognition judgments. Performance is analyzed using signal detection measures (hits, false alarms, d') and can be further decomposed into familiarity-based (rapid, automatic) and recollection-based (slower, effortful) processes using confidence ratings or remember/know judgments. Neuroimaging consistently implicates the hippocampus, angular gyrus, and default mode network in successful recognition.

procedure: Participants study a list of items, then view a test list containing studied (old) items and unstudied (new) items and classify each as old or new.

variations.name: Standard Old/New
variations.description: The participant studies a list of words or pictures. Later the studied items are mixed with an equal number of new ones, and the participant says 'old' or 'new' to each. The hit rate for old items and the false alarm rate for new items are the measures.
variations.justification: Canonical yes/no recognition judgment

variations.name: Remember-Know (R/K)
variations.description: For each item judged old, the participant also says whether they actually recollect something about studying it (remember) or just find it familiar (know). Cataloged in its own right as the Remember/Know Task.
variations.justification: Participant distinguishes recollection from familiarity; different response scale

variations.name: Source Memory
variations.description: Items are studied under different conditions, such as spoken by a male or female voice or shown on the left or right. At test the participant says not only whether an item is old but also which condition it was studied in. Cataloged in its own right as the Source Memory Task.
variations.justification: Identify source context of recognized item; adds contextual retrieval judgment

variations.name: Associative Recognition
variations.description: Items are studied in pairs. At test the participant sees intact pairs, pairs made by re-pairing studied items, and new pairs, and must say which pairs were studied together. Recognizing the individual words is not enough.
variations.justification: Judge intact vs. rearranged pairs; tests associative vs. item memory

variations.name: Forced-Choice Recognition
variations.description: Each test trial shows two (or more) items, one studied and one new, and the participant picks the studied one, rather than judging items one at a time.
variations.justification: Select target from foil array; different response structure

variations.name: Continuous Recognition
variations.description: There is no separate study phase. Items appear in one long stream and some repeat after various numbers of intervening items. The participant judges every item as new or repeated as it appears.
variations.justification: Study and test interleaved in ongoing stream; different trial structure

variations.name: DRM (Deese-Roediger-McDermott) False Memory Variant
variations.description: The study lists are made of words all related to one unpresented word (bed, rest, awake, tired... for SLEEP). At test the unpresented related word is included, and participants often confidently call it old.
variations.justification: Semantically related lures elicit false recognition; distinct false memory paradigm

families.rationale: Studied items among new lures

short_definition: Alternating arithmetic verification and word/letter memory items; complex-span score indexes working memory capacity under processing load.
description: The Operation Span Task is a complex span measure of working memory capacity. Participants alternate between a processing task (verifying simple math equations, e.g., "Is (2 x 3) + 1 = 8?") and a memory task (remembering letters or words presented after each equation). After a set of 3-7 equation-letter pairs, participants recall the letters in order. The OSPAN score reflects the ability to maintain memory representations while engaging in concurrent processing - a hallmark of working memory capacity (WMC). OSPAN scores are strong predictors of fluid intelligence, reading comprehension, and general executive function.

procedure: Participants alternate between processing a distractor task (verifying math equations) and remembering items (letters or words).
At the end of each set, they recall items in order.
measurements: Operation span score (items recalled in correct position)
Processing accuracy (to verify engagement with distractor task)

variations.name: Automated OSPAN (AOSPAN)
variations.description: The participant alternates between checking whether a simple arithmetic equation is correct and seeing a letter to remember. After three to seven such pairs they recall the letters in order by clicking them. The computer paces the arithmetic from the participant's own practice speed.
variations.justification: Canonical computerized OSPAN with math distractor

variations.name: Reading Span (RSPAN)
variations.description: The interleaved processing task is reading a sentence and judging whether it makes sense, instead of arithmetic. A word or letter to remember follows each sentence.
variations.justification: Sentence comprehension distractor; different processing demand

variations.name: Symmetry Span (SYMSPAN)
variations.description: The processing task is judging whether a pattern is symmetric about its vertical axis, and the items to remember are positions of red squares in a grid, recalled in order. A spatial version of the task.
variations.justification: Spatial symmetry judgment distractor; visuospatial storage component

variations.name: Counting Span
variations.description: The participant counts the target shapes (for example dark circles among squares) in each display and says the total aloud, then after several displays recalls the totals in order.
variations.justification: Counting shapes distractor; different processing requirement

variations.name: Shortened OSPAN
variations.description: A version with fewer sets and shorter maximum set sizes that takes around half the time but has been shown to give similar scores.
variations.justification: Abbreviated protocol; recognized efficient version for time-limited settings

variations.name: Adaptive OSPAN
variations.description: The number of items in each set is increased after correct recall and decreased after errors, so the task spends most of its trials near the participant's limit rather than running a fixed series of set sizes.
variations.justification: Adaptive set sizes based on performance; different difficulty trajectory

families.rationale: Complex span with interleaved arithmetic

short_definition: Study of cue-target pairs followed by cued recall; proportion recalled indexes associative encoding and retrieval.
description: Participants learn arbitrary associations between stimuli and their locations (or between word pairs). In a typical computerized version (CANTAB PAL), abstract patterns appear in boxes around the screen during the study phase, and during test, patterns are presented centrally and participants must identify the correct box location. Difficulty increases across stages from 1-2 to 6-8 pairs. Performance is measured by patterns correctly learned and errors made. The PAL task is particularly sensitive to hippocampal function and shows early sensitivity to amyloid-beta pathology in preclinical Alzheimer's disease.

procedure: Participants study pairs of items (word-word, face-name, object-location) and are later cued with one member to recall the other.

variations.name: Verbal Paired Associates (Cued Recall)
variations.description: The participant studies pairs of words such as 'window - cheese'. At test the first word of each pair is shown and the participant must produce the second. The proportion correct is the measure.
variations.justification: Canonical word-word pairs with cued recall test

variations.name: Face-Name Paired Associates
variations.description: Each pair is a photograph of a face and a name. At test the face is shown and the participant must recall the name, or choose it from a list. Sensitive to age-related memory decline.
variations.justification: Face-name binding; social memory domain

variations.name: Object-Location Pairs
variations.description: Each object is shown at a particular place on the screen or in a scene. At test the object is shown and the participant indicates where it was, or a location is shown and the participant names the object.
variations.justification: Object-location binding; spatial memory component

variations.name: CANTAB PAL
variations.description: A touchscreen test from the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery. Boxes on the screen open one by one to reveal abstract patterns; then each pattern is shown in the center and the participant touches the box it came from. The number of patterns increases across stages.
variations.justification: Touchscreen object-location paradigm; named computerized instrument

variations.name: Arbitrary vs. Semantically Related Pairs
variations.description: Some pairs are related in meaning (baby - cries) and some are not (obey - inch). Related pairs are learned faster, and the difference shows how much the participant relies on existing knowledge.
variations.justification: Relatedness manipulation changes encoding strategy

variations.name: Cross-Modal Paired Associates
variations.description: The two members of a pair come through different senses or formats, for example a sound paired with a picture, or a spoken word paired with a screen location.
variations.justification: Pairs span sensory modalities; cross-modal binding demand

variations.name: Multi-Trial Learning Curves
variations.description: The same pairs are studied and tested several times in alternation, and the number correct on each test is plotted to give a learning curve.
variations.justification: Repeated study-test cycles; tests learning rate over trials

variations.name: Retroactive/Proactive Interference Variants
variations.description: After learning one list of pairs (A-B), the participant learns a second list in which the same cue words are paired with new responses (A-C). Memory for the first list after the second (retroactive interference) or for the second given the first (proactive interference) is tested.
variations.justification: Competing pairs introduced; tests interference in associative memory

variations.name: Incidental vs. Intentional Encoding
variations.description: In the intentional version the participant is told to learn the pairs for a later test. In the incidental version they do some other task with the pairs, such as rating how well the words go together, and the memory test is a surprise.
variations.justification: Encoding goal manipulation; tests depth and intentionality of encoding

families.rationale: Cued recall of studied pairs

short_definition: A neutral CS is paired with an aversive US (shock, loud sound); conditioned responses (SCR, startle, amygdala BOLD) index fear learning.
description: A neutral conditioned stimulus (CS; auditory tone or visual cue) is paired with an aversive unconditioned stimulus (US; mild shock, loud noise). After conditioning, the CS alone elicits conditioned fear responses including skin conductance increases, heart rate changes, freezing (in animals), and subjective fear ratings (in humans). Extinction is measured in a subsequent phase where the CS is presented without the US. The task is fundamental to understanding emotional learning and has been used extensively to study the amygdala's role in fear acquisition and the prefrontal cortex's role in extinction.

procedure: Participants view a neutral stimulus (CS+) paired with an aversive unconditioned stimulus (US, typically mild shock or loud noise).
Another stimulus (CS-) is never paired.
Acquisition is followed by extinction (CS+ presented without US).

variations.name: Delay Conditioning
variations.description: A neutral cue such as a colored shape or tone is presented for several seconds, and a mild electric shock or loud noise arrives at the end of the cue while it is still on. After several pairings the cue alone produces a fear response such as increased skin conductance.
variations.justification: CS and US overlap; canonical associative fear learning

variations.name: Trace Conditioning
variations.description: The cue ends and there is a silent gap of a few seconds before the shock arrives, so the participant must bridge the gap in memory to link cue and shock. Harder to learn than the overlapping version.
variations.justification: Trace interval between CS offset and US onset; different temporal structure

variations.name: Contextual Conditioning
variations.description: No discrete cue predicts the shock. Instead shocks occur at unpredictable times in a particular setting, such as one of two virtual rooms or a background color, and fear becomes attached to the setting itself.
variations.justification: Context (environment) as CS; different stimulus type

variations.name: Differential Conditioning (CS+/CS-)
variations.description: Two cues are used: one is followed by the shock and the other never is. Fear to the paired cue minus fear to the safe cue shows that the participant learned the specific prediction, not just a general wariness.
variations.justification: Two CSs with different US contingencies; adds discrimination demand

variations.name: Extinction Training
variations.description: After conditioning, the cue is presented many times without any shock. The fear response gradually fades as the participant learns that the cue no longer predicts the shock.
variations.justification: CS presented without US; tests extinction learning

variations.name: Extinction Recall
variations.description: A day or more after extinction, the cue is presented again without shock. Whether the fear stays low or returns measures how well the extinction learning was retained.
variations.justification: Test of extinguished fear after delay; different memory phase

variations.name: Renewal (Context Change)
variations.description: Conditioning takes place in one setting and extinction in another. The cue is then tested back in the original setting (or a new one), where the fear response typically returns, showing extinction is tied to where it happened.
variations.justification: Extinguished CS tested in new context; tests context-specificity of extinction

variations.name: Reinstatement
variations.description: After extinction, a few shocks are given with no cue present. When the cue is then tested, the fear response comes back even though the cue was never paired again.
variations.justification: Unsignaled US presentations revive extinguished fear; different recovery procedure

variations.name: Reconsolidation Paradigm
variations.description: A day after conditioning, the cue is presented once to reactivate the memory, and extinction training follows within a window of about ten minutes to a few hours. Extinction given in this window can prevent fear from returning later.
variations.justification: Reactivation + interference during reconsolidation; different intervention timing

variations.name: Generalization Gradient
variations.description: After conditioning to one cue (for example a circle of a given size), cues that differ from it by increasing amounts are tested. Plotting fear against similarity shows how far fear spreads to similar things.
variations.justification: CS-similar stimuli tested; measures perceptual generalization

variations.name: Instructed vs. Uninstructed
variations.description: Some participants are told in advance which cue will be followed by shock; others find out only by experience. Compares fear learned through words with fear learned through direct experience.
variations.justification: Verbal instruction about CS-US relationship; tests instructed vs. experiential fear

variations.name: Compound CS Conditioning
variations.description: Two or more cues are presented together (such as a light and a tone) before the shock. Later the cues are tested separately and together to see whether the participant learned about each element or about the combination.
variations.justification: CS compound with multiple elements; different stimulus structure

families.rationale: CS paired with an aversive US

short_definition: Rhyme judgment, phoneme deletion, or phoneme blending tasks index sensitivity to the sound structure of language.
description: Participants view or hear pairs of words and judge whether they rhyme. The task requires analysis of the sound structure of words, comparison of phonological representations, and a binary decision. Control conditions involve matching for orthographic similarity or judging word identity. fMRI reveals activation in left inferior frontal regions (pars opercularis), left temporoparietal areas, and left superior temporal cortex. The task is widely used in reading research and dyslexia studies, as phonological awareness is a strong predictor of reading ability.

procedure: Participants make explicit judgments about the sound structure of spoken words: rhyme detection, phoneme deletion, phoneme segmentation, or blending.
manipulations: Task type (rhyme, onset, phoneme deletion, blending)
measurements: Correlation with reading ability in developmental populations

variations.name: Rhyme Detection
variations.description: Two spoken words are presented and the participant says whether they rhyme, for example 'cat' and 'hat' (yes) or 'cat' and 'cup' (no).
variations.justification: Participant judges whether words rhyme; canonical phonological awareness task

variations.name: Rhyme Oddity
variations.description: Three or four spoken words are presented, all but one rhyming, and the participant picks the one that does not rhyme, such as 'book' from 'cat, hat, book'.
variations.justification: Identify non-rhyming word in set; different task structure from detection

variations.name: Rhyme Production
variations.description: A word is spoken and the participant produces one or more words that rhyme with it.
variations.justification: Generate rhyming words; different output requirement

variations.name: Onset Detection
variations.description: A word is spoken and the participant says its first sound, or judges whether two words begin with the same sound.
variations.justification: Judge initial consonant; different phonological unit (onset)

variations.name: Phoneme Deletion
variations.description: A word is spoken and the participant says what is left when a given sound is removed, for example 'boat' without the /b/ gives 'oat'.
variations.justification: Delete specified phoneme and report result; manipulation task

variations.name: Phoneme Substitution
variations.description: A word is spoken and the participant replaces one sound with another, for example changing the /k/ in 'cat' to /h/ to give 'hat'.
variations.justification: Replace phoneme in word; different manipulation operation

variations.name: Phoneme Segmentation
variations.description: A word is spoken and the participant says each of its sounds separately in order, or counts them, for example 'dog' has three sounds: /d/, /o/, /g/.
variations.justification: Segment word into constituent phonemes; decomposition task

variations.name: Blending
variations.description: The sounds of a word are spoken one at a time with gaps (/s/ ... /u/ ... /n/) and the participant says the word they make ('sun').
variations.justification: Combine phonemes to form word; synthesis operation

variations.name: Spoonerisms
variations.description: Two words are spoken and the participant swaps their first sounds, for example 'fed bull' becomes 'bed full'. Requires holding both words while rearranging them.
variations.justification: Transpose onset phonemes of two words; complex transposition manipulation

variations.name: Alliteration Detection
variations.description: Two or more spoken words are presented and the participant says whether they begin with the same sound, or picks the one that does not.
variations.justification: Detect shared onset consonant; different phonological judgment

variations.name: Syllable Awareness Tasks
variations.description: The units are syllables rather than single sounds: the participant counts the syllables in a word, taps them out, deletes one ('sunshine' without 'sun'), or blends syllables into a word. Easier than the sound-level tasks and used with younger children.
variations.justification: Syllable-level operations instead of phoneme-level; different linguistic unit

families.rationale: Rhyme and phoneme manipulation judgments

short_definition: Naming of pictured objects; RT and errors index lexical retrieval and are sensitive to name agreement, frequency, and age of acquisition.
description: Participants view photographs or line drawings of common objects, animals, or scenes and name each item aloud as quickly and accurately as possible. Naming latency (RT from stimulus onset to vocal response onset) is the primary measure. The task engages multiple stages of language production: conceptual identification, lemma retrieval, phonological encoding, and articulation. fMRI reveals activation in left inferior frontal regions (Broca's area) and temporal cortex. The task is widely used in aphasia research and studies of language production.

procedure: Line drawings or photographs of objects are presented one at a time.
Participants name each object as quickly as possible.
manipulations: Phonological or semantic context (blocked naming, picture-word interference)

variations.name: Standard Single-Object Naming
variations.description: Line drawings or photographs of objects appear one at a time and the participant says the name of each as quickly as possible. A microphone records the time from picture onset to the start of speech.
variations.justification: Canonical overt naming to pictured objects

variations.name: Blocked-Cyclic Naming
variations.description: A small set of pictures is named repeatedly in cycles. In some blocks all pictures in the set are from one category (all animals); in others they are mixed. Naming slows over cycles in the same-category blocks because related words compete.
variations.justification: Same items repeat in blocked cycles; cumulative interference paradigm

variations.name: Continuous Naming
variations.description: A long list of pictures is named once each, with pictures from the same category scattered through the list. Each additional picture from a category is named a little more slowly than the one before, showing interference building up.
variations.justification: Rapid successive naming; tests sustained lexical access

variations.name: Picture-Word Interference (PWI)
variations.description: A written or spoken word is presented with each picture, and the participant names the picture while ignoring the word. A word related in meaning (cat for a picture of a dog) slows naming; a word that sounds similar (doll) speeds it.
variations.justification: Distractor word accompanies picture; lexical competition paradigm

variations.name: Delayed Naming
variations.description: The picture is shown but the participant must wait for a signal, typically one to two seconds later, before saying the name. Because the name is ready before the signal, response time reflects only speech production.
variations.justification: Delay between picture onset and response signal; isolates planning from execution

variations.name: Object + Action Naming
variations.description: Pictures show actions as well as objects, and the participant names the action with a verb ('running') or the object with a noun, in separate or mixed blocks.
variations.justification: Name actions as well as objects; different grammatical category

variations.name: Bilingual Picture Naming
variations.description: A cue on each trial (such as a flag or color) tells a bilingual participant which language to name the picture in. Naming is slower just after a switch of language.
variations.justification: Language cue specifies response language; language control demand

variations.name: Tip-of-the-Tongue (TOT) Paradigm
variations.description: Pictures of rarely named things or people (famous faces, unusual objects) are used to provoke states in which the participant knows the name but cannot produce it. The participant reports whether they know it, are in that state, or do not know, and may report partial information such as the first letter.
variations.justification: Naming under word-finding difficulty conditions; different metacognitive state

variations.name: Naming with Phonological/Semantic Cues
variations.description: When the participant cannot name a picture, a hint is given, such as the first sound of the name or a description of its meaning, and whether the hint produces the name is recorded.
variations.justification: Partial cues provided after TOT; different cueing structure

families.rationale: Name pictured objects

short_definition: A central or peripheral cue indicates the likely target location; RT differences between valid, neutral, and invalid cues index covert spatial orienting.
description: The Posner Spatial Cueing Task measures covert orienting of visual attention. Participants fixate on a central point with two peripheral locations marked. A cue stimulus appears (exogenous: at the target location; or endogenous: a central arrow) followed by a target stimulus at one of the peripheral locations. Cues can be valid (same location as target) or invalid (opposite location). The cueing effect (faster RT to validly cued targets vs. invalidly cued) reflects the cost and benefit of attentional orienting. The task dissociates different components of attention: engaging, disengaging, and shifting.

procedure: A cue (peripheral flash or central arrow) indicates a likely target location.
The target then appears at the cued or uncued location and participants detect or discriminate it.
measurements: RT difference between valid and invalid trials (attention effect)

variations.name: Exogenous (Peripheral) Cueing
variations.description: The participant fixates the center while two boxes sit to the left and right. One box briefly brightens, and shortly afterwards a target appears in one of the boxes. The participant responds to the target as fast as possible. The flash pulls attention to that side automatically, so targets there are detected faster.
variations.justification: Peripheral onset cue drives automatic orienting; canonical exogenous attention

variations.name: Endogenous (Central) Cueing
variations.description: The cue is an arrow or other symbol at fixation pointing to the side where the target is likely to appear. The participant must interpret the cue and shift attention deliberately, which takes longer than a flash.
variations.justification: Central arrow cue drives voluntary orienting; different mechanism

variations.name: Valid, Invalid, and Neutral Cue Conditions
variations.description: Three kinds of trial are mixed: the cue correctly indicates the target side (valid), indicates the wrong side (invalid), or gives no side information (neutral). The benefit of a valid cue and the cost of an invalid one are measured against the neutral trials.
variations.justification: Three cue validity conditions test benefit and cost of orienting

variations.name: Inhibition of Return (IOR) Paradigm
variations.description: A flash cue is used and the delay before the target is lengthened beyond about 300 ms. At these delays targets at the flashed location are detected more slowly, not faster, as attention has moved on and is reluctant to return.
variations.justification: Long SOA reverses validity benefit; distinct temporal structure

variations.name: Gap vs. Overlap Conditions
variations.description: The fixation point either disappears shortly before the cue (gap) or stays on (overlap). Removing fixation makes it easier to disengage attention and speeds responses.
variations.justification: Fixation offset before/during cue changes alerting

variations.name: Double-Cue Paradigm
variations.description: Both boxes flash at the same time, so the participant is alerted that a target is coming but gets no information about which side. Comparing with single flashes separates the alerting effect from the orienting effect.
variations.justification: Both locations cued simultaneously; tests alerting without orienting

variations.name: Predictive vs. Non-Predictive Cues
variations.description: The proportion of trials on which the cue correctly indicates the target side is varied, for example 50 percent (uninformative), 75 percent or 100 percent. Only informative cues encourage the participant to shift attention deliberately.
variations.justification: Cue validity changes attentional weight given to cue

variations.name: Feature-Based Cueing
variations.description: The cue indicates a feature of the target, such as its color or orientation, rather than its location. Tests whether attention can be directed to a feature across the whole display.
variations.justification: Feature rather than location cued; tests feature-based attention

variations.name: Object-Based Cueing
variations.description: Two elongated objects are shown and the cue appears at one end of one object. Targets at the uncued end of the same object are detected faster than targets at an equally distant location on the other object.
variations.justification: Object defines cued location; tests object-based attention

variations.name: Cross-Modal Cueing
variations.description: The cue is a sound from the left or right, or a touch on one hand, and the target is visual. Tests whether attention directed by one sense benefits another.
variations.justification: Auditory or tactile cue precedes visual target; cross-modal orienting

variations.name: Detection vs. Discrimination Targets
variations.description: In the detection version the participant presses one key as soon as any target appears. In the discrimination version the target has one of two forms and the participant reports which, for example its orientation or identity.
variations.justification: Simple detection vs. identity discrimination; different response task

families.rationale: Canonical spatial cueing paradigm

short_definition: Two-player one-shot or iterated game with cooperate/defect choices and asymmetric payoffs; choice patterns index cooperation and strategic reasoning.
description: The Prisoner's Dilemma is a canonical game theory paradigm for studying cooperation and defection under strategic interdependence. Two players simultaneously choose to cooperate or defect. Mutual cooperation yields moderate rewards for both; mutual defection yields low rewards for both; but if one defects while the other cooperates, the defector receives the highest reward and the cooperator receives nothing (or a penalty). The dominant strategy in single-shot play is to defect, yet human participants frequently cooperate, particularly in iterated versions. The task is central to research on trust, reciprocity, altruism, and the neural substrates of social decision-making.

procedure: Two players simultaneously choose to cooperate or defect.
Payoffs depend on both choices according to a matrix where mutual cooperation beats mutual defection but defection is individually tempting.

variations.name: Single-Shot (One-Round) PD
variations.description: Two players each choose at the same time, without communicating, to cooperate or defect. Both cooperating pays each a moderate amount; both defecting pays each little; if one defects while the other cooperates, the defector gets the most and the cooperator the least. They play once with an anonymous partner.
variations.justification: Canonical one-round anonymous PD; no reputation effects

variations.name: Iterated PD (Repeated Games)
variations.description: The same two players make the cooperate-or-defect choice repeatedly, seeing each other's past choices, so that strategies such as responding in kind become possible.
variations.justification: Multiple rounds with same partner; reputation and strategy accumulate

variations.name: Sequential PD
variations.description: One player chooses first and the second player sees that choice before making their own. The second player's choice shows whether they reciprocate cooperation.
variations.justification: One player acts before observing other's choice; different temporal structure

variations.name: Multiplayer/Public Goods Version
variations.description: Several players each decide how much of their money to put into a shared pool, which is multiplied and divided equally among everyone regardless of contribution. Contributing helps the group but each player does best by holding back.
variations.justification: More than two players; group dilemma structure

variations.name: PD with Communication
variations.description: The players can talk or exchange messages before choosing, either freely with no binding force, or with the option of making promises that are enforced.
variations.justification: Players communicate before deciding; cheap talk changes decision context

variations.name: PD with Punishment Option
variations.description: After the choices are revealed, a player (or an observing third party) can pay some of their own money to reduce the earnings of a player who defected.
variations.justification: Third-party punishment available; adds enforcement mechanism

variations.name: PD with Varying Payoff Matrices
variations.description: The amounts in the payoff table are changed between games, for example making defection more or less tempting, to see how cooperation depends on the stakes.
variations.justification: Different temptation/sucker payoffs; tests sensitivity to game parameters

variations.name: PD against Computer Opponents
variations.description: The other player is a computer program following a known or unknown fixed strategy, such as always cooperating, always defecting, or copying the participant's last move. The participant may or may not be told it is a computer.
variations.justification: Computer opponent instead of human; per section 5.6 structural change (deterministic vs. human partner)

variations.name: PD with Reputation Information
variations.description: Before choosing, the participant is shown how often their current partner cooperated in previous games with other people.
variations.justification: Partner's past cooperation history visible; changes social information available

variations.name: Continuous PD
variations.description: Instead of a binary choice, each player chooses how much to cooperate on a scale, for example how much of an endowment to transfer to the partner, with payoffs that depend on both amounts.
variations.justification: Continuous contribution instead of binary; different action space

variations.name: Asymmetric Prisoner's Dilemma
variations.description: The two players face different payoff tables, so that one stands to gain more from defecting or to lose more from being exploited than the other. Players may or may not know the other's payoffs.
variations.justification: Different payoff structures for each player; breaks symmetry of standard PD

variations.name: Optional Prisoner's Dilemma
variations.description: Each player has a third option: to not play, taking a guaranteed small payoff instead. Those who choose to play then face the usual cooperate-or-defect choice.
variations.justification: Third option to not participate; changes strategic choice set

families.rationale: Cooperate or defect with asymmetric payoffs

short_definition: Multi-cue probabilistic prediction of a binary outcome with trial-by-trial feedback; learning curves index gradual procedural category learning.
description: The Weather Prediction Task presents 1-3 cues from a set of 4 possible cards; participants predict a binary outcome (rain/sunshine). Each cue is probabilistically associated with outcomes (e.g., 75%/25%), requiring participants to learn from statistical patterns. Feedback is provided after each prediction. Critically, amnesic patients with medial temporal lobe damage show intact learning despite impaired conscious awareness of the task structure, implicating basal ganglia and striatal systems in implicit probabilistic learning.

procedure: Participants predict an outcome (e.g., rain/sun) based on combinations of cues (cards), where each cue is probabilistically (not deterministically) related to outcomes.
Learning is incremental across hundreds of trials.
measurements: Comparison to Parkinson patients (basal ganglia involvement)

variations.name: Standard Weather Prediction (4 cues, binary outcome)
variations.description: One to three cards from a set of four, each with a geometric pattern, are shown on each trial, and the participant predicts whether the weather will be rain or sunshine. Each card is linked to rain with its own probability, and feedback after each guess lets the participant gradually learn the odds.
variations.justification: Canonical probabilistic categorization with cue combinations

variations.name: Deterministic Version
variations.description: Each combination of cards always predicts the same outcome, so a rule can be learned exactly rather than approximately. The task then measures explicit rule learning rather than gradual probabilistic learning.
variations.justification: Cues perfectly predict outcome; removes probabilistic uncertainty

variations.name: Varying Probability Levels
variations.description: The strength of the link between cards and outcome is varied, from barely better than chance (60/40) to nearly certain (90/10). Learning is faster and more complete with stronger links.
variations.justification: Cue-outcome reliability systematically manipulated; different learning statistics

variations.name: Information-Integration Category Learning
variations.description: The stimuli vary continuously on two or more dimensions (such as the length and tilt of a line), and the correct category depends on combining both dimensions in a way that cannot be stated as a simple rule. Learned gradually from feedback.
variations.justification: Categories defined by integration of dimensions; different decision rule

variations.name: Rule-Based Category Learning (comparison)
variations.description: The stimuli vary on several dimensions but the category is determined by one dimension alone (for example, long lines are category A), so the participant can find the rule by testing hypotheses. Used as a contrast with the integration version.
variations.justification: Explicit rule applicable; contrasts implicit vs. explicit learning systems

variations.name: Feedback vs. Observation Learning
variations.description: In the observation version, each set of cards is shown together with its outcome and the participant just watches, rather than guessing and being told right or wrong. Both versions are then tested without feedback.
variations.justification: Active feedback vs. observational learning; different learning mechanism

variations.name: Transfer Test Variants
variations.description: After learning, the participant is tested on card combinations never seen during training, or on the same cards with the outcome links reversed, to see whether what was learned generalizes or can be updated.
variations.justification: Probe generalization with novel cue combinations; different test phase

families.rationale: Multi-cue prediction with trial feedback

short_definition: Learn to choose between stimulus pairs through probabilistic feedback, then select among novel recombinations; choose-A vs. avoid-B accuracy dissociates positive and negative reinforcement learning.
description: The Probabilistic Selection Task, developed by Frank and colleagues, assesses the separable contributions of positive and negative reinforcement learning, linked to striatal Go and NoGo pathway function respectively. During training, participants learn to choose between pairs of stimuli (AB, CD, EF) where each stimulus has a fixed probability of reward (e.g., A=80%, B=20%). At test, stimuli are recombined into novel pairs (e.g., A vs. C, B vs. D). Choosing A in novel contexts indexes Go learning (approach from positive feedback), while avoiding B indexes NoGo learning (avoidance from negative feedback). The task was specifically designed to probe basal ganglia dopaminergic mechanisms and is sensitive to dopaminergic medication effects in Parkinson's disease.

procedure: Participants learn to choose between stimulus pairs through probabilistic feedback (80/20 or 70/30 contingencies), then are tested on novel recombinations without feedback to dissociate Go learning (choose A) from NoGo learning (avoid B).
measurements: Transfer test accuracy (choose-A vs. avoid-B dissociation)
Fit to actor-critic or opponent-actor learning models

variations.name: Standard PST (3 Stimulus Pairs)
variations.description: Three pairs of symbols are shown, one pair at a time, and the participant picks one symbol from each pair. Feedback is 'correct' or 'incorrect' but is only probabilistic: in pair AB, A is correct 80 percent of the time; in CD, 70 percent; in EF, 60 percent. After training, all symbols are recombined into new pairs with no feedback, and choosing A (learned from wins) is compared with avoiding B (learned from losses).
variations.justification: Canonical Frank et al. learn-then-test with choose/avoid pairs

variations.name: Extended Training Versions
variations.description: More training trials are given, or training continues until the participant reaches a set accuracy on each pair, so that everyone is fully trained before the test phase.
variations.justification: More training trials; tests asymptotic learning

variations.name: 4-Pair Version
variations.description: A fourth pair of symbols with its own reward probability is added to the three standard pairs, giving more test combinations and more reliable scores for each participant.
variations.justification: Additional stimulus pairs; larger choice set

variations.name: Gain-Only and Loss-Only Variants
variations.description: In some blocks the feedback is winning money or nothing; in others it is losing money or nothing. This separates learning from rewards from learning from punishments more directly than the standard 'correct' and 'incorrect' feedback.
variations.justification: Separate gain vs. loss feedback conditions; isolates approach vs. avoidance learning

variations.name: PST with Volatility
variations.description: The probabilities attached to the symbols change partway through training, so the participant must notice the change and adjust which symbol they prefer.
variations.justification: Contingencies shift over time; tests learning in non-stationary environment

families.rationale: Learn stimulus pairs from probabilistic feedback

short_definition: Two tasks presented with a short SOA; RT for the second task lengthens as SOA shortens, indexing a central response-selection bottleneck.
description: Two stimuli are presented in rapid succession (S1 then S2, separated by a variable stimulus onset asynchrony or SOA), each requiring its own speeded response (R1 and R2). The robust finding is that R2 is slowed as the SOA decreases - the psychological refractory period effect - because central response-selection processes for S2 must wait until response selection for S1 is complete. Pashler (1994) provided the definitive review establishing the central bottleneck model: perceptual processing and motor execution can overlap between tasks, but response selection (choosing which response to make) represents a serial bottleneck. The PRP paradigm remains the primary tool for mapping the architecture of cognitive processing stages and understanding the limits of multitasking.

procedure: Two stimuli requiring separate speeded responses are presented in rapid succession with a variable stimulus-onset asynchrony (SOA).
Both responses are required.
manipulations: SOA between S1 and S2 (50-1000 ms)
measurements: RT2 as a function of SOA (PRP effect: RT2 slowing at short SOAs)
Locus of interference per bottleneck models

variations.name: Standard Auditory-Visual PRP
variations.description: On each trial a tone sounds and, a short and variable time later, a letter or digit appears. The participant responds to the tone (for example high or low pitch, with one hand) and then to the visual item (with the other hand). The shorter the gap between them, the slower the second response.
variations.justification: Canonical PRP: auditory then visual stimulus with variable SOA

variations.name: Visual-Visual PRP
variations.description: Both stimuli are visual, shown at different positions so they can be told apart, for example a colored patch followed by a letter. Tests whether the slowing of the second response depends on using two senses.
variations.justification: Both stimuli visual; tests modality effects on bottleneck

variations.name: Variable SOA Design
variations.description: The gap between the first and second stimulus is varied across a wide range, from about 50 ms up to a second, so that the second response time can be plotted against the gap.
variations.justification: Multiple SOAs parametrically varied; standard PRP SOA manipulation

variations.name: PRP with Practice
variations.description: Participants perform thousands of trials across several sessions, to see whether the slowing of the second response shrinks or disappears with extensive practice.
variations.justification: Extended practice changes PRP magnitude; tests dual-task automatization

variations.name: PRP with Ideomotor-Compatible Tasks
variations.description: The tasks are chosen so the response naturally matches the stimulus, such as saying 'A' when hearing 'A' or pressing a key under a finger that is touched. Such tasks produce little or no slowing of the second response.
variations.justification: Ideomotor-compatible S-R mappings eliminate bottleneck; tests structural bottleneck theory

variations.name: Triple-Task PRP
variations.description: Three stimuli are presented in quick succession, each needing its own response, to test how the slowing builds up when more than two tasks overlap.
variations.justification: Three concurrent tasks; extends bottleneck theory to three tasks

families.rationale: Dual-task response-selection bottleneck; no dual-task family exists yet

short_definition: Simple reaction to visual or auditory stimuli appearing at random intervals over 5-10 minutes; mean RT, lapses, and false starts index sustained attention.
description: The Psychomotor Vigilance Task is a sustained-attention reaction time task widely used in sleep research and fatigue monitoring. Participants monitor a display and respond as quickly as possible to a visual stimulus (typically a millisecond counter) that appears at random inter-stimulus intervals (2-10 seconds) over a 5-10 minute period. The primary measure is the number of lapses (responses >500 ms), reflecting momentary failures of sustained attention. The PVT is considered the gold-standard behavioral measure of vigilance and sleepiness because it is simple, has minimal learning effects, and is highly sensitive to sleep deprivation, circadian misalignment, and time-on-task.

procedure: A visual stimulus (counter or light) appears at random intervals (2-10 s).
Participants press a button as quickly as possible upon detection.
The task runs for 10 minutes.

variations.name: Standard 10-Minute PVT
variations.description: For ten minutes the participant watches a screen and presses a button as fast as possible whenever a counter or light appears, which happens at random intervals of two to ten seconds. Responses slower than 500 ms are counted as lapses and presses before the stimulus as false starts.
variations.justification: Canonical 10-min RT task with variable ISI

variations.name: Brief PVT (PVT-B)
variations.description: A three-minute version with shorter waits between stimuli (one to four seconds) and a lapse threshold of 355 ms, designed for repeated testing when ten minutes is too long.
variations.justification: 3-min version; recognized published abbreviated instrument

variations.name: Palm PVT / Mobile PVT
variations.description: The task runs on a handheld device or smartphone, with a tap on the screen as the response, so it can be used outside the laboratory, for example in sleep studies at home or in the field.
variations.justification: Handheld or mobile device; different motor and environmental context

variations.name: Auditory PVT
variations.description: The stimulus is a tone through headphones rather than a visual signal, and the participant presses the button as soon as the tone is heard. Usable with eyes closed or in darkness.
variations.justification: Auditory tone instead of visual stimulus; different sensory modality

families.rationale: Simple reactions to unpredictable stimuli over minutes

short_definition: Virtual multi-arm maze in which participants retrieve rewards from each arm once; working-memory and reference-memory errors index spatial memory.
description: The Virtual Radial Arm Maze is a spatial memory task adapted from the rodent paradigm. Participants navigate a central platform connected to 8 (or more) radial arms, some of which contain rewards. They must visit all rewarded arms while avoiding revisits (working memory errors) and unbaited arms (reference memory errors). The task dissociates reference memory (knowing which arms are baited across trials) from working memory (remembering which arms have been visited within a trial). Virtual versions rendered on computer screens or in VR maintain the spatial navigation demands while enabling human testing with precise measurement. The task engages hippocampal spatial memory systems and has been used extensively in pharmacological and developmental research.

procedure: In a virtual radial arm maze (typically 8 arms radiating from a center), some arms are baited with reward.
Participants visit arms to collect rewards, using spatial cues to remember which arms have been visited.
measurements: Working memory errors (re-entering already-visited baited arms)

variations.name: Standard 8-Arm Radial Maze
variations.description: The participant stands at the center of a virtual maze with eight corridors radiating outward, each with a reward at the far end. They visit arms to collect rewards; once an arm has been visited its reward is gone. Returning to an already emptied arm is a working-memory error.
variations.justification: Canonical 8-arm maze with bait at end of each arm

variations.name: Partially Baited Maze (4 of 8)
variations.description: Only four of the eight arms ever contain rewards, and it is always the same four across trials. Entering a never-rewarded arm is a reference-memory error (failing to learn the fixed rule), while re-entering an arm already emptied on this trial is a working-memory error.
variations.justification: Only subset of arms baited; tests working memory for visited arms

variations.name: 12-Arm or 16-Arm Versions
variations.description: The maze has twelve or sixteen arms instead of eight, so more locations have to be kept in mind before the trial is complete.
variations.justification: Increased arm number; higher memory load

variations.name: Virtual Reality (Immersive VR)
variations.description: The maze is presented in a head-mounted display that updates with the participant's head and body movement, so they turn and look around as they would in a real maze.
variations.justification: Head-mounted display VR; full immersive spatial navigation

variations.name: Desktop Virtual Maze
variations.description: The maze is shown on an ordinary monitor from a first-person viewpoint and the participant moves with a keyboard, mouse or joystick.
variations.justification: Screen-based navigation; different motor control

variations.name: Maze with Landmarks
variations.description: Distinctive objects or pictures are placed around the maze, either on the walls of the room (far landmarks) or within the arms (near landmarks), so that arms can be told apart and remembered by what is near them.
variations.justification: Salient landmarks aid navigation; tests landmark use

variations.name: Cue-Removed Conditions
variations.description: After learning with landmarks, the landmarks are removed or the maze is rotated so that landmarks no longer help. The participant must rely on remembering their own movements.
variations.justification: Landmarks removed mid-experiment; tests spatial memory without cues

variations.name: Delay Variants
variations.description: After visiting some of the arms, the participant is held at the center or taken out of the maze for a delay of minutes before being allowed to finish, so that the visited arms must be remembered across the delay.
variations.justification: Delay between choices tests retention

variations.name: Probabilistic Reward Maze
variations.description: Each arm pays off only some of the time rather than always, so the participant must learn which arms are most often rewarded instead of simply avoiding arms already visited.
variations.justification: Arms probabilistically rather than deterministically rewarded

families.rationale: Visit rewarded arms without repetition

short_definition: A field of moving dots in which a variable fraction move coherently; direction judgments and RT under varying coherence support drift-diffusion modeling of perceptual decisions.
description: The random dot kinematogram presents a field of moving dots in which a variable proportion move coherently in one direction while the remainder move randomly. Participants judge the direction of coherent motion, and the proportion of coherently moving dots parametrically controls task difficulty. This paradigm is the foundational tool for studying perceptual decision-making and has been central to establishing the neural basis of evidence accumulation, linking single-neuron recordings in area MT/V5 and LIP to drift-diffusion models of choice. It bridges sensory processing and decision-making in a way no other paradigm does as cleanly.

procedure: A field of moving dots is displayed.
a proportion move coherently in one direction while the rest move randomly.
Participants judge the direction of coherent motion.
measurements: Accuracy and RT as functions of coherence
Drift rate and threshold parameters from diffusion model fits

variations.name: Two-Alternative Forced Choice (Standard)
variations.description: A patch of moving dots is shown in which some fraction move together to the left or right while the rest move randomly. The participant reports the direction of the coherent motion with a key press or eye movement. The fraction of coherent dots sets the difficulty.
variations.justification: Canonical 2AFC motion direction discrimination

variations.name: Free Response vs. Interrogation Protocol
variations.description: In the free-response version the dots keep moving until the participant answers, so they can take as long as they want. In the interrogation version the dots are shown for a fixed time chosen by the experimenter and the participant then answers.
variations.justification: Self-paced vs. fixed-duration decision; different temporal control

variations.name: Pulse Paradigm
variations.description: Most of the display has zero or low coherence, and a brief burst of coherent motion of about 100 ms is inserted at a chosen moment. How much that burst sways the final decision shows when evidence is being weighed.
variations.justification: Brief coherence pulses instead of sustained motion; different stimulus structure

variations.name: Multi-Alternative Motion Discrimination
variations.description: The coherent motion can be in one of four or more directions rather than just left or right, and the participant indicates which, for example by moving the eyes to one of several targets.
variations.justification: More than two motion directions; higher-order discrimination

families.rationale: Motion direction judgment under varying coherence
