short_definition: Matrix completion items requiring induction of a rule from a 3x3 array of figures; items correct is a standard measure of non-verbal reasoning.
description: Participants view a matrix pattern with a missing element and select the correct completion from a set of alternatives. The patterns involve systematic variations in features such as shape, size, color, orientation, and number, governed by rules that increase in complexity across test items. Solving each item requires extracting the governing rules and applying them to predict the missing element. Raven's Progressive Matrices is the most widely used culture-reduced measure of fluid intelligence (Gf) and abstract relational reasoning, and is among the most extensively studied psychometric instruments in all of psychology. It has been central to debates about the neural basis of general intelligence, g-loading, and the structure of reasoning.

procedure: Participants view a 3x3 matrix of geometric patterns with one cell missing and select the pattern that completes the matrix from a set of alternatives.
manipulations: Number of relational rules to integrate
Rule types (distribution of values, quantitative progression, figure addition)
measurements: Number correct (raw score, often converted to IQ-scale)

variations.name: Standard Progressive Matrices (SPM)
variations.description: Sixty items, each a grid of abstract patterns with one cell missing. The participant chooses the piece that completes the pattern from six or eight options. Items are arranged in five sets that get harder. The score is the number correct.
variations.justification: Canonical general ability measure

variations.name: Advanced Progressive Matrices (APM)
variations.description: A set of 36 harder matrix items intended for adults of above-average ability, so that the test still distinguishes people at the top of the range.
variations.justification: Harder item set for higher ability; different item difficulty range

variations.name: Colored Progressive Matrices (CPM)
variations.description: An easier 36-item set with colored backgrounds, designed for young children, older adults and people with impairments. The first items are simple pattern completion.
variations.justification: Colored figures, simpler items for children/elderly; different stimulus format

variations.name: Computerized Adaptive Version
variations.description: Items are presented on a computer, and which item comes next is chosen from the participant's answers so far, giving harder items after correct answers and easier ones after errors. Fewer items are needed for a precise score.
variations.justification: Per section 5.6: adaptive algorithm changes which items presented; procedural change beyond interface

variations.name: Matrix Reasoning (WAIS subtest)
variations.description: The matrix reasoning subtest of the Wechsler intelligence scales, with 26 items of the same kind administered as part of the full scale, with its own norms.
variations.justification: Standardized 26-item version with WAIS norms; named published instrument

variations.name: Sandia Matrices
variations.description: A freely available set of matrix items generated by software so that the number and type of rules in each item are known and controlled, allowing new items of chosen difficulty to be made for experiments.
variations.justification: Open-source item set with verified psychometrics; distinct published test

variations.name: Time-Limited vs. Untimed Administration
variations.description: The test is given either with a strict overall time limit (such as 20 minutes) or with as much time as the participant wants. Under time pressure the score depends partly on speed rather than only on reasoning ability.
variations.justification: Time pressure changes response strategy and performance profile

variations.name: Shortened Versions (15-Item)
variations.description: A selection of 15 items from the full test chosen to give a reasonable estimate of the full score in a few minutes, used when a quick screen is needed.
variations.justification: Abbreviated protocols validated for efficiency; recognized published short form

canonical_name: Reading the Mind in the Eyes Task
aliases: Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test
short_definition: Choice of the best-matching mental-state word for a photograph of the eye region; accuracy indexes complex emotion and mental-state inference.
description: Participants view photographs showing only the eye and eyebrow region of actors and select which of four mental state descriptors best describes the person's thoughts or feelings. The revised version contains 36 photographs, each with four choices ranging from basic emotions to complex cognitive states (e.g., "sarcastic," "despondent"). The task indexes affective theory of mind and shows deficits in autism spectrum conditions. Performance correlates with amygdala and left inferior frontal gyrus activity.

procedure: Participants view photographs of the eye region of faces and select the mental state (from four word options) that best describes what the person is thinking or feeling.

variations.name: RMET Revised (36 items)
variations.description: Thirty-six black-and-white photographs of just the eye region of a face are shown one at a time, each with four mental-state words (such as 'nervous', 'playful', 'hostile', 'reflective'). The participant picks the word that best describes what the person is thinking or feeling. A glossary of the words is available.
variations.justification: Canonical Baron-Cohen RMET with 36-item set

variations.name: RMET Short Form (15-18 items)
variations.description: A subset of 15 to 18 of the items selected to give a score that correlates well with the full version in about half the time.
variations.justification: Abbreviated form; recognized efficient version

variations.name: RMET Child Version
variations.description: A 28-item version for children in which the word choices are simpler (such as 'kind', 'cross', 'bored') and the photographs are chosen to suit a younger audience.
variations.justification: Simplified vocabulary and reduced items for children; adapted per section 5.3

variations.name: Dynamic Eyes Task
variations.description: Short video clips of the eye region in motion replace the still photographs, so that blinks, gaze shifts and changes in the eyes are available as cues.
variations.justification: Moving eyes instead of static photographs; different stimulus type

variations.name: Full-Face vs. Eyes-Only
variations.description: The same mental-state choices are made for whole faces in one condition and for the eye region alone in another, to see how much is lost when only the eyes are visible.
variations.justification: Full face context vs. isolated eyes region; different stimulus scope

short_definition: Classify recognition hits as 'remember' (vivid recollection) or 'know' (familiarity without context); proportions index the relative contributions of recollection and familiarity to recognition memory.
description: During a recognition memory test, participants classify each item they judge as "old" according to the subjective quality of their memory: "remember" if they can recollect specific contextual details from the encoding episode (e.g., what they were thinking, where the item appeared), or "know" if the item feels familiar but retrieval of contextual details fails. Tulving (1985) introduced this distinction to operationalize the difference between episodic recollection and noetic familiarity. The paradigm has become the primary behavioral tool for dual-process theories of recognition memory and has been extensively validated with neuroimaging, revealing dissociable hippocampal (recollection) and perirhinal (familiarity) contributions.

procedure: During a recognition memory test, participants first judge each item as old or new, then classify old responses as 'remember' (vivid recollection of encoding context) or 'know' (familiarity without recollection).
measurements: Proportion remember and know responses for hits and false alarms
Estimates of recollection and familiarity (dual-process model parameters)

variations.name: Standard Remember/Know
variations.description: After studying a list, the participant sees old and new items. For each item they call old, they then say whether they 'remember' it, meaning they can recollect something specific about seeing it (what they thought, what came before), or just 'know' it was there without any such detail.
variations.justification: Canonical R/K: recollection vs. familiarity distinction

variations.name: Remember/Know/Guess (RKG)
variations.description: A third option, 'guess', is added for items called old without either recollection or a feeling of familiarity, so that 'know' responses are not contaminated by guesses.
variations.justification: Third Guess category added; different response scale

variations.name: Remember/Know with Source Memory
variations.description: After the remember or know judgment, the participant is asked a question about the study context of the item, such as which list it was in or which voice spoke it, to check whether 'remember' responses really come with retrievable detail.
variations.justification: Source judgment added to R/K; adds contextual memory component

variations.name: Associative Remember/Know
variations.description: Items are studied as pairs, and at test the participant judges pairs as intact or rearranged and gives remember or know judgments for the pairing, measuring recollection of the link between items.
variations.justification: R/K for associative pairs; tests recollection of binding

families.rationale: Recognition with a remember or know judgment

short_definition: Three cue words linked to a single fourth word; solution rate and solution time index semantic search and insight.
description: The Remote Associates Test measures creative thinking through convergent semantic association. On each trial, participants are given three seemingly unrelated words (e.g., "cottage," "Swiss," "cake") and must find a single word that connects all three (answer: "cheese"). The task requires searching semantic memory broadly, suppressing dominant but incorrect associations, and recognizing the linking concept. RAT performance correlates with measures of creativity, insight problem-solving, and divergent thinking. The task has also been used to study the "Aha!" moment - the subjective experience of sudden insight - and its neural correlates in the right anterior superior temporal gyrus.

procedure: Three seemingly unrelated words are presented (e.g., PINE, CRAB, SAUCE).
Participants find a single word that forms a compound or common phrase with each (APPLE).
manipulations: Item difficulty (associative strength of solution to each cue)
measurements: Solution probability as a function of associative strength

variations.name: Standard RAT (Mednick)
variations.description: Each item gives three words, such as 'cottage, swiss, cake', and the participant must find a fourth word that goes with all three ('cheese'). Thirty items are given with a time limit of 15 to 40 seconds each, and the number solved and time to solve are recorded.
variations.justification: Canonical three-word compound remote associate task

variations.name: Compound RAT (CRAT)
variations.description: The items are restricted to those where the answer forms a compound word or common phrase with each of the three cue words (cottage cheese, swiss cheese, cheesecake), rather than being related by meaning alone. The normed set by Bowden and Jung-Beeman is the usual source.
variations.justification: Compound word solutions instead of single words; different solution structure

variations.name: Timed vs. Untimed RAT
variations.description: Items are given either with a strict time limit per item or with no limit, sometimes with a break before unsolved items are retried, to study whether solutions arrive after a pause.
variations.justification: Time pressure changes solving strategy

variations.name: RAT with Hint/Priming
variations.description: Before or during an item, the answer or a related word is shown, either briefly and masked so it is not consciously seen, or openly as a hint. The effect on solving is measured.
variations.justification: Semantic prime precedes problem; changes solution accessibility

families.rationale: Insight problem solving over words; could be filed under language

short_definition: After initial stimulus-reward learning, the contingencies switch; perseveration and reversal speed index behavioral flexibility.
description: Participants learn a stimulus-outcome association (e.g., stimulus A is rewarded, B is not), then contingencies are reversed. Participants must flexibly adapt their behavior to the new associations. Performance measures include trials to criterion and perseverative errors (continued selection of the previously rewarded stimulus). The task can use deterministic or probabilistic contingencies. Neuroimaging consistently implicates the orbitofrontal cortex and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex in reversal learning, particularly for updating stimulus-outcome associations based on feedback.

procedure: Participants learn to choose the rewarded stimulus over an unrewarded one.
After reaching criterion, contingencies reverse - the previously correct stimulus becomes incorrect and vice versa.
measurements: Errors to criterion on initial discrimination and on reversals
Perseverative errors (continuing to choose previously correct stimulus)

variations.name: Deterministic Reversal
variations.description: Two stimuli are shown and the participant picks one. One is always rewarded and the other never. Once the participant reliably picks the rewarded one, the assignment is switched without warning, and the participant must learn to pick the other.
variations.justification: Contingency fully reverses; canonical reversal learning

variations.name: Probabilistic Reversal
variations.description: The better stimulus is rewarded only most of the time (for example 80 percent) and the worse one sometimes. The participant must decide whether a non-reward is just bad luck or a sign that the rule has switched.
variations.justification: Stochastic contingency reversal; different uncertainty structure

variations.name: Serial Reversal
variations.description: The assignment is switched several times within the session, each time after the participant has adapted. Later reversals are usually handled faster than the first.
variations.justification: Multiple reversals in sequence; tests reversal learning rate

variations.name: Stimulus-Outcome vs. Action-Outcome Reversal
variations.description: In one version the rewarded thing is a particular stimulus wherever it appears; in the other it is a particular response (such as the left key) whatever stimulus is shown. The reversal switches the stimulus rule or the response rule.
variations.justification: Reversal of stimulus or action contingency; different associative structure

variations.name: Multi-Dimensional Reversal
variations.description: The stimuli differ in several features (such as shape, color and position) and only one feature predicts reward. A reversal can switch which value of that feature is rewarded, or switch to a different feature altogether.
variations.justification: Reversal involves change in relevant stimulus dimension; more complex

variations.name: Reward vs. Punishment Reversal
variations.description: Feedback is winning versus not winning in some blocks and losing versus not losing in others, so that the speed of adapting after a reversal can be compared for reward-based and punishment-based learning.
variations.justification: Valence manipulation changes learning signal

families.rationale: Learned contingencies switch

short_definition: Repeated presentation of a 15-word list with immediate free recall over five trials, an interference list, and delayed recall; indexes verbal learning and forgetting.
description: The RAVLT is a comprehensive measure of verbal episodic memory. A list of 15 unrelated words (List A) is read aloud five times, with free recall tested after each presentation, yielding a learning curve. After the fifth trial, an interference list (List B) is presented once and recalled, followed by immediate recall of List A without re-presentation (retroactive interference). After a 20-30 minute delay, delayed recall and recognition of List A are tested. The RAVLT provides a rich profile of memory processes including acquisition rate, learning plateau, susceptibility to interference, retention over delay, and recognition discrimination.

procedure: A 15-word list (List A) is read aloud five times with free recall after each.
A single interference list (List B) is then read once and recalled.
Immediate and delayed recall of List A follow, plus a recognition test.

variations.name: Standard RAVLT (List A * 5 + List B + Recall + Delayed Recall)
variations.description: A list of 15 unrelated words is read aloud and the participant recalls as many as possible, five times in a row. A second 15-word list is then read and recalled once. The participant then recalls the first list again without hearing it, and once more after a delay of 20 to 30 minutes.
variations.justification: Canonical multi-trial verbal learning with interference and delayed recall

variations.name: Recognition Trial
variations.description: After the delayed recall, the participant hears or reads a longer list containing the first-list words mixed with second-list words and new words, and says yes or no to each. Separates failure to retrieve from failure to store.
variations.justification: Target list embedded in foil words for recognition test; different retrieval task

variations.name: Shortened RAVLT
variations.description: Fewer learning trials (such as three instead of five) or a shorter word list, for participants who tire easily or when testing time is limited.
variations.justification: Fewer study trials; recognized abbreviated protocol

variations.name: Proactive Interference Paradigm
variations.description: The order is rearranged so that the second list is learned first, and the effect of that earlier learning on recall of the main list is measured, rather than the usual effect of the interference list on recall of what came before.
variations.justification: List B interference on List A recall; tests proactive interference effects

variations.name: Cued Recall Addition
variations.description: After free recall, the participant is given category hints for words not recalled (for example 'one was a kind of animal'). Words produced with a hint were stored but could not be retrieved unaided.
variations.justification: Category cues added to recall phase; tests cueing benefit on verbal learning

families.rationale: Repeated list learning with delayed recall

short_definition: Lexical or semantic decision on targets preceded by semantically related or unrelated primes; RT facilitation indexes automatic semantic activation.
description: Word pairs are presented in sequence: a prime word followed by a target. Prime-target relationships are manipulated (semantically related, unrelated, or neutral). Participants typically make lexical decisions on the target. Semantic priming is measured as faster RT to related versus unrelated pairs, reflecting automatic spreading activation through semantic memory networks. SOA manipulation distinguishes automatic (short SOA) from strategic (long SOA) priming.

procedure: A prime word is followed by a target word.
Participants make a lexical decision or naming response to the target.
Prime-target pairs are semantically related or unrelated.
manipulations: SOA (short for automatic priming, long for strategic)
measurements: N400 ERP amplitude reduction for related pairs

variations.name: Short SOA (< 250 ms)
variations.description: The prime word is followed by the target word within a quarter of a second, too soon for the participant to form an expectation about what the target will be. Faster responses to related targets reflect automatic activation of related meanings.
variations.justification: Brief prime-target interval; automatic spreading activation

variations.name: Long SOA (> 500 ms)
variations.description: Half a second or more passes between prime and target, giving the participant time to anticipate likely targets. Priming can then include deliberate expectation as well as automatic activation.
variations.justification: Long interval; strategic processing contributes

variations.name: Masked Priming
variations.description: The prime is shown for about 50 ms between masking patterns so it is not consciously seen, and the target follows immediately. Priming that survives masking is taken to be automatic.
variations.justification: Prime below awareness; unconscious semantic activation

variations.name: Relatedness Proportion Manipulation
variations.description: The share of trials on which prime and target are related is set high (such as 75 percent) in one condition and low (25 percent) in another. When related pairs are common, participants use the prime to predict the target and priming is larger.
variations.justification: Varies proportion of related pairs; changes strategic context

variations.name: Semantic Relation Types
variations.description: The prime and target are related in different ways on different trials: by association (bread - butter), by category (cat - dog), by situation (broom - floor) or by function (hammer - nail). Priming is compared across relation types.
variations.justification: Taxonomic vs. thematic vs. associative relations; different prime-target relationships

variations.name: Mediated Priming
variations.description: The prime and target are not directly related but share a common link, for example 'lion' and 'stripes' through 'tiger'. Priming between them shows that activation spreads beyond immediate associates.
variations.justification: Prime activates mediator that activates target; tests spread of activation

variations.name: Cross-Modal Priming
variations.description: The prime is spoken through headphones and the target is written on the screen, or vice versa, so that priming must cross from one sense to the other.
variations.justification: Auditory prime + visual target; cross-modal semantic activation

variations.name: Sentence Context Priming
variations.description: The prime is a sentence frame rather than a single word, and the target word either fits the sentence or does not. Measures how a whole context prepares the reader for a word.
variations.justification: Sentence prime instead of single word; higher-level context

variations.name: Picture-Word Priming
variations.description: The prime is a picture and the target a word (or the reverse), so that the relationship is in meaning rather than in the words themselves.
variations.justification: Picture prime for word target; conceptual rather than lexical priming

variations.name: Morphological Priming
variations.description: The prime and target share a word stem, such as 'teach' and 'teacher', or a prefix. Priming from shared structure is compared with priming from shared meaning or shared spelling to see whether words are broken into parts during reading.
variations.justification: Morphologically related prime; tests morphological representation

variations.name: Phonological Priming
variations.description: The prime and target sound alike, for example they rhyme (cat - hat) or share a first sound (cat - cup), without being related in meaning. Measures the role of sound in recognizing words.
variations.justification: Phonologically similar prime; tests phonological overlap effects

variations.name: Orthographic Priming
variations.description: The prime and target share letters but nothing else, for example 'corner' and 'corn'. Usually a control condition for morphological priming, showing how much priming comes from spelling overlap alone.
variations.justification: Orthographically similar prime; tests spelling overlap effects

families.rationale: Lexical decision with related or unrelated primes

short_definition: Reading or listening to locally ambiguous sentences; reading-time disruptions and offline comprehension indexes syntactic reanalysis.
description: Participants read sentences containing temporary syntactic ambiguities (garden-path sentences) that initially lead to an incorrect parse before disambiguating information forces reanalysis. Classic example: "The horse raced past the barn fell." Sentences may be presented word-by-word (self-paced reading) or while eye movements are tracked. Comprehension is assessed via subsequent questions. Neuroimaging reveals left inferior frontal and temporal activation during syntactic reanalysis. The task probes how the parser uses syntactic, semantic, and probabilistic cues in real-time language processing.

procedure: Participants read sentences word-by-word or in regions.
Some sentences contain temporary syntactic ambiguities that lead the reader down a wrong parse (garden path) before disambiguation.
manipulations: Ambiguity type (main verb/reduced relative, NP/S, etc.)
measurements: Reading time at disambiguating region (self-paced reading, eye tracking)

variations.name: Self-Paced Reading (Word-by-Word)
variations.description: A sentence is revealed one word at a time, each key press showing the next word. The time spent on each word is recorded, and longer times at a particular word show where the reader had difficulty.
variations.justification: Canonical sentence processing paradigm with reading time measure

variations.name: Eye-Tracking Reading
variations.description: The whole sentence is shown at once and an eye tracker records where the reader looks. Measures include how long the eyes first rest on a word, how often they go back to earlier words, and total time on each region.
variations.justification: Natural reading with eye-tracking; different response modality and richer time course

variations.name: Main Verb/Reduced Relative Ambiguity
variations.description: Sentences like 'The horse raced past the barn fell', where 'raced' is first read as the main verb and must be reinterpreted as a description of the horse when 'fell' arrives. Reading slows at the point where the first reading breaks down.
variations.justification: Syntactic ambiguity at main verb/relative clause; canonical garden path structure

variations.name: PP-Attachment Ambiguity
variations.description: Sentences like 'Put the book on the table in the box', where 'on the table' could say where to put the book or which book is meant. The ambiguity is resolved later in the sentence.
variations.justification: Prepositional phrase attachment ambiguity; different syntactic decision point

variations.name: NP/S Ambiguity
variations.description: Sentences like 'The doctor told the patient that he was having trouble with...', where 'that...' could be a description of the patient or the thing that was told. Readers slow when the less expected reading turns out to be correct.
variations.justification: Noun phrase vs. sentence ambiguity; different structural ambiguity type

variations.name: Temporarily Ambiguous vs. Unambiguous Controls
variations.description: Each ambiguous sentence is paired with a version that says the same thing without the ambiguity (for example 'The horse that was raced past the barn fell'). The reading-time difference between them isolates the cost of the misreading.
variations.justification: Matched unambiguous controls; tests processing cost of ambiguity

variations.name: Speed-Accuracy Tradeoff (SAT) Studies
variations.description: The participant must judge whether each sentence is acceptable at a signal that comes at one of several delays after the sentence ends, from very early to late. Plotting accuracy against the delay shows how quickly an interpretation becomes available.
variations.justification: Response deadline method; different temporal measurement approach

families.rationale: Read or hear syntactically ambiguous sentences

short_definition: Sequential key-press responses to cued locations; RT speedup on repeating vs random sequences indexes implicit sequence learning.
description: The SRTT measures implicit motor sequence learning. Visual stimuli appear sequentially at different spatial locations, each corresponding to a response button. Participants respond as quickly as possible, unaware that stimuli follow a repeating sequence interspersed with random blocks. Learning is inferred from decreasing RT for the repeating sequence relative to random sequences. The dissociation between improved performance and lack of conscious awareness of the sequence structure is a hallmark of implicit learning and provides evidence for procedural memory systems.

procedure: Stimuli appear at one of several spatial locations in a repeating (but covert) sequence.
Participants respond to each location with a spatially mapped keypress.
Sequence awareness is typically not disclosed.
measurements: RT slowing when sequence is replaced by random order (sequence learning effect)

variations.name: Deterministic SRTT
variations.description: A marker appears at one of four positions and the participant presses the matching key. Unknown to the participant, the positions follow a fixed repeating sequence of about ten to twelve items. Responses speed up over blocks and slow down when a random block is inserted.
variations.justification: Fixed repeating sequence; canonical implicit sequence learning

variations.name: Probabilistic SRTT
variations.description: Instead of a fixed sequence, each position is followed by a particular next position most of the time but not always, so the structure is statistical. Faster responses to the likely transitions show learning.
variations.justification: High-probability sequence structure; tests learning under uncertainty

variations.name: Alternating Serial Reaction Time (ASRT)
variations.description: Fixed-sequence positions alternate with random positions (pattern, random, pattern, random...), so the regularity can only be picked up over every other item. Learning shows as faster responses to the predictable items.
variations.justification: Alternating random and patterned elements; tests learning of alternating structure

variations.name: SRTT with Awareness Assessment
variations.description: After the main task the participant is asked whether they noticed a sequence, asked to reproduce it, or shown fragments to recognize, to find out how much of the learning was conscious.
variations.justification: Explicit sequence knowledge probed after implicit learning; adds awareness component

variations.name: Second-Order Conditional (SOC) Sequences
variations.description: The sequence is built so that no single position predicts the next; only the last two positions together do. This prevents learning simple pair associations and requires sensitivity to longer runs.
variations.justification: Each response depends on two preceding; different sequence order

variations.name: Arm-Reaching/Foot-Stepping SRTT
variations.description: The responses are reaches to targets on a table or steps onto floor pads rather than finger presses, to test whether the learned sequence depends on which body part performs it.
variations.justification: Full-limb movements instead of finger presses; different motor effector

variations.name: Cross-Modal SRTT
variations.description: The cues are sounds (for example tones of four pitches, each mapped to a key) instead of visual positions, or the modality switches between learning and test.
variations.justification: Auditory sequence instead of visual; different sensory modality

families.rationale: Implicit sequence learning through key presses; could be filed under motor performance

short_definition: Non-spatial feature (e.g. color) dictates a left/right response while task-irrelevant stimulus location varies; RT cost on incongruent trials indexes spatial response conflict.
description: The Simon Task measures the effect of spatial stimulus-response correspondence on performance. Participants respond to a non-spatial stimulus attribute (e.g., color: press left for red, right for blue) while the stimulus appears on either the left or right side of the screen. When stimulus location corresponds with the assigned response side (congruent), responses are faster and more accurate than when they do not correspond (incongruent). The Simon effect reflects automatic activation of a spatially corresponding response that must be overridden when incongruent. The task is a foundational paradigm for studying stimulus-response compatibility and dimensional overlap.

procedure: Stimuli varying on a non-spatial attribute (color, shape) appear on the left or right.
Participants respond with spatially mapped keys.
On incongruent trials, stimulus location conflicts with response location.
manipulations: Spatial congruency (stimulus side matches or conflicts with response side)
measurements: Delta-plot analysis of time-course of interference

variations.name: Visual Simon Task (Standard)
variations.description: A colored shape appears to the left or right of center, and the participant presses a left key for one color and a right key for the other. Position is irrelevant, but responses are slower when the stimulus appears on the side opposite the required key.
variations.justification: Canonical: respond to color/shape despite irrelevant spatial position

variations.name: Auditory Simon Task
variations.description: A tone is played to the left or right ear and the participant presses a key based on its pitch. Responses are slower when the required key is on the opposite side from the ear that heard the tone.
variations.justification: Auditory stimulus location as irrelevant dimension; different sensory modality

variations.name: Vertical Simon Task
variations.description: The stimulus appears above or below center and the response keys are arranged one above the other, so the conflict is between up-down position and up-down response.
variations.justification: Vertical rather than horizontal spatial dimension; different axis of conflict

variations.name: Simon Task with Accessory Stimuli
variations.description: An irrelevant tone is played at the same time as the visual stimulus, from the same or opposite side, or centrally, to study how an extra event affects the position conflict.
variations.justification: Non-response-relevant accessory stimulus added; tests alerting-compatibility interaction

variations.name: Reversed Simon Task
variations.description: The participant is told to press the key opposite to where the stimulus appears, or practices such a mapping, before the standard task. This can reverse the usual effect.
variations.justification: Stimulus-response mapping reversed; opposite compatibility mapping

variations.name: Joint Simon Task
variations.description: Two people sit side by side and each is responsible for one response key and one color, so each has a simple go/no-go task. The position conflict reappears for each person as if they were doing the whole task alone.
variations.justification: Two participants share one Simon task; tests social simulation of co-actor's response

variations.name: Hybrid Simon-Flanker Task
variations.description: The lateral stimulus is also surrounded by flanker items that match or conflict with it, so that position conflict and flanker conflict are present in the same trial.
variations.justification: Integrates flanker conflict with Simon conflict; combined interference paradigm

variations.name: Emotional Simon Task
variations.description: The stimuli are emotional faces or words shown to the left or right, with the response based on their emotion, or the response keys are labeled with positive and negative meanings so that the irrelevant emotional content can conflict with the response.
variations.justification: Emotional content as irrelevant dimension; retained per section 5.1 (EMOT retired)

variations.name: Mouse-Tracking Simon
variations.description: The participant responds by moving a mouse to a target in the upper left or right of the screen, and the whole path of the cursor is recorded. Curvature toward the wrong side shows the pull of the stimulus position.
variations.justification: Continuous mouse trajectory as response; different response modality

variations.name: Simon with Proportion-Congruent Manipulation
variations.description: The share of trials on which position and response agree is varied between blocks, for example mostly agreeing in one block and mostly conflicting in another, to see how the effect changes when conflict is expected.
variations.justification: Varies conflict frequency; adaptation context manipulation per section 5.2

families.rationale: Irrelevant location conflicts with response side

short_definition: MID variant in which cues predict potential social (smiling/frowning face) rather than monetary outcomes; indexes social reward anticipation.
description: The Social Incentive Delay Task is a variant of the Monetary Incentive Delay Task (Task 63) that replaces monetary outcomes with social rewards and punishments. Cues signal the potential for positive social feedback (e.g., a smiling face with a thumbs-up), negative social feedback (e.g., a frowning face with a thumbs-down), or neutral outcomes. Participants then respond to a target stimulus, and outcome delivery depends on response speed. The SID was developed to compare the neural substrates of social versus non-social reward anticipation and consumption, testing whether social rewards engage the same striatal dopaminergic circuitry as monetary rewards. The task has been particularly impactful in autism spectrum disorder research, where reduced social reward sensitivity is hypothesized.

procedure: Cues signal potential social reward (smiling face), social non-reward (neutral face), or control (geometric shape).
After a delay, participants respond to a target.
Outcome is contingent on response speed.
manipulations: Cue type (social reward, social non-reward, non-social control)
measurements: Comparison of social vs. monetary reward anticipation signals

variations.name: Standard SID (Smiling Face Reward)
variations.description: A cue signals whether a fast enough response to the coming target will earn a smiling face with approving words, avoid an angry face, or produce nothing. The participant presses a button when the target flashes, and the face feedback follows.
variations.justification: Canonical SID with face as social incentive

variations.name: SID with Personalized Social Stimuli
variations.description: The faces used as rewards are of people the participant knows, such as friends or family, photographed in advance, rather than strangers.
variations.justification: Stimuli customized to individual's social network; different stimulus content

variations.name: SID vs. MID within-Subjects
variations.description: The participant performs both the social version and the monetary version in the same session, with the cues indicating which kind of reward is at stake, so the two kinds of anticipation can be compared directly.
variations.justification: Both social and monetary incentives in same session; direct contrast paradigm

variations.name: SID with Graded Social Reward
variations.description: The cues signal different intensities of social reward, such as a faint smile versus a broad smile with strong praise, to see whether anticipation scales with the size of the social reward.
variations.justification: Multiple social reward magnitudes; tests social reward sensitivity

variations.name: SID with Real Social Interaction
variations.description: The social reward is delivered by a real person, for example an experimenter or confederate who smiles and praises the participant through a video link, rather than by a stored photograph.
variations.justification: Actual social partner rather than photograph; different social context

families.rationale: Incentive delay with social outcomes

short_definition: Short memory set followed by a probe; yes/no judgment of set membership. RT typically scales linearly with set size.
description: The Sternberg task measures the speed of short-term memory scanning. On each trial, participants encode a brief study list of 1-6 items, then after a retention interval, judge whether a test probe was in the studied list. The critical finding is that RT increases linearly with memory set size for both positive and negative probes, suggesting serial exhaustive scanning. The slope of the RT-by-set-size function indexes memory scanning speed, while the intercept indexes stimulus encoding and response execution time.

procedure: Participants memorize a small set of items (1-6 digits or letters), then a probe appears and they indicate whether it was in the memory set.
manipulations: Varied vs. fixed set across trials
measurements: RT as a function of set size (slope = scanning rate, ~38 ms/item)

variations.name: Visual Sternberg
variations.description: A small set of letters or digits (one to six items) is shown, followed by a short delay and then a single probe item. The participant presses one key if the probe was in the set and another if not. Response time grows with the number of items in the set.
variations.justification: Canonical memory set presented visually; recognition probe after delay

variations.name: Auditory Sternberg
variations.description: The memory set and probe are spoken through headphones rather than displayed, and the participant decides whether the spoken probe was among the spoken set.
variations.justification: Auditory memory set; different sensory modality

variations.name: Cross-Modal Sternberg
variations.description: The set is presented in one modality and the probe in another, for example letters shown on screen and a spoken probe, so the match must be made on identity rather than on how the item looked or sounded.
variations.justification: Study in one modality, test in another; cross-modal recognition

variations.name: Sternberg with Irrelevant Items
variations.description: The set includes items marked as not to be remembered, or extra items are shown during the delay, and the probe sometimes matches one of these. Slower rejection of such probes shows the irrelevant items still interfere.
variations.justification: Distractors added during retention; tests interference resistance

variations.name: Recent-Probes Sternberg
variations.description: Some probes that are not in the current set were in the set on the previous trial. Rejecting these familiar-but-wrong probes takes longer, which measures interference from recent memory.
variations.justification: Probes match previous trials; tests proactive interference

families.rationale: Memory set followed by a membership probe

short_definition: Choice RT task in which an occasional stop signal requires response cancellation; stop-signal reaction time (SSRT) estimates inhibitory latency.
description: The Stop-Signal Task measures the ability to inhibit a prepotent motor response after it has been initiated. Participants perform a primary go task (button press to go signals) but on a subset of trials, a stop signal (auditory tone or visual cue) appears after a variable delay (stop-signal delay, SSD), instructing them to cancel their response. SSD is adjusted dynamically using a staircase procedure converging on 50% inhibition probability. The key measure is stop-signal reaction time (SSRT), estimated using the race model framework, which indexes the latency of the internal inhibitory process.

procedure: On most trials, participants make a speeded response to a go stimulus.
On a minority of trials, a stop signal (tone or visual cue) appears after the go stimulus, instructing them to withhold their response.
measurements: Stop-signal reaction time (SSRT, estimated via race model)
Probability of stopping at each SSD

variations.name: Standard SST with Staircase SSD
variations.description: The participant makes a quick left-or-right choice to each stimulus. On about a quarter of trials a beep or visual signal follows the stimulus and the participant must try not to respond. The delay before the signal is increased after successful stops and decreased after failures so that stopping succeeds about half the time, which allows the stopping speed to be estimated.
variations.justification: Canonical adaptive stop-signal delay tracking

variations.name: Fixed SSD Procedure
variations.description: The stop signal comes at a few preset delays after the stimulus (for example 100, 200, 300 and 400 ms) rather than being adjusted to the participant. Stopping success is plotted against delay.
variations.justification: Non-adaptive fixed delays; different trial structure

variations.name: Stop-Change Task
variations.description: Instead of simply withholding, the participant must cancel the planned response and make a different one, for example pressing a third key, when the signal occurs.
variations.justification: Stop signal replaced by change signal; different inhibition-and-substitute

variations.name: Selective Stop-Signal
variations.description: Only one of the signals, or one of the responses, requires stopping. For example, a high tone means stop but a low tone means carry on, or stopping is needed only for left-hand responses. The participant must identify the signal before deciding whether to stop.
variations.justification: Stop signal applies to one response type only; selective inhibition

variations.name: Proactive vs. Reactive Inhibition Manipulation
variations.description: A cue or block instruction tells the participant how likely a stop signal is on coming trials (for example none, some, or many). Responses slow when stopping is likely, which shows the participant preparing to stop before any signal appears.
variations.justification: Pre-signal preparatory inhibition vs. post-signal reactive; different inhibition timing

variations.name: Stop-Signal in Reaching/Saccade Tasks
variations.description: The response to be stopped is an arm reach to a target or an eye movement to a target rather than a key press, and movement or eye position is recorded to see whether the action was cancelled.
variations.justification: Arm reaching or eye movement response; different motor effector

variations.name: Context-Dependent Stop-Signal
variations.description: Features of the display or environment, such as a background color, are associated with different stop-signal probabilities, and the participant learns to adjust their readiness to stop from these features.
variations.justification: Stop signal context varies; tests context-sensitive inhibition

variations.name: Conditional Stop-Signal
variations.description: A stop signal always appears, but stopping is required only when it has a particular property, such as a specific color, and otherwise the response should go ahead.
variations.justification: Inhibit only under specific conditions; conditional stopping logic

families.rationale: Cancel an initiated response on a stop signal

short_definition: Naming the ink color of color words while ignoring word meaning; RT and error costs on incongruent trials index selective attention and conflict control.
description: The Stroop Color-Word Task is a classic measure of selective attention and cognitive control that requires participants to identify the ink color of printed words while ignoring the semantic content. In the standard version, participants view color names (e.g., "RED," "BLUE") printed in incongruent ink colors and must respond with the ink color rather than reading the word. The task measures reaction time and accuracy across congruent trials (word and color match), incongruent trials (word and color conflict), and neutral trials. Performance reflects the ability to overcome automatic word-reading processes and requires engagement of executive control mechanisms. The Stroop interference effect (slowed RT on incongruent trials) is one of the most robust findings in cognitive psychology.

procedure: Color words (RED, BLUE) are printed in incongruent ink colors.
Participants name the ink color while ignoring the word.

variations.name: Classic Color-Word Stroop
variations.description: Color words are printed in colored ink, for example RED printed in blue, and the participant names the ink color while ignoring the word. Naming is slower and more error-prone when the word and the ink disagree than when they agree or the item is a neutral string.
variations.justification: Canonical color naming of congruent/incongruent color words

variations.name: Manual (Button-Press) Stroop
variations.description: The participant presses one of several keys, one per ink color, instead of saying the color aloud. Common in brain imaging where speaking would cause head movement.
variations.justification: Button press instead of vocal response; different response modality

variations.name: Vocal Response Stroop
variations.description: The participant says the ink color aloud, as in the original task, and voice onset is recorded with a microphone. Interference is larger than with key presses because reading and color naming both use speech.
variations.justification: Vocal naming; distinct from manual version

variations.name: Counting Stroop
variations.description: A number word is printed one to four times (for example 'two' printed three times) and the participant reports how many words there are, ignoring what the word says. Neutral items use animal names.
variations.justification: Count number of words instead of naming color; different task dimension

variations.name: Spatial Stroop
variations.description: A direction word (such as LEFT or ABOVE) or an arrow appears at a position on the screen, and the participant reports either the word's meaning or its position while ignoring the other.
variations.justification: Spatial word/location conflict; different conflict dimension

variations.name: Numerical Stroop
variations.description: Two digits are shown in different physical sizes, and the participant chooses the one that is numerically larger (ignoring size) or physically larger (ignoring value). Responses slow when the larger number is printed smaller.
variations.justification: Number magnitude vs. physical size conflict; different domain

variations.name: Reverse Stroop
variations.description: The participant reads the word and ignores the ink color. Interference from the ink is usually small, but it appears when the response is made by pointing to a color patch rather than speaking.
variations.justification: Name the word rather than the color; reversed task demand

variations.name: Proportion-Congruent Manipulation
variations.description: The share of trials on which word and ink agree is varied between blocks or between particular words, for example mostly agreeing in one block and mostly conflicting in another. Interference is smaller when conflict is expected.
variations.justification: Conflict frequency variation; adaptation context per section 5.2

variations.name: Face-Word Stroop
variations.description: A face with an emotional expression has an emotion word written across it. The participant names the expression while ignoring the word, and responses slow when the word names a different emotion.
variations.justification: Face emotion vs. color word conflict; different stimulus domain

variations.name: Color-Shape Stroop
variations.description: Objects with a strongly associated color are shown in the wrong color, such as a blue banana, and the participant names the displayed color while the known color of the object interferes.
variations.justification: Color word/shape conflict instead of ink color; different conflict structure

variations.name: Priming Stroop
variations.description: Each color-word item is preceded by a prime, such as a word or cue that is neutral, matches or conflicts with the coming item, to study how advance information changes the interference.
variations.justification: Prime precedes Stroop item; temporal context manipulation

variations.name: Negative Priming Stroop
variations.description: Trials are arranged so that the word to be ignored on one trial is the ink color to be named on the next (for example RED in green, then any word in red). Naming the previously ignored color is slower, which shows it was suppressed.
variations.justification: Previously ignored item becomes target; tests ignored repetition effect

families.rationale: Canonical interference task

short_definition: Speeded responses to frequent non-targets with withholding on rare targets; commission errors and RT variability index sustained attention lapses.
description: The Sustained Attention to Response Task is a Go/No-Go variant specifically designed to measure sustained attention failures and mind-wandering. Participants respond (button press) to every digit presented (1-9) except for one designated target digit (typically "3"), to which they must withhold their response. Digits are presented at a fixed rate (e.g., every 1150 ms), and the high frequency of Go responses (89%) creates a monotonous, routinized response pattern that promotes attentional lapses. Errors of commission (responding to the No-Go target) serve as the primary index of attention failure. The SART has become the standard behavioral measure for studying mind-wandering, task-unrelated thought, and attentional lapses.

procedure: Single digits (1-9) are presented one at a time.
Participants respond to every digit except a designated target (typically 3).
The high go-probability induces a prepotent response tendency.
measurements: Commission errors (responses to the no-go target)

variations.name: Standard SART (Fixed Sequence)
variations.description: The digits 1 to 9 appear one at a time, about one per second, repeatedly in order. The participant presses a key for every digit except 3, to which they must withhold. Because the sequence is predictable, lapses of attention show up as presses to 3.
variations.justification: Canonical: respond to digits except 3; fixed pseudo-random sequence

variations.name: Random SART
variations.description: The digits appear in random order rather than counting up, so the participant cannot predict when the no-go digit will come. Fewer errors are made than in the fixed version.
variations.justification: Random digit order; removes sequential predictability

variations.name: SART with Thought Probes
variations.description: At unpredictable points the task pauses and asks the participant what they were just thinking about, for example whether they were focused on the task or thinking of something else. Reports are linked to performance just before the probe.
variations.justification: Mind-wandering probes inserted; adds metacognitive reporting

variations.name: Perceptual SART
variations.description: The items are shapes, colors or lines of different orientation instead of digits, with one of them as the rare withhold item, for participants for whom digits are unsuitable.
variations.justification: Perceptual variants (lines, shapes); different stimulus type

variations.name: Sustained Attention Task with Response Switching
variations.description: The rule for which key to press changes periodically during the task, so the participant must keep track of the current rule as well as watch for the withhold item.
variations.justification: Response switches during task; adds rule-change demand

variations.name: SART with Multiple Targets
variations.description: Two or more digits are withhold items rather than only the 3, which changes how often the participant must stop and how many rules must be kept in mind.
variations.justification: Multiple no-go digits instead of one; different inhibition load

variations.name: Sustained Attention with Clock Task
variations.description: The participant watches a clock hand that moves in regular jumps and presses a key when it occasionally makes a double jump. The task continues for a long period and misses increase over time.
variations.justification: Clock face rather than digit sequence; different stimulus format

variations.name: Child-Adapted SART
variations.description: Pictures of animals or objects replace the digits, with one picture as the withhold item, and the pace is slowed to suit children.
variations.justification: Modified timing and stimuli for children; adapted per section 5.3

families.rationale: Go/no-go structure with rare withhold targets; also a vigilance measure
Thought probes inserted in the stream sample mind wandering

short_definition: Alternation between two or more simple tasks on cue; switch-cost RT and errors index task-set reconfiguration.
description: Task Switching paradigms measure cognitive flexibility by requiring participants to alternate between two or more classification tasks. Participants view stimuli (e.g., bivalent alphanumeric characters like "G3") and perform different classifications depending on a task cue (letter: vowel/consonant; digit: odd/even). Tasks alternate in predictable sequences (e.g., AABB) or are cued on each trial. The primary measures are switch costs (increased RT and errors when switching tasks vs. repeating the same task) and mixing costs (increased RT in mixed-task blocks vs. single-task blocks). Switch costs reflect the time for task-set reconfiguration.

procedure: Participants alternate between two (or more) simple tasks on the same stimuli, cued by an explicit cue or a predictable alternation schedule.
measurements: Switch cost (switch - repeat RT and accuracy)
Preparation effect (switch cost reduction with longer CSI)

variations.name: Cued Task-Switching
variations.description: Each trial starts with a cue, such as a word or a colored frame, telling the participant which of two tasks to do on the coming stimulus (for example, judge a digit as odd or even, or as bigger or smaller than 5). Responses are slower when the task differs from the previous trial.
variations.justification: Canonical cue specifies task each trial

variations.name: Alternating Runs (AABB)
variations.description: No cue is given; instead the tasks alternate in a fixed pattern, usually two trials of one then two of the other, often with the stimulus moving around a grid to mark position in the pattern. The participant must keep track of where they are.
variations.justification: Predictable alternation without explicit cue; different task structure

variations.name: Voluntary Task Switching
variations.description: The participant decides on each trial which task to perform, with the instruction to do both about equally often in a random order. The choice is read from which response keys are used. How often people choose to switch is measured as well as the cost.
variations.justification: Participant chooses task; measures voluntary switching rates

variations.name: Mixing Cost Paradigm
variations.description: Blocks in which only one task is done are compared with blocks in which the two tasks are mixed. Even trials in the mixed blocks that repeat the task are slower than single-task trials, a cost of keeping both tasks ready.
variations.justification: Compares mixed-block to pure-block performance; different block structure

variations.name: Cue-Stimulus Interval (CSI) Manipulation
variations.description: The time between the cue and the stimulus is varied, from almost none to a second or more. Longer preparation time reduces the switch cost but does not remove it.
variations.justification: Varies preparation time; tests proactive preparation

variations.name: Response-Stimulus Interval (RSI) Manipulation
variations.description: The time between one trial's response and the next trial's stimulus is varied, without changing the preparation time, to see how the previous task's influence fades on its own.
variations.justification: Varies post-response interval; tests backward inhibition decay

variations.name: Task Switching with N>2 Tasks
variations.description: Three or more tasks are cued. Returning to a task that was done two trials ago (A-B-A) is slower than coming to a task not done recently (C-B-A), which shows that a task is inhibited when it is abandoned.
variations.justification: Three or more tasks; different reconfiguration demands

variations.name: Univalent vs. Bivalent Stimuli
variations.description: Stimuli either allow only one of the tasks (for example letters for a letter task, digits for a digit task) or allow both (a letter and a digit together). Switch costs are larger when the stimulus could be used for either task.
variations.justification: Stimuli compatible with one vs. both tasks; different interference structure

variations.name: Predictable vs. Random Task Sequences
variations.description: The order of tasks is either known in advance (a fixed alternation) or random with a cue, to see how much knowing what comes next helps preparation.
variations.justification: Known vs. unknown switch sequence; tests preparation strategies

variations.name: Task Switching with Conflict
variations.description: The stimuli are also designed to create response conflict, for example a Stroop or flanker item, so that the cost of switching tasks and the cost of resolving conflict can be studied together.
variations.justification: Bivalent stimuli with competing responses; combined switching and conflict

families.rationale: Alternate between tasks on cue

short_definition: Cue words are presented with instructions to either retrieve or suppress their learned associate; later memory for suppressed items indexes retrieval-induced forgetting through inhibition.
description: Participants first learn cue-target word pairs (e.g., "ordeal-roach"). In the critical phase, cues are presented and participants are instructed either to recall the target (Think) or to prevent the target from coming to mind (No-Think). On a final test, suppressed (No-Think) items show reduced recall relative to baseline items that were learned but not presented during the critical phase. Anderson and Green (2001) introduced this paradigm as a memory analog of the Go/No-Go motor inhibition task, arguing that just as people can stop a motor action, they can suppress retrieval of unwanted memories. The paradigm has become central to research on memory suppression, PTSD, and the role of prefrontal control over hippocampal memory retrieval.

procedure: Participants learn cue-target word pairs to criterion.
In the critical phase, cues are presented and participants either actively recall the target (think) or suppress retrieval (no-think).
A final test probes all pairs.
manipulations: Think vs. no-think vs. baseline (not presented in critical phase)
Independent probe test (IP: novel cue for same target)
measurements: IP test (demonstrates inhibitory vs. associative interference account)

variations.name: Standard Think/No-Think (TNT)
variations.description: The participant learns word pairs until they can give the second word for each first word. Then first words are shown in green (recall and think of the partner) or red (look at the word but keep the partner out of mind) many times. Finally all first words are given and the participant recalls every partner. Partners that were repeatedly kept out of mind are recalled less well than untrained pairs.
variations.justification: Canonical Anderson & Green: cue-directed recall suppression

variations.name: Independent Probe Test
variations.description: In the final test, instead of the learned first word, a new cue is given, such as a category plus a first letter ('insect R___' for 'roach'). If suppressed words are still harder to recall from a new cue, the memory itself has been weakened, not just the link from the trained cue.
variations.justification: Test with novel cues not seen in TNT phase; isolates suppression from retrieval practice

variations.name: TNT with Intrusion Reporting
variations.description: After each suppress trial the participant reports whether the partner word came to mind anyway. The share of trials with intrusions falls across repetitions, tracking how suppression improves.
variations.justification: Participant signals intrusions during no-think; adds metacognitive monitoring report

variations.name: Emotional TNT
variations.description: The items to be suppressed are negative or trauma-related, such as unpleasant words or pairs of faces with disturbing scenes, to test whether distressing memories can be suppressed.
variations.justification: Emotional paired associates; retained per section 5.1 (EMOT retired)

variations.name: TNT with Thought Substitution
variations.description: Instead of blocking the partner word directly, the participant is given a different word to think about whenever the red cue appears. Compares two strategies for keeping a memory out of mind.
variations.justification: Replace suppressed thought with substitute; different suppression strategy

variations.name: Dose-Response TNT
variations.description: Different pairs are given different numbers of suppress trials (such as 0, 2, 4, 8, 12 or 16), and final recall is plotted against the number of suppressions.
variations.justification: Varies number of suppression repetitions; tests suppression as function of dose

families.rationale: Retrieve or suppress an associate on cue

short_definition: Rearrange colored beads on pegs to match a goal state in the minimum number of moves; pre-execution latency and move efficiency index planning.
description: The Tower of London Task is a planning and problem-solving task. Participants are presented with two configurations of colored beads on pegs: a start state and a goal state. They must plan and execute a sequence of moves to transform the start state into the goal state in the minimum number of moves, following movement constraints (one bead at a time, peg capacity limits). Problem difficulty is manipulated by the minimum number of moves required (2-7). Performance is measured by moves to solution, planning time, and accuracy. The task is a key measure of prefrontal executive function, particularly planning and look-ahead.

procedure: Three pegs hold colored discs in a start configuration.
Participants move discs one at a time to reach a goal configuration in the minimum number of moves.
measurements: Number of problems solved in minimum moves

variations.name: Standard Tower of London (3 pegs, 3 balls)
variations.description: Three colored balls sit on three pegs of different heights (holding one, two and three balls). The participant is shown a goal arrangement and must move the balls one at a time to reach it in the fewest moves, usually with the minimum number stated. Problems need two to seven moves.
variations.justification: Canonical Shallice ToL: rearrange colored balls across pegs

variations.name: Tower of Hanoi
variations.description: A related puzzle with disks of different sizes on three pegs. All disks must be moved to another peg, one at a time, without ever placing a larger disk on a smaller one. More moves are needed and the rule about sizes must be kept in mind.
variations.justification: Different rule structure (disk size constraint); distinct classic puzzle

variations.name: Tower of London - Drexel (TOL-DX)
variations.description: A standardized clinical version with ten problems of increasing difficulty, fixed administration rules, and norms for scoring the number of moves, planning time and rule violations.
variations.justification: Standardized 10-item version with normative data; published clinical instrument

variations.name: Tower of London - Freiburg (TOL-F)
variations.description: A computerized version whose problems are selected to control features that affect difficulty, such as the number of moves and whether intermediate steps are obvious, for research use.
variations.justification: Computer version with different item set and constraints

variations.name: Computerized vs. Physical Versions
variations.description: The balls and pegs are shown on a screen and moved by dragging or clicking, rather than being real objects picked up by hand. Move times are recorded precisely but no physical handling is involved.
variations.justification: Per section 5.6: grasping 3D beads vs. drag-and-drop changes motor activity

variations.name: Tower with Time Pressure
variations.description: A time limit is set for each problem, or the participant is told to be fast, so that the trade-off between planning carefully and acting quickly can be studied.
variations.justification: Response deadline imposed; changes planning strategy

families.rationale: Plan a sequence of moves to a goal state

short_definition: Paper-and-pencil sequencing: connect numbered circles (Part A) or alternate numbers and letters (Part B) as fast as possible. B-A difference indexes set switching.
description: The Trail Making Test is a widely used neuropsychological assessment consisting of two parts. In Part A, participants draw lines connecting consecutively numbered circles (1->2->3->...) as quickly as possible, measuring visual scanning and psychomotor speed. In Part B, participants alternate between numbers and letters (1->A->2->B->3->C->...), adding demands for cognitive flexibility and task-switching. The derived score (B-A) isolates the switching cost from baseline motor and visual search speed. The TMT is among the most sensitive measures of general brain dysfunction and is included in virtually every neuropsychological test battery. Digital tablet versions now capture rich kinematic data (velocity, pressure, pauses).

procedure: Participants connect numbered circles in order (Part A: 1-2-3...) or alternate between numbers and letters (Part B: 1-A-2-B-3-C...), drawing lines as quickly as possible.
measurements: Completion time for Part A and Part B

variations.name: TMT-A (Number Sequencing)
variations.description: Twenty-five numbered circles are scattered on a page, and the participant draws a line from 1 to 2 to 3 and so on as fast as possible without lifting the pencil. Time to finish is the score.
variations.justification: Canonical: connect numbers in order; processing speed measure

variations.name: TMT-B (Number-Letter Alternation)
variations.description: The circles contain both numbers and letters, and the participant connects them alternating between the two sequences: 1, A, 2, B, 3, C and so on. The extra time compared with the number-only version measures switching.
variations.justification: Alternating numbers and letters; adds cognitive flexibility demand

variations.name: Oral Trail Making Test
variations.description: The participant says the alternating sequence aloud (1, A, 2, B...) without any page, so that drawing and visual search are not needed. For people who cannot write or see well.
variations.justification: Verbal response instead of pencil tracing; different response modality

variations.name: Color Trails Test
variations.description: The letters are replaced by a second set of numbers in a different color, and the participant alternates between pink and yellow circles (1 pink, 2 yellow, 3 pink...). Usable in any language.
variations.justification: Color-coded circles instead of letters; tests same construct in different format

variations.name: Comprehensive Trail Making Test (CTMT)
variations.description: A published battery of five trail-making subtests of increasing difficulty, adding distractor circles and switching between numbers and number words, with norms.
variations.justification: Extended standardized version with additional subtests; named published instrument

variations.name: D-KEFS Trail Making
variations.description: The trail-making test from the Delis-Kaplan Executive Function System, with five conditions: scanning for a target, number sequencing, letter sequencing, number-letter switching and a motor speed condition, so that switching can be separated from the other components.
variations.justification: Delis-Kaplan version with additional conditions; named published instrument

families.rationale: Part B alternates sequences; Part A is a speeded motor task

short_definition: Two-stage exchange in which an investor transfers a fraction of an endowment (multiplied on receipt), and a trustee returns some fraction; amounts transferred index trust and reciprocity.
description: A sequential two-player game in which the investor decides how much of an endowment to send to the trustee; the sent amount is multiplied (typically 3x), and the trustee decides how much to return. The investor faces a dilemma: trusting yields potentially higher mutual payoffs but risks exploitation. fMRI reveals that trust decisions engage theory-of-mind regions (medial PFC, temporoparietal junction) and reward regions (ventral striatum) that track mutual cooperation and reciprocity.

procedure: An investor receives an endowment and chooses how much to send to a trustee.
The amount is multiplied (typically tripled).
The trustee decides how much to return to the investor.

variations.name: Standard Two-Stage Trust Game
variations.description: The first player (investor) is given money and chooses how much to send to a second player (trustee). The sent amount is tripled. The trustee then decides how much of the tripled amount to send back. The investor's transfer measures trust and the trustee's return measures trustworthiness.
variations.justification: Canonical Berg et al.: investor sends, trustee returns

variations.name: One-Shot vs. Repeated
variations.description: The exchange happens either once with a stranger or repeatedly with the same partner over several rounds, so that partners can build or lose trust based on earlier rounds.
variations.justification: Single vs. multiple rounds; repeated play enables reputation building

variations.name: Multiplier Variation
variations.description: The amount sent is doubled, tripled or quadrupled, which changes how much there is to gain from trusting and how much the trustee could return.
variations.justification: Different multiplication factors; changes investment incentive

variations.name: Trust Game with Reputation
variations.description: Before deciding how much to send, the investor is shown the trustee's record of returns in earlier games with other people.
variations.justification: Trustee reputation history visible; changes available social information

variations.name: Partner Selection Trust Game
variations.description: The investor first chooses which of several possible trustees to play with, based on information about them, and then plays the usual game with that person.
variations.justification: Participant selects partner before trust game; adds partner choice

variations.name: Anonymous vs. Face-to-Face
variations.description: Players either never see or learn anything about each other, or meet, see a photograph, or interact over video before playing, so the effect of knowing who the partner is can be measured.
variations.justification: Social identification manipulation changes accountability

variations.name: Social Identity Manipulation
variations.description: The investor is told that the trustee belongs to the same group as them (such as the same university, nationality or team) or to a different group, and transfers to in-group and out-group partners are compared.
variations.justification: In-group vs. out-group trustee; tests trust as function of group membership

families.rationale: Investment returned at the partner's discretion

short_definition: Sequential two-choice task with probabilistic transitions to second-stage states and drifting rewards; choice patterns dissociate model-based from model-free control.
description: Participants make two sequential choices per trial. The first-stage choice leads (with fixed transition probabilities - 70% common, 30% rare) to one of two second-stage states, each containing its own pair of options. Second-stage options yield rewards with slowly drifting probabilities. Daw et al. (2011) designed this task to dissociate model-based reinforcement learning (using knowledge of the transition structure to plan) from model-free reinforcement learning (repeating previously rewarded actions regardless of transition type). The diagnostic signature is the interaction between reward and transition type on subsequent first-stage choices: model-based agents show opposite stay/switch patterns after common vs. rare transitions, while model-free agents show the same pattern regardless of transition type.

procedure: First stage: choose between two options that lead probabilistically (70/30) to one of two second-stage choice sets.
Second stage: choose between two options with drifting reward probabilities.
This separates model-based from model-free learning.
measurements: Stay probability as a function of previous trial outcome x transition type
Computational model fits (hybrid MB/MF learning rates, mixing weight)

variations.name: Standard Daw et al. (2011) Version
variations.description: The participant chooses one of two symbols. Each symbol usually (70 percent) leads to one of two second-stage pairs and sometimes (30 percent) to the other. In the second stage they choose again and may win a reward, with each option's reward probability drifting slowly over the session. Whether the participant's next first-stage choice depends on the transition that occurred shows whether they are using a model of the task.
variations.justification: Canonical two-step Markov decision task; measures model-based vs. model-free

variations.name: Shortened/Simplified Versions
variations.description: Fewer trials, fewer options or a story (for example spaceships and planets) that makes the transition structure easier to understand, for use with children or patients.
variations.justification: Fewer trials or simplified state structure; recognized efficient version

variations.name: Enhanced Model-Based Version
variations.description: The task is extended with more stages or more states, or rewards that make planning more worthwhile, so that using a model of the structure makes a bigger difference to earnings.
variations.justification: Design features that enhance model-based learning; different incentive structure

variations.name: Devaluation Manipulation
variations.description: After learning, the participant is told that the reward in one second-stage state is now worthless or has changed value. Whether their first-stage choices adjust immediately shows whether they are planning rather than repeating what worked.
variations.justification: Reward devalued after training; tests habitual vs. goal-directed control

variations.name: Two-Stage with Instructed Knowledge
variations.description: The participant is taught the transition probabilities explicitly before starting, instead of having to discover them from experience, to see whether explicit knowledge increases planned choice.
variations.justification: Transition structure explicitly taught; tests instructed vs. learned model

families.rationale: Two-step choice dissociating model-based and model-free learning
