short_definition: Proposer offers a division of an endowment; responder accepts or rejects. Rejection of unfair offers indexes inequity aversion and strategic punishment.
description: Two players divide a sum of money. The proposer suggests a division; the responder accepts (both get the proposed split) or rejects (both get nothing). Typically played with computer-controlled offers varying from fair (50-50) to unfair (90-10). Unfair offers activate the anterior insula (negative emotion, inequity aversion) and are rejected at high rates, even at personal cost. The task demonstrates the interplay between emotional reactions and rational economic considerations in social decision-making.

procedure: A proposer splits a sum of money.
The responder can accept (both keep their shares) or reject (neither gets anything).
measurements: Rejection rate as function of offer
fMRI anterior insula activation to unfair offers

variations.name: Standard Ultimatum
variations.description: One player (the proposer) is given a sum and offers a split to a second player (the responder). If the responder accepts, both get the proposed amounts; if the responder rejects, neither gets anything. Responders typically reject offers much below a fair share even though rejecting costs them money.
variations.justification: Canonical: proposer offers split, responder accepts/rejects

variations.name: Strategy Method
variations.description: Instead of reacting to one actual offer, the responder states in advance the smallest offer they would accept, or gives an accept-or-reject answer for every possible offer. The proposer's actual offer is then matched against these answers.
variations.justification: Responder states acceptance threshold for all possible offers; different elicitation

variations.name: Multi-Round Ultimatum
variations.description: The same two players repeat the game over several rounds, possibly swapping roles, so that offers and rejections can respond to what happened in earlier rounds.
variations.justification: Repeated rounds; tests learning and adaptation

variations.name: Third-Party Punishment
variations.description: An observer who is not part of the split can spend some of their own money to reduce the proposer's earnings after seeing an unfair offer. Measures willingness to punish unfairness that does not affect oneself.
variations.justification: Observer can punish unfair proposer; adds external enforcement

variations.name: Proposer Competition
variations.description: Several proposers each make an offer to a single responder, who can accept at most one. Competition pushes offers toward more generous splits.
variations.justification: Multiple proposers compete for responder; changes market structure

variations.name: Asymmetric Information
variations.description: The responder does not know the size of the sum being divided, or the proposer does not know what the responder knows, so offers can be judged only on their absolute size.
variations.justification: Responder does not know pie size; different information structure

variations.name: Stake Variation
variations.description: The sum to be divided is varied from a dollar or two up to large amounts (sometimes a month's wages in low-income settings), to see whether rejection of unfair offers persists when the cost of rejecting is high.
variations.justification: Systematically varies total pie size; tests stake sensitivity

variations.name: Anonymous vs. Identified Partners
variations.description: Players either remain anonymous or learn who their partner is, see a photo, or meet them, which changes how accountable each feels for their choices.
variations.justification: Social identification changes accountability

variations.name: Ultimatum with Earned vs. Windfall Endowment
variations.description: Before the game the proposer either earns the sum by doing a task or is simply given it. Proposers who earned the money tend to offer less and responders tend to accept lower offers.
variations.justification: Endowment from effort vs. luck; changes perceived legitimacy

families.rationale: Accept or reject a proposed split

short_definition: Brief central identification combined with peripheral localization under increasing distractor and divided-attention load; thresholds index processing speed and divided attention.
description: The Useful Field of View test measures the visual field area over which information can be rapidly extracted without eye or head movements. It consists of three subtests of increasing complexity: (1) central target identification (processing speed), (2) central identification with simultaneous peripheral target localization (divided attention), and (3) the same dual-task with embedded distractors (selective attention). Each subtest uses a staircase procedure to determine the shortest display duration achieving 75% accuracy. The UFOV was originally developed for assessing driving fitness in older adults and has become the standard measure of functional visual attention, with strong predictive validity for crash risk, instrumental activities of daily living, and cognitive decline.

procedure: Three subtests of increasing demand: central target identification, divided attention (central + peripheral targets simultaneously), and selective attention (peripheral target among distractors).
measurements: Display duration threshold for 75% accuracy per subtest

variations.name: Subtest 1: Central Processing Speed
variations.description: A picture of a car or a truck is flashed in the center of the screen for a variable time and then masked, and the participant reports which it was. The shortest exposure at which they are reliably correct is the score.
variations.justification: Central target discrimination; measures processing speed component

variations.name: Subtest 2: Divided Attention
variations.description: While identifying the central car or truck, the participant must also report where a second car appeared at the edge of the display, which was shown at the same time. The exposure needed to do both is measured.
variations.justification: Central + peripheral target; divided attention component

variations.name: Subtest 3: Selective Attention
variations.description: As in the divided-attention subtest, but the display is filled with distracting triangles, so the peripheral car must be found among clutter while the central item is identified.
variations.justification: Peripheral target with distractors; selective attention component

variations.name: UFOV with Varying Eccentricities
variations.description: The peripheral target is placed at several distances from the center, and performance is measured at each to map how far out attention extends.
variations.justification: Peripheral target at different distances; tests eccentricity function

families.rationale: Peripheral target localization among distractors

short_definition: Produce a verb associated with each presented noun; indexes lexical-semantic retrieval and inhibition of prepotent responses, with well-known left-prefrontal activation.
description: The Verb Generation Task is a semantic retrieval and language production paradigm. Participants see or hear a concrete noun (e.g., "hammer") and must generate an associated verb (e.g., "hit" or "pound"). The task requires accessing semantic knowledge, selecting among competing responses, and executing a language production response. It robustly activates left inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area) and anterior cingulate cortex, and is one of the most frequently used language tasks in neuroimaging. Performance is measured by response latency, accuracy, and the specificity/typicality of verb selections.

procedure: A concrete noun is presented (e.g., HAMMER).
Participants generate an associated verb (e.g., 'hit' or 'pound') as quickly as possible.
measurements: Competition effect (slower for nouns with many associates)

variations.name: Standard Overt Verb Generation
variations.description: A noun such as 'hammer' is shown or spoken, and the participant says aloud a verb that goes with it ('hit'). Response time and the verb produced are recorded.
variations.justification: Canonical Petersen et al.: say verb aloud in response to noun

variations.name: Covert Verb Generation
variations.description: The participant thinks of the verb without saying it, usually pressing a key when a verb has come to mind. Used in brain imaging to avoid movement from speaking.
variations.justification: Internal silent generation; different response mode

variations.name: High vs. Low Selection Demand
variations.description: Nouns are chosen so that some have one obvious verb (scissors - cut) and others have many equally likely verbs (ball - throw, kick, bounce). Choosing among many candidates takes longer and engages selection processes.
variations.justification: Dominant vs. non-dominant verb associations; tests selection difficulty

variations.name: Verb Generation with Practice
variations.description: The same nouns are presented repeatedly across blocks. Responses get faster and the brain activity associated with the task declines as the verb for each noun becomes automatic. A new noun list restores the effort.
variations.justification: Repeated generation reduces demand; tests automatization

variations.name: Noun Generation (Reverse)
variations.description: A verb is given and the participant produces a noun that goes with it ('cut' - 'paper'), used as a comparison for the standard direction.
variations.justification: Generate noun to verb cue; reversed direction

variations.name: Written Verb Generation
variations.description: The participant types or writes the verb instead of saying it, so that the response is a written word and no speech is involved.
variations.justification: Written response instead of vocal; different response modality

families.rationale: Generate a verb for a presented noun

short_definition: Navigate a virtual circular arena to find a hidden platform using distal spatial cues; latency and search patterns index allocentric spatial learning and navigation ability.
description: In the Virtual Morris Water Maze, participants navigate a virtual environment to find a hidden goal location using environmental landmarks. During acquisition, participants start from different positions and learn the goal location across trials; performance is indexed by path length, latency, and heading error. Probe trials (goal removed) assess retention by measuring search distribution. The task engages hippocampal spatial mapping and is highly sensitive to hippocampal dysfunction. It dissociates place-based (allocentric) from response-based (egocentric) navigation strategies.

procedure: Participants navigate a virtual circular arena to find a hidden platform using distal visual cues.
Across trials, they learn the platform's fixed spatial location.
manipulations: Probe trials (platform removed to assess spatial knowledge)
measurements: Path length and latency to reach the hidden platform
Probe trial time in target quadrant
Probe trial proximity to platform location

variations.name: Hidden Platform (Allocentric)
variations.description: The participant moves through a virtual circular pool using a joystick or keys, looking for a platform hidden below the surface. Pictures or objects on the surrounding walls are the only guide. They start from different points on each trial and must learn where the platform is relative to the landmarks.
variations.justification: Canonical allocentric navigation to hidden platform using distal cues

variations.name: Visible Platform (Cue-Based)
variations.description: The platform is marked with a visible flag or shown above the surface, so the participant can head straight for it without learning its position from the room. Serves as a control for moving and seeing.
variations.justification: Platform marked visibly; cue-based navigation without spatial learning

variations.name: Probe Trials
variations.description: After learning, the platform is removed without telling the participant and they search for a fixed time. The share of time spent in the quarter of the pool where the platform used to be measures memory for its location.
variations.justification: Platform removed; tests memory for trained location

variations.name: Reversal
variations.description: After the platform's location has been learned, it is moved to a new place, usually the opposite side, and the participant must stop going to the old place and find the new one.
variations.justification: Platform moved to opposite quadrant; tests behavioral flexibility

variations.name: Dual-Solution Design
variations.description: The pool is arranged so the platform can be found either by remembering its place relative to the room or by following a route or a nearby landmark. Later probe trials that separate the two cues reveal which strategy the participant used.
variations.justification: Landmark and allocentric routes both available; tests strategy preference

variations.name: Virtual Star Maze
variations.description: A maze of corridors radiating from a central area, or a simple Y or T shaped maze, replaces the open pool. The participant learns which arm leads to the goal, and a probe from a new start arm shows whether they learned a place or a turn.
variations.justification: Star-shaped corridors in VR; different maze geometry

variations.name: Path Integration Tasks
variations.description: The landmarks are removed or the scene goes dark after the participant has moved along a path, and they must return to the start or point to it using only their sense of how they moved.
variations.justification: Navigation without visual landmarks; dead reckoning demand

variations.name: Large-Scale Virtual Cities
variations.description: The environment is a virtual town or a game-like world with streets, buildings and multiple destinations, such as the Sea Hero Quest game, and the participant navigates to goals over longer distances.
variations.justification: City-scale environment; different scale and complexity

variations.name: Boundary-Based vs. Landmark-Based Navigation
variations.description: The environment provides either the shape of the enclosure (walls, boundaries) or discrete landmark objects, or both, and these are moved separately on test trials to see which the participant uses to find the goal.
variations.justification: Systematically varies cue type; tests geometric vs. landmark navigation

families.rationale: Find a hidden platform in a virtual pool

short_definition: A brief target is rendered invisible or reduced in visibility by a preceding or following mask; variants include metacontrast, paracontrast, pattern, forward, backward, common-onset, and object-substitution masking.
description: Participants attempt to detect or discriminate brief, near-threshold visual stimuli that are rendered difficult to see through low contrast, brief duration, or metacontrast masking (a spatially adjacent, temporally trailing mask that suppresses visibility of the target without overlapping it spatially). The key dependent variable is not only accuracy but the relationship between trial-by-trial detection success and prestimulus brain states - particularly the phase and power of ongoing alpha (~10 Hz) and theta (~7 Hz) oscillations recorded via EEG. This paradigm demonstrates that conscious visual perception is not a passive, deterministic process but is gated by rhythmic fluctuations in cortical excitability, supporting pulsed-inhibition and perceptual-sampling theories.

procedure: A brief target stimulus is rendered invisible or reduced in visibility by a temporally adjacent mask.
Participants detect, identify, or discriminate the target.
manipulations: Mask type (metacontrast, pattern, backward, forward, common-onset, object-substitution)
measurements: Target detection/identification accuracy or d-prime as a function of SOA (U-shaped or monotonic masking functions)

variations.name: Standard Metacontrast Masking
variations.description: A small shape (such as a disk) is flashed briefly, and after a short delay a ring that surrounds but does not touch its location is flashed. At delays of around 50 to 100 ms the disk becomes hard or impossible to see. The participant reports whether the disk was present or which shape it was.
variations.justification: Canonical metacontrast: annular mask suppresses disc

variations.name: Phosphene Detection at Threshold
variations.description: A faint flash of light at the edge of visibility is presented on a plain background with no mask, and the participant reports whether they saw it. Used to study the moment-to-moment state of the visual system without any masking.
variations.justification: TMS-evoked phosphenes measured at perceptual threshold

variations.name: TMS-Evoked Phosphene Detection
variations.description: A magnetic pulse applied to the back of the head produces a brief spot of light in the participant's vision, and they report whether they saw it. The pulse is timed relative to the phase of the participant's brain rhythms.
variations.justification: Visual cortex stimulation produces phosphene; different masking mechanism

variations.name: Object Substitution Masking
variations.description: The target appears among other items surrounded by four small dots. If the dots remain on screen after the target and the other items have disappeared, the target is hard to report, even though the dots never touch it.
variations.justification: Four-dot surround mask replaces object representation; different mechanism

variations.name: Pattern Masking at Threshold
variations.description: The mask is a dense pattern of lines, letters or random dots that covers the same location as the target, presented just before or after it. The target is reported at reduced visibility.
variations.justification: Pattern mask overlapping in space and time; different mask type

variations.name: Continuous Flash Suppression Threshold
variations.description: A rapidly changing colorful pattern is shown to one eye while a faint image is shown to the other. The flashing pattern dominates and the image stays invisible for seconds. The participant reports when the image finally breaks through or whether it was present.
variations.justification: Monocular suppression by rapidly alternating masks; binocular suppression paradigm

variations.name: Rhythmic Entrainment + Detection
variations.description: A regular series of flashes at a chosen rate is shown before the faint target, and whether the target is detected is measured as a function of when it falls relative to the rhythm.
variations.justification: Rhythmic stimulation before target; tests oscillatory effects on detection

variations.name: Masked Priming Variant
variations.description: The masked item is not reported at all. Instead it serves as a prime for a later visible target, and its effect on the response to that target shows that the masked item was processed.
variations.justification: Masked prime before target; tests subliminal priming via masking

variations.name: Backward Masking with Attentional Manipulation
variations.description: The masked target is embedded in a situation where attention is limited, such as a second task or a rapid stream of items, to see how attention changes what the mask hides.
variations.justification: Attention directed during masking; tests attentional modulation of masking

variations.name: Auditory Backward Masking
variations.description: A brief tone is followed by a burst of noise after a variable delay, and the participant reports whether the tone was heard. The sound version of the masking task.
variations.justification: Auditory masking paradigm; different sensory modality

families.rationale: Target visibility reduced by a mask

short_definition: Detection of a target in a display of distractors; search slopes across set size dissociate feature (parallel) from conjunction (serial) search.
description: Visual Search Tasks present participants with a display containing multiple items among which they must locate a target. In feature search, the target is defined by a single distinctive feature (e.g., a red item among blue) and "pops out" preattentively, with search time independent of set size. In conjunction search, the target is defined by a combination of features (e.g., a red square among red triangles and green squares) requiring serial, attention-dependent search with RT increasing linearly with set size. The task measures search efficiency, reaction time slopes, and accuracy, providing insights into parallel versus serial attentional processing.

procedure: An array of items is displayed.
Participants search for a target defined by a feature or feature conjunction among distractors and indicate its presence/absence or identity.
measurements: RT x set size slope (search efficiency)
Miss rate at low target prevalence

variations.name: Feature Search (Pop-Out)
variations.description: The participant looks for a target that differs from all the distractors in one simple feature, such as a red item among green ones, and reports whether it is present. The target stands out at once and search time does not increase with more distractors.
variations.justification: Canonical preattentive pop-out; target defined by single feature

variations.name: Conjunction Search
variations.description: The target shares one feature with some distractors and another with the rest, for example a red X among red Os and green Xs. The target does not stand out, and search time grows with the number of items.
variations.justification: Target defined by conjunction of features; requires serial search

variations.name: Spatial Configuration Search
variations.description: The target and distractors are made of the same parts in different arrangements, such as a T among rotated Ls. Each item has to be inspected, making this one of the slowest kinds of search.
variations.justification: Learned spatial configuration guides search; contextual cueing component

variations.name: Absent Trials and Target-Present/Absent Ratio
variations.description: The share of trials on which a target is actually present is varied, for example 50 percent in one block and 2 percent in another. When targets are rare, participants miss far more of them.
variations.justification: Systematically varies target presence probability; changes decision criteria

variations.name: Multiple-Target Search (Foraging)
variations.description: A display contains several targets, and the participant collects as many as they can, or decides when to stop and move to a new display. Finding one target makes further targets more likely to be missed.
variations.justification: Multiple targets per display; foraging paradigm with different decision structure

variations.name: Real-World/Naturalistic Search
variations.description: The participant searches for a named object in a photograph of a real scene, or in a 3D environment, rather than in an array of simple shapes.
variations.justification: Natural scenes as search arrays; different stimulus class and recognition demands

variations.name: Guided Search Variants
variations.description: Before the display, the participant is told or shown what the target looks like, or part of the display is shown in advance, so that knowledge of the target can guide attention to likely items.
variations.justification: Top-down feature guidance provides target template; changes attentional control

variations.name: Additional-Singleton Paradigm
variations.description: On some trials one distractor is given a highly salient but irrelevant feature, such as a unique color, while the participant searches for a target defined by shape. The salient distractor slows search by drawing attention.
variations.justification: Color singleton distractor captures attention; distinct capture paradigm

variations.name: Preview Search
variations.description: Half the distractors are shown first and the rest of the display, including the target, is added about a second later. Search is efficient among the new items only, as if the old ones were marked and ignored.
variations.justification: Subset of items previewed before search display; different temporal structure

variations.name: Adaptive Choice Visual Search
variations.description: Two targets are present, one defined by each of two colors, and the participant chooses which to search for. The numbers of each color change gradually, and whether the participant switches to the easier target measures how well they adjust their strategy.
variations.justification: Participant chooses between search types; tests cost-benefit of different strategies

variations.name: Hybrid Search (Visual + Memory)
variations.description: The participant memorizes a set of possible targets (from a few to a hundred) and then searches each display for any of them. Search time depends on both the number of items on screen and the number of targets in memory.
variations.justification: Memory set held while visual search proceeds; combined memory-search paradigm

families.rationale: Find a target among distractors

short_definition: Four cards with letters and numbers under a conditional rule; participants choose cards to turn over to test the rule. Indexes conditional reasoning and content effects.
description: The Wason Selection Task is the classic test of conditional reasoning. Participants see four cards, each showing information on both sides. A conditional rule is stated (e.g., "If a card has an A on one side, then it has a 2 on the other"). Cards show one side each (e.g., A, B, 2, 7), and participants must select which cards need to be turned over to test the rule. The correct answer is the card showing A (potentially confirming) and the card showing 7 (potentially falsifying), but most participants incorrectly select A and 2 (confirmation bias). When the rule is reframed in terms of social contracts (e.g., "If you drink alcohol, you must be over 21"), performance dramatically improves, supporting evolutionary theories of cheater-detection modules.

procedure: Participants see four cards showing one side each and a conditional rule (if P then Q).
They select which cards must be turned over to test the rule.
measurements: Proportion selecting logically correct cards (P and not-Q)

variations.name: Abstract Wason Task (Standard)
variations.description: Four cards show, for example, A, D, 4 and 7, with the rule 'if a card has a vowel on one side it has an even number on the other'. The participant chooses which cards must be turned over to check the rule. Most people fail to choose the 7, which could reveal a violation.
variations.justification: Canonical abstract conditional reasoning; select cards to test rule

variations.name: Thematic/Concrete Versions
variations.description: The same logical structure is dressed in a familiar situation, for example cards showing drinks and ages with the rule 'if a person is drinking beer, they must be over 18'. People choose the correct cards far more often.
variations.justification: Concrete familiar content; tests facilitation of abstract reasoning

variations.name: Social Contract Versions
variations.description: The rule is framed as a social exchange in which a benefit must be paid for ('if you take the benefit, you must meet the requirement'), and the participant looks for cheaters. These versions reliably produce correct selections.
variations.justification: Cheater-detection framing; different evolutionary content domain

variations.name: Precaution Rules
variations.description: The rule is a safety precaution, such as 'if you work with toxic chemicals, you must wear gloves', and the participant checks for people who are in danger because they broke it.
variations.justification: Safety precaution framing; different pragmatic rule type

variations.name: Deontic vs. Indicative Rules
variations.description: The task is run with rules about what people must or may do (deontic) and with rules describing how things are (indicative), using matched content, to compare how the two kinds of rule are tested.
variations.justification: Permission/obligation vs. descriptive conditional; different rule semantics

variations.name: Negated Rules
variations.description: The rule contains a negation in one of its parts, such as 'if a card has an A, it does not have a 3'. Negations change which cards are logically relevant and make the task considerably harder.
variations.justification: Negation in conditional changes logical structure

variations.name: Probabilistic Selection Task
variations.description: The rule is treated as a claim that is probably rather than certainly true, and the participant chooses which cards would be most informative for deciding whether to believe it, rather than which could prove it false.
variations.justification: Probabilistic card selection instead of binary; different decision format

variations.name: Wason 2-4-6 Task (Related)
variations.description: A different rule-discovery task by the same author. The participant is told that the triple 2-4-6 fits a hidden rule and proposes their own triples, learning whether each fits, until they are ready to state the rule. People tend to test only triples that confirm their guess.
variations.justification: Hypothesis-testing number sequence task; related reasoning paradigm

short_definition: Speeded categorization of tools vs weapons primed by faces of varying race; congruence effects index implicit racial bias in perception.
description: Participants view face primes (typically Black and White faces, presented briefly) followed by target objects that are either weapons (guns, knives) or non-threatening objects (tools, household items). Participants must rapidly classify the target object while ignoring the face prime. The paradigm measures implicit racial bias through two routes: behavioral errors (misclassifying tools as weapons more often after Black face primes) and EEG markers of error monitoring (enhanced ERN on racially biased error trials). The ERN enhancement on bias-consistent errors indicates that the anterior cingulate cortex detects the conflict between egalitarian goals and automatic stereotype-driven responses, with ERN amplitude predicting subsequent behavioral correction. This paradigm bridges social psychology, implicit cognition, and cognitive neuroscience by providing a neural signature of bias detection.

procedure: A face (Black or White) is flashed briefly, followed by an object (weapon or tool).
Participants classify the object.
Racial bias is indexed by differential accuracy or speed.
measurements: Signal-detection measures of racial bias (criterion shift)
Error rate for weapon/tool by face race

variations.name: First-Person Shooter Task (Correll et al., 2002)
variations.description: Photographs of men in realistic settings, either holding a gun or holding a harmless object such as a phone, appear briefly. The participant presses 'shoot' for armed men and 'don't shoot' for unarmed men within a deadline. Errors and response times are compared by the race of the person shown.
variations.justification: Video-game format shooter task; different motor response and scenario structure

variations.name: Weapons Task in Virtual Reality
variations.description: The scenes are presented in an immersive virtual environment, and the participant responds by aiming and pulling a trigger on a hand-held controller, so that the decision is made with the body in the scene rather than at a keyboard.
variations.justification: Immersive VR environment; full-body spatial and motor engagement

families.rationale: Race prime creates a congruence effect on categorization; could be filed under social cognition

short_definition: Sort cards by a hidden rule (color, form, or number) using only correct/incorrect feedback; after runs of correct sorts the rule silently switches. Perseverative errors index set-shifting.
description: The WCST tests cognitive flexibility, set-shifting, and learning from feedback. Participants match cards displaying varying numbers of colored symbols to four reference cards according to an unannounced sorting rule (color, shape, or number). After 10 consecutive correct sorts, the rule changes without warning. Feedback ("correct"/"incorrect") is provided after each sort. The test measures categories completed, perseverative errors (continued use of the previous rule), non-perseverative errors, and the ability to maintain set. It is the gold-standard clinical test of prefrontal executive function.

procedure: Cards vary on three dimensions (color, form, number).
Participants sort cards to match a target according to an undisclosed rule (e.g., color), receiving feedback.
After a run of correct sorts, the rule changes without warning.
manipulations: Number of consecutive correct before shift
measurements: Perseverative errors (continuing to sort by old rule)

variations.name: Standard WCST (128 Cards)
variations.description: Four reference cards differ in the color, shape and number of their symbols. The participant places each of 128 cards under one reference card, and is told only 'right' or 'wrong'. After ten correct placements the hidden rule (sort by color, shape or number) silently changes. Continuing to sort by the old rule is a perseverative error.
variations.justification: Canonical 128-card version with shifting sorting rules

variations.name: Short Form WCST (64 Cards)
variations.description: Only the first 64 cards are used, halving the time while keeping the same rules and scoring.
variations.justification: 64-card abbreviated version; recognized efficient form

variations.name: Modified WCST with Explicit Cues
variations.description: The participant is told when the rule changes, or told which rules are possible, or both. Comparing with the standard version separates difficulty in discovering the rule from difficulty in switching to it.
variations.justification: Explicit cues about sorting dimension; tests rule use vs. rule discovery

variations.name: Berg Card Sorting Test
variations.description: A simpler version with fewer cards and clearly separated sorting features, used in early studies and as a freely available computerized form.
variations.justification: Simplified precursor with fewer cards and dimensions; named related instrument

variations.name: Intra-/Extra-Dimensional Set Shifting (IED)
variations.description: A touchscreen test from the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery. The participant learns which of two shapes is correct through feedback. The rule changes in stages: first to a new pair of shapes with the same feature relevant, then to a different feature (line patterns superimposed on the shapes). The latter shift is the hard one.
variations.justification: CANTAB analog with distinct dimension-shifting structure; different stimuli and shift types

variations.name: Reversal-Only WCST
variations.description: Only two sorting rules are used and the rule simply switches between them, so the task measures reversal rather than discovery of a new rule among several.
variations.justification: Only reversal phase; isolates reversal from acquisition

variations.name: Probabilistic WCST
variations.description: The feedback is wrong some of the time, for example 'wrong' on 20 percent of correct sorts, so the participant must decide whether a 'wrong' means the rule has changed or is just noise.
variations.justification: Sorting feedback probabilistic rather than deterministic; different uncertainty structure

families.rationale: Discover and switch a hidden sorting rule

short_definition: Generate as many words as possible within a time limit matching a phonemic (letter) or semantic (category) constraint; production count and clustering/switching patterns index executive-lexical retrieval.
description: Participants produce as many unique words as possible in a fixed interval (typically 60 seconds) that satisfy a constraint: a starting letter (phonemic/letter fluency, e.g., F, A, S) or a semantic category (e.g., animals, fruits). Phonemic fluency loads heavily on left frontal executive systems involved in strategic search and self-monitoring, while semantic fluency additionally engages temporal-lobe semantic stores. Beyond raw word count, temporal analyses of clustering (runs of semantically or phonemically similar words) and switching (transitions between clusters) dissociate automatic retrieval from effortful executive search. Verbal fluency is one of the most widely administered neuropsychological tasks, sensitive to frontal-lobe lesions, neurodegenerative disease (especially Alzheimer's vs. frontotemporal dementia), schizophrenia, and normal aging. Its brevity, minimal equipment needs, and robust normative data make it a cornerstone of clinical assessment batteries.

procedure: Participant generates words aloud matching a letter or category constraint within a timed interval.
An examiner records all responses.
manipulations: Constraint type (phonemic letter vs. semantic category)
measurements: Number of perseverations and rule violations
Cluster size (mean words per semantic/phonemic cluster)

variations.name: Phonemic / Letter Fluency (FAS)
variations.description: The participant says as many words as they can that begin with a given letter in one minute, excluding names and repeats of the same word with different endings. Usually three letters (F, A and S) are given in turn. The score is the total number of acceptable words.
variations.justification: Generate words by initial letter; canonical phonemic fluency

variations.name: Semantic / Category Fluency
variations.description: The participant names as many members of a category as they can in one minute, such as animals or things in a supermarket. Usually easier than letter fluency, and the two are impaired differently by different brain conditions.
variations.justification: Generate words from category; different retrieval strategy and structure

variations.name: Action / Verb Fluency
variations.description: The participant names as many different things that people can do (verbs) as they can in one minute.
variations.justification: Generate verbs/actions; different grammatical category

variations.name: Switching Fluency
variations.description: The participant alternates between two categories with each word, for example a fruit, then a piece of furniture, then a fruit, and so on, for one minute.
variations.justification: Alternate between two categories; adds cognitive flexibility demand

variations.name: Design Fluency
variations.description: A non-verbal version in which the participant draws as many different designs as they can by connecting dots in a small grid with a fixed number of lines, within a minute.
variations.justification: Draw novel designs instead of words; different modality

variations.name: Excluded-Letter Fluency
variations.description: The participant says as many words as they can that do not contain a given letter (such as 'e'), which requires checking each candidate word against the constraint.
variations.justification: Generate words avoiding a letter; adds constraint that changes retrieval strategy

families.rationale: Generate words to a category or letter

short_definition: Participants perform an ongoing task while remembering to execute a deferred intention when a target event occurs (event-based) or after a time interval (time-based); PM hit rate indexes the ability to remember to remember.
description: Prospective memory (PM) is the ability to remember to carry out an intended action in the future. In the standard Einstein-McDaniel paradigm, participants perform a continuous ongoing task (e.g., pleasantness rating, lexical decision) while simultaneously holding the intention to execute a secondary action when a specific cue appears (event-based PM: e.g., press a key when an animal word appears) or after a fixed time interval (time-based PM: e.g., press a key every 2 minutes). The critical measure is whether the participant detects the PM cue and executes the intended action. PM is theoretically distinct from retrospective memory: the challenge is not remembering the content of the intention but spontaneously retrieving it at the right moment without an external prompt. The multiprocess framework (McDaniel & Einstein, 2000) proposes that PM retrieval can be supported by automatic, reflexive-associative processes or by resource-demanding strategic monitoring, depending on cue focality, ongoing-task absorption, and individual differences. PM failures are a leading cause of real-world memory complaints and are sensitive to aging, traumatic brain injury, ADHD, and schizophrenia.

procedure: Participant performs a continuous ongoing task while holding a delayed intention.
On designated trials (event cue) or at designated times (time cue), the participant must interrupt the ongoing task to execute the prospective action.
manipulations: Cue focality (focal cue processed as part of ongoing task vs. non-focal cue requiring monitoring)
Delay between intention formation and PM window
measurements: PM hit rate (proportion of cues correctly detected and acted upon)
Ongoing-task cost (RT and accuracy difference between PM blocks and baseline blocks)
Time-monitoring behavior (clock-checking frequency in time-based PM)

variations.name: Event-Based PM (Focal Cue)
variations.description: The participant performs an ongoing task, such as deciding whether letter strings are words, and is also asked to press a special key whenever a particular word (such as 'tiger') appears. Because the ongoing task already requires reading each word, the cue is noticed with little extra effort.
variations.justification: PM cue is focal target of ongoing task; different resource demand from non-focal

variations.name: Event-Based PM (Non-Focal Cue)
variations.description: The special key must be pressed when a word has some feature the ongoing task does not require looking at, for example when a word contains the syllable 'tor' while the participant is rating words for pleasantness. The participant must keep checking for the feature, which slows the ongoing task.
variations.justification: PM cue is non-focal; requires additional monitoring attention

variations.name: Time-Based PM
variations.description: The special response must be made at set times, for example every two minutes, with no external reminder. A clock is available but must be checked deliberately, and how often the participant checks it is recorded.
variations.justification: Time check required at specified interval; different PM cue type

variations.name: Activity-Based PM
variations.description: The special response must be made when a particular activity ends, such as at the end of a block of trials or when a questionnaire is finished, rather than at a set time or on seeing a particular item.
variations.justification: PM intention linked to completing an activity; different cue type

variations.name: Multiple-Intention PM
variations.description: The participant holds several delayed intentions at once, each triggered by a different cue and requiring a different response, so that the limits on keeping several intentions in mind can be tested.
variations.justification: Several PM intentions simultaneously maintained; different load

variations.name: Naturalistic PM
variations.description: The intended actions are everyday ones outside the laboratory, such as mailing a postcard on a given day, phoning at a set time, or completing errands in a virtual town, and whether they are done is recorded.
variations.justification: Real-world task context instead of lab; different ecological setting

families.rationale: Execute a deferred intention during an ongoing task; the only prospective paradigm in the Catalog

short_definition: After studying items presented in distinct contexts (speaker, location, modality, time), participants judge each item's encoding source; source accuracy dissociates contextual recollection from item familiarity.
description: Source memory tests assess the ability to remember the contextual details of an encoding episode - not just whether an item was encountered (item memory) but where, when, how, or from whom it was learned. In the standard paradigm, items are presented under two or more source conditions (e.g., spoken by a male vs. female voice; shown on the left vs. right of the screen; read vs. imagined). At test, participants first make an old/new recognition judgment, then indicate the source of each recognized item. Source accuracy (correct source attributions conditional on item recognition) is the primary measure, dissociating recollection-based contextual retrieval from familiarity-based item recognition. Johnson's source monitoring framework (Johnson, Hashtroudi, & Lindsay, 1993) distinguishes external source monitoring (which person said it), internal source monitoring (did I do it or imagine it), and reality monitoring (internal vs. external origin). Source memory failures underlie false memories, eyewitness misattributions, and confabulation. The paradigm recruits prefrontal cortex (especially right and medial PFC for monitoring) and hippocampus (binding items to contexts), with a characteristic dissociation from item memory in aging and frontal lesion patients.

procedure: Items are studied under two or more contextually distinct source conditions.
At test, participants recognize studied items and judge the source (context) in which each item was encoded.
manipulations: Source type (voice, spatial location, temporal position, modality, cognitive operation)
Response format (forced-choice source vs. source confidence rating)
measurements: Source accuracy (proportion of recognized items with correct source attribution)

variations.name: Voice Source Monitoring
variations.description: Words are spoken by two different voices, such as a man and a woman, during study. At test the participant sees or hears each word and says whether it was new, said by the man, or said by the woman.
variations.justification: Speaker identity as source attribute; canonical source monitoring

variations.name: Spatial Source Monitoring
variations.description: Each item is studied at one of several positions on the screen, or in one of several rooms or containers, and the participant later reports where each item was.
variations.justification: Location as source attribute; different source dimension

variations.name: Temporal Source Monitoring
variations.description: Items are studied in two or more separate lists or sessions, and the participant later reports which list (or which session, earlier or later) each item came from.
variations.justification: Time of occurrence as source; different temporal memory dimension

variations.name: Reality Monitoring
variations.description: During study, some items are seen or heard and others are only imagined or generated by the participant, for example completing a word from its first letters. At test the participant says whether each item was actually presented or self-generated.
variations.justification: Internal vs. external origin judgment; distinct reality monitoring paradigm

variations.name: Internal Source Monitoring
variations.description: All items are generated by the participant, but in two different ways, for example some said aloud and some only thought, or some written and some imagined. At test the participant reports which way each item was generated.
variations.justification: Self-generated vs. experimenter-presented items; different internal/external distinction

variations.name: Modality Source Monitoring
variations.description: Some items are presented visually and others auditorily at study, and the participant later reports whether each was seen or heard.
variations.justification: Auditory vs. visual presentation as source; different sensory source

variations.name: Encoding Task Source Monitoring
variations.description: Each item is studied with one of two different judgments, for example rating its pleasantness or counting its letters, and the participant later reports which judgment they made for each item.
variations.justification: Which encoding task was used as source; different procedural context

variations.name: Multi-Source (3+ Sources)
variations.description: Items come from three or more sources, such as three different speakers or three screen positions, so that the participant has to choose among more options and confusions between particular sources can be analyzed.
variations.justification: Three or more source attributes; higher discrimination demand

families.rationale: Recognition with an attribution of encoding context

short_definition: Participants choose between a low-effort/low-reward option and a high-effort/high-reward option on each trial; the indifference point indexes effort discounting and motivational willingness to exert effort for reward.
description: Effort-based decision-making tasks measure the willingness to exert physical or cognitive effort in exchange for reward. In the Effort Expenditure for Rewards Task (EEfRT; Treadway et al., 2009), participants on each trial choose between an easy task (e.g., pressing a button with the dominant index finger 30 times in 7 seconds for a small reward) and a hard task (pressing with the non-dominant pinky finger 100 times in 21 seconds for a larger, variable reward). Reward magnitude and probability are manipulated across trials to map the effort-reward tradeoff. The proportion of hard-task choices is the primary measure, indexing motivational drive. Effort discounting variants (Botvinick, Huffstetler, & McGuire, 2009) use a titration procedure to find the reward value at which effortful and easy options are equally preferred (the indifference point). The paradigm has become central to research on motivational anhedonia - the reduced willingness to exert effort for reward that characterizes depression, schizophrenia, and Parkinson's disease. Computational models decompose behavior into effort sensitivity, reward sensitivity, and probability weighting parameters. The framework connects to dopaminergic theories of motivation: effort willingness is modulated by dopamine function in the ventral striatum and anterior cingulate cortex.

procedure: On each trial, participants choose between a low-effort/low-reward option and a high-effort/high-reward option, then execute the chosen action.
Trials vary reward magnitude and probability.
manipulations: Effort demand level (physical vs. cognitive; graded difficulty)
Effort type (button pressing, grip force, N-back)
measurements: Effort indifference point (reward at which hard and easy options are equally chosen)
Computational model parameters (effort sensitivity, reward sensitivity, probability weighting)

variations.name: EEfRT (Physical Effort)
variations.description: On each trial the participant chooses between an easy task (about 30 presses with the index finger in 7 seconds for a small fixed reward) and a hard task (about 100 presses with the little finger in 21 seconds for a larger reward). The size of the larger reward and the probability of being paid vary across trials. How often the hard task is chosen measures willingness to work for reward.
variations.justification: Canonical effort-reward task: grips vs. reward levels

variations.name: Cognitive Effort Discounting
variations.description: The effort is mental rather than physical. After experiencing working-memory tasks of different difficulty (such as 1-back to 4-back), the participant repeatedly chooses between doing an easy level for a smaller amount or a harder level for a larger amount, with the amounts adjusted until they are indifferent.
variations.justification: Cognitive task difficulty vs. reward; different effort type

variations.name: Grip-Force Effort Task
variations.description: The participant squeezes a hand-grip device. Offers pair a reward with a required squeeze force as a share of the participant's maximum, and the participant accepts or rejects each offer, or chooses between offers. Force can be varied finely.
variations.justification: Graded grip force as effort measure; different motor requirement

variations.name: Effort Discounting Titration
variations.description: For each effort level, the reward for the easy option is raised or lowered after each choice until the participant is indifferent between the easy and hard options. The resulting reward difference is the subjective cost of that effort level.
variations.justification: Adaptive titration of effort-reward indifference points; different method

variations.name: Progressive Ratio Task
variations.description: Each successive reward requires more presses or squeezes than the one before. The participant may stop at any time, and the effort level at which they quit (the breakpoint) measures the most they are willing to do for the reward.
variations.justification: Escalating effort requirement for each reward; different effort schedule

variations.name: Demand Selection Task
variations.description: Two decks or locations are offered that lead to the same kind of task, but one involves more frequent rule switches than the other. No reward depends on the choice. Participants are not told the difference, and a preference for the easier option shows avoidance of mental effort.
variations.justification: Freely choose between high/low demand tasks; choice behavior reveals effort avoidance

variations.name: Apple-Gathering Task
variations.description: The participant picks apples from a virtual tree, where each press yields fewer apples than the last, and decides when to leave for the next tree, which costs travel time. When they leave shows how they weigh continued effort against diminishing returns.
variations.justification: Virtual navigation effort for rewards; different effort modality (locomotion)

families.rationale: Choice between low and high effort for reward

short_definition: After failing to recall a studied item, participants rate the likelihood they could recognize the answer; the accuracy of these predictions (gamma correlation with recognition) indexes metacognitive monitoring of unretrieved memory.
description: The Feeling-of-Knowing task measures the accuracy of metacognitive judgments about information that cannot currently be recalled. In the standard Hart (1965) paradigm, participants study cue-target pairs, attempt cued recall, and then - for items they failed to recall - rate their confidence that they would recognize the correct answer among alternatives. A subsequent recognition test determines the accuracy of these predictions. The key dependent measure is resolution - the correspondence between feeling-of-knowing magnitude and recognition performance, typically quantified by the Goodman-Kruskal gamma correlation. Feeling-of-knowing judgments are thought to rely on partial retrieval of target attributes, cue familiarity, and accessibility of related information, rather than direct access to trace strength. The paradigm dissociates from Judgment-of-Learning tasks in timing (post-retrieval-failure vs. post-encoding), prediction target (recognition vs. recall), and cognitive basis (partial retrieval and cue familiarity vs. encoding fluency). Feeling-of-knowing accuracy is sensitive to frontal lobe damage, aging, Alzheimer's disease, and schizophrenia, and is more closely tied to executive functioning than Judgment-of-Learning accuracy.

procedure: Participants study cue-target pairs, attempt cued recall, and for each unrecalled item rate their feeling of knowing (likelihood of future recognition).
a subsequent recognition test assesses prediction accuracy.
manipulations: Delay between judgment and recognition test
measurements: Resolution (gamma correlation between ratings and recognition accuracy)
Calibration (correspondence between predicted and actual recognition probabilities)

variations.name: Episodic Feeling-of-Knowing
variations.description: The participant studies word pairs. Later, given the first word, they try to recall the second. For each pair they cannot recall, they rate how likely they would be to recognize the answer if shown it. A recognition test follows, and the match between ratings and recognition is the measure.
variations.justification: FOK for episodic memories; unrecalled episode-specific items

variations.name: Semantic / General-Knowledge Feeling-of-Knowing
variations.description: The questions are general-knowledge items such as 'What is the capital of Australia?' rather than studied pairs. For each answer the participant cannot recall, they rate the likelihood of recognizing it, and a multiple-choice test follows.
variations.justification: FOK for semantic facts; different memory system

variations.name: Cue-Only vs. Cue-Target Paradigm
variations.description: At the time of the rating, either only the question or cue word is shown, or the cue is shown together with some partial information about the answer. Compares ratings based on the cue alone with ratings that can draw on fragments of the answer.
variations.justification: Study with or without target; tests whether target exposure affects FOK accuracy

variations.name: Tip-of-the-Tongue Variant
variations.description: The participant indicates when they are in a tip-of-the-tongue state, feeling the answer is on the verge of coming, and may report partial information such as the first letter or number of syllables. These items are analyzed separately from ordinary failures to recall.
variations.justification: TOT state as extreme FOK; different phenomenology and partial information access

variations.name: Feeling-of-Knowing with Feedback
variations.description: After each recognition test the participant is told whether they were right, and the task continues with further items, to see whether the accuracy of their ratings improves with this information.
variations.justification: Accuracy feedback after recognition test; tests calibration learning

families.rationale: Rate recognizability after failed recall

short_definition: After studying each item, participants predict the likelihood they will recall it on a later test; calibration and resolution of these predictions index metacognitive monitoring of encoding.
description: The Judgment-of-Learning task measures the accuracy of metacognitive predictions made during or shortly after encoding. In the standard Nelson and Dunlosky (1991) paradigm, participants study word pairs and, after each pair (immediate) or after a delay (delayed), rate the likelihood (0-100%) that they will recall the target when given the cue on a later test. A cued recall test follows, and prediction accuracy is assessed through resolution (gamma correlation between judgments and recall) and calibration (mean judgment vs. mean recall). A landmark finding is the delayed-judgment-of-learning effect: predictions made after a brief delay are far more accurate than immediate ones, because delayed judgments rely on retrieval fluency (a valid cue) rather than short-term memory availability (a poor cue). Judgment-of-Learning research connects to self-regulated learning: learners use these judgments to allocate study time, select items for restudy, and decide when to terminate study. The paradigm is foundational in metamemory research and dissociates from Feeling-of-Knowing tasks in timing (post-encoding vs. post-retrieval-failure), prediction target (recall vs. recognition), and underlying basis (encoding fluency vs. partial retrieval).

procedure: Participants study items (typically word pairs), then predict the likelihood of recalling each item on a future test.
a subsequent recall test assesses prediction accuracy.
manipulations: Encoding conditions (number of presentations, elaborative vs. rote)
Cue type (cue-only vs. cue-target at judgment)
measurements: Resolution (gamma correlation between judgments and recall)
Study-time allocation as a behavioral consequence of judgments

variations.name: Immediate Judgment-of-Learning
variations.description: The participant studies a word pair and, right after it, rates how likely they are to recall the second word when given the first on a later test. After all pairs, the recall test is given and ratings are compared with actual recall.
variations.justification: JOL made immediately after study; foresight-based monitoring

variations.name: Delayed Judgment-of-Learning
variations.description: The rating is made some time after studying the pair, typically after several other pairs have been studied, rather than right away. Delayed ratings predict later recall far better than immediate ones.
variations.justification: JOL made after delay; improves accuracy via delayed-JOL effect

variations.name: Aggregate vs. Item-by-Item Judgments
variations.description: Instead of (or in addition to) rating each item, the participant estimates how many of the whole list they will recall. The overall estimate is compared with the number actually recalled.
variations.justification: Global confidence vs. per-item monitoring; different judgment granularity

variations.name: Cue-Only vs. Cue-Target Delayed Judgment
variations.description: When the delayed rating is made, either only the first word of the pair is shown, which forces the participant to try to retrieve the second word, or both words are shown. Ratings made from the cue alone are the most accurate.
variations.justification: JOL prompted by cue alone vs. cue+target; tests forward vs. backward recall fluency

variations.name: Self-Regulated Study Paradigm
variations.description: After rating the items, the participant chooses which items to study again, or how long to spend on each. Whether they choose items they rated as poorly learned shows how the ratings are used to guide study.
variations.justification: Participant allocates study time based on JOL; adds metacognitive control component

variations.name: Pre-Study Judgment (Ease-of-Learning)
variations.description: The participant sees each item briefly before studying it and rates how easy it will be to learn. These judgments are made before any learning and measure estimates of difficulty rather than of learning achieved.
variations.justification: Judgment made before study; different pre-learning prediction task

families.rationale: Predict later recall of each studied item

short_definition: Participants count or discriminate their own heartbeats without external feedback; the correspondence between perceived and actual heartbeat counts (or discrimination accuracy) indexes interoceptive sensitivity.
description: The Heartbeat Detection Task is the standard paradigm for measuring interoceptive accuracy - the ability to perceive internal physiological signals. In the Schandry (1981) heartbeat counting variant, participants silently count their heartbeats during timed intervals (e.g., 25, 35, 45 seconds) without taking their pulse; an interoceptive accuracy score is computed from the discrepancy between counted and actual heartbeats (recorded via ECG or pulse oximetry). In the Whitehead heartbeat discrimination variant, participants judge whether an external stimulus (tone or light) is presented synchronously or asynchronously with their heartbeat; d-prime indexes perceptual sensitivity. Interoceptive accuracy is central to theories of emotion (the somatic marker hypothesis; Damasio, 1994), anxiety (interoceptive hypersensitivity models), and embodied cognition (predictive interoception). Individual differences in heartbeat detection correlate with emotional intensity, anxiety sensitivity, and decision-making quality. The paradigm has generated substantial methodological debate: the counting variant may partially reflect beliefs about heart rate rather than true perception, motivating the discrimination variant and newer alternatives.

procedure: Participants perceive their own heartbeats - either counting them during timed intervals (counting variant) or judging synchrony between external stimuli and cardiac events (discrimination variant) - while actual heartbeats are recorded physiologically.
manipulations: Stimulus timing relative to R-wave (synchronous vs. delayed)
Attention condition (interoceptive focus vs. exteroceptive distraction)
measurements: Heart rate variability as a covariate
Heartbeat-evoked potential (HEP) amplitude as a neural index

variations.name: Heartbeat Counting (Schandry)
variations.description: The participant sits quietly and, between a start and stop signal, silently counts their own heartbeats without feeling for a pulse. The count is compared with the number of beats recorded by an electrocardiogram over intervals of about 25 to 60 seconds.
variations.justification: Count heartbeats over interval; canonical interoception measure

variations.name: Heartbeat Discrimination (Whitehead)
variations.description: A series of tones is played, each triggered by a heartbeat either immediately or after a delay, so the tones are in time with the heart or slightly out of step. The participant judges whether the tones were synchronous with their heartbeat.
variations.justification: Judge whether tone is synchronous with heartbeat; different detection task

variations.name: Confidence-Accuracy Paradigm
variations.description: After each counting or discrimination trial the participant also rates how confident they are in their answer, and separately fills in a questionnaire about how aware of bodily sensations they generally are. The match between confidence and accuracy is a third measure alongside the two.
variations.justification: Sole confidence-rating exception per section 5.5; Garfinkel et al. (2015) interoception model

variations.name: Interoceptive Attention Manipulation
variations.description: In some blocks the participant is told to attend to their heartbeat, and in others to attend to an external stimulus such as a tone or a visual display, while heartbeats and brain responses to them are recorded. Compares cardiac processing with and without attention on it.
variations.justification: Instructions to attend to vs. distract from heartbeat; changes attentional focus

variations.name: Respiratory Interoception Variant
variations.description: The participant breathes through a mouthpiece and on some breaths a small resistance is added. They report whether each breath was harder than normal, and the smallest resistance they can detect is the measure. Tests sensitivity to breathing rather than to the heart.
variations.justification: Respiratory signals instead of cardiac; different physiological channel

short_definition: Participants judge whether trait adjectives describe themselves vs. another person or a semantic property; the self-reference effect (superior recall for self-encoded items) and endorsement patterns index self-concept and self-referential processing.
description: The Self-Referential Encoding Task exploits the robust finding that information encoded in relation to the self is remembered better than information encoded in other ways (the self-reference effect; Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977). In the standard paradigm, participants view trait adjectives and make judgments under different encoding conditions: 'Does this word describe you?' (self-reference), 'Does this word describe [other person]?' (other-reference), 'Is this a positive word?' (semantic), or 'Is this word in uppercase?' (structural). A surprise recall or recognition test follows. The self-reference effect is the recall advantage for self-encoded items over semantic or other-reference conditions. Beyond the memory effect, the pattern of adjective endorsement (which traits are endorsed as self-descriptive) provides a direct window into self-concept content. This has made the task central to depression research: depressed individuals endorse more negative and fewer positive adjectives as self-descriptive, and show reduced or reversed self-reference memory effects for positive material. The paradigm engages cortical midline structures (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate) associated with self-referential processing, making it a standard fMRI probe of the default mode network.

procedure: Participants judge trait adjectives under self-reference and comparison encoding conditions (other-reference, semantic, structural).
a subsequent memory test assesses the self-reference effect on recall or recognition.
manipulations: Other-reference target (close other vs. distant other vs. celebrity)
measurements: Self-reference effect (recall/recognition advantage for self-encoded items)
Endorsement rate by valence and condition
Recall bias (proportion positive vs. negative recalled)
Cortical midline activation (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate)

variations.name: Standard Trait Adjective Encoding
variations.description: Trait words such as 'honest' or 'lazy' are shown, each with a question: does this describe you (self), does it describe another person such as a public figure (other), does it mean the same as a given word (meaning), or is it printed in capitals (appearance). After all words, a surprise recall test follows. Words judged about the self are recalled best.
variations.justification: Canonical: judge whether adjective describes self; incidental encoding

variations.name: Positive/Negative Valence Split
variations.description: The trait words are balanced between positive (kind) and negative (selfish), and endorsement and recall are analyzed separately for each. Depressed participants endorse and recall more negative words about themselves.
variations.justification: Valence-matched sets tested separately; tests self-relevance by valence

variations.name: Close vs. Distant Other-Reference
variations.description: The 'other' person in the question is varied from someone very close (mother, best friend) to a celebrity or a stranger, to see whether the memory advantage for self-judged words shrinks as the other becomes closer.
variations.justification: Encoding with reference to close vs. distant others; tests reference specificity

variations.name: Incidental vs. Intentional Encoding
variations.description: In the usual version the participant does not know a memory test is coming. In the intentional version they are told to remember the words as well as answering the questions, to see whether the self-reference advantage holds when people are trying to learn.
variations.justification: Explicit memory instruction vs. incidental; changes encoding goal

variations.name: Endorsement-Only (No Memory Test)
variations.description: Only the self-judgment phase is run: the participant says yes or no to whether each trait word describes them, and the pattern of positive and negative endorsements is the measure. No recall test is given.
variations.justification: Task without memory test phase; tests self-referential processing in isolation

variations.name: Source Memory for Self-Encoded Items
variations.description: At test the participant must say not only whether a word was studied but which question it was studied with (self, other, meaning), to check whether self-reference improves memory for the context as well as for the word.
variations.justification: Retrieval includes source judgment for self vs. other items; adds source component

families.rationale: Encoding instruction manipulates later recall
The participant reports on themselves; no answer can be checked

short_definition: Participants retrieve specific personal memories in response to cue words or structured prompts; specificity, detail, and temporal distribution of retrieved episodes index autobiographical memory function.
description: Autobiographical memory tasks assess the ability to retrieve specific personal episodes from one's past. The Galton-Crovitz cue-word task presents generic words (e.g., 'garden,' 'river,' 'knife') and asks participants to retrieve a specific personal memory associated with each and date it. The Autobiographical Memory Interview (Kopelman, Wilson, & Baddeley, 1989) uses a structured interview format probing both personal semantic knowledge (names, addresses) and autobiographical incidents across life periods (childhood, early adulthood, recent). The Autobiographical Memory Test (Williams & Broadbent, 1986) presents positive and negative cue words and measures whether participants retrieve specific episodes (bounded in time and place) vs. overgeneral memories (categories or extended periods). Overgeneral autobiographical memory - the tendency to retrieve categorical summaries rather than specific episodes - is a robust marker of depression, PTSD, and suicidality. The temporal distribution of memories typically shows a reminiscence bump (disproportionate recall of events from ages 10-30), recency effect, and childhood amnesia gradient. The paradigm engages a distributed network including hippocampus, medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate, and lateral temporal cortex.

procedure: Participants retrieve specific personal memories in response to cue words, category prompts, or structured interview questions.
Retrieved memories are scored for specificity, detail, emotional content, and temporal distribution.
manipulations: Retrieval instruction (specific episode vs. free retrieval)
Time period constraint (childhood, recent, specific decade)
measurements: Specificity (proportion of specific vs. overgeneral memories)
Phenomenological detail ratings (vividness, emotional intensity, sensory detail)
Autobiographical Memory Interview scores (personal semantic + autobiographical incident)

variations.name: Cue-Word Task (Galton-Crovitz)
variations.description: A single word such as 'river' or 'party' is presented, and the participant describes a specific personal memory it brings to mind and estimates when it happened. The time to find a memory and how specific it is are recorded.
variations.justification: Single word cues; participant freely generates memories in response

variations.name: Autobiographical Memory Test (Williams & Broadbent)
variations.description: A standardized clinical version with positive and negative cue words (such as 'happy', 'sorry'). The participant must describe an event that happened on one particular day. Responses are scored as specific, general (repeated or extended events), or not a memory, with over-general memories being the clinical sign.
variations.justification: Cued recall with specificity scoring and suicidal ideation variant; named standardized instrument

variations.name: Autobiographical Memory Interview (Kopelman)
variations.description: A structured interview covering childhood, early adulthood and recent years. For each period the participant answers factual questions about their life (such as school names) and describes specific incidents, scored separately for facts and incidents.
variations.justification: Structured interview with childhood, early adult, and recent life sections; different retrieval protocol

variations.name: Sentence-Cue Variant
variations.description: The cue is a sentence stem such as 'A time when I felt proud was...' instead of a single word, which directs retrieval toward particular kinds of events or emotions.
variations.justification: Sentence-length cues instead of single words; richer cueing structure

variations.name: Odor-Cued Autobiographical Memory
variations.description: The cue is a smell presented in a jar or on a strip, such as coffee or cinnamon, and the participant describes the personal memory it evokes. Smell-cued memories tend to be older and more emotional than word-cued ones.
variations.justification: Olfactory cues evoke memories; different sensory modality and involuntary retrieval characteristics

variations.name: Future Episodic Simulation
variations.description: Given a cue word, the participant imagines and describes a specific event that might happen to them in the future, rather than recalling a past one. The descriptions are scored for detail in the same way as memories.
variations.justification: Participant imagines future events instead of recalling past; different cognitive operation (projection vs. retrieval)
