short_definition: Participants observe cue-outcome pairings across trials and judge the causal strength of the relationship; judgment profiles across contingency conditions index causal induction and associative learning mechanisms.
description: Causal learning tasks measure how people acquire and represent causal relationships from observed co-occurrences. In the standard contingency judgment paradigm, participants observe a series of trials in which a candidate cause (e.g., a food, a medicine, a button press) is either present or absent and an outcome (e.g., an allergic reaction, a health improvement, a light turning on) either occurs or does not. After observing multiple trials, participants rate the causal strength of the relationship (typically -100 to +100 or 0 to 100). The normative benchmark is delta-P (P(outcome|cause) - P(outcome|no cause)), but human judgments systematically deviate: they are sensitive to outcome density, show cue competition effects (blocking, overshadowing), and are influenced by prior causal beliefs. Associative models (Rescorla-Wagner) and statistical models (causal power; Cheng, 1997) compete to explain these patterns. The paradigm bridges associative learning, causal reasoning, and Bayesian inference literatures. It is the human analogue of animal conditioning studies and is foundational for understanding how people learn cause-effect relationships in medicine, engineering, and everyday reasoning.

procedure: Participants observe a series of trials presenting the presence/absence of candidate causes and occurrence/non-occurrence of outcomes, then judge the causal strength of cause-outcome relationships.
manipulations: Outcome base rate (common vs. rare outcomes)
Temporal contiguity between cause and outcome
measurements: Sensitivity to contingency components (P(O|C) and P(O|~C) separately)
Correspondence between judgments and normative models (delta-P, causal power, Rescorla-Wagner)

variations.name: Allergy Prediction Task
variations.description: On each trial the participant sees which foods a fictional patient ate and then learns whether the patient had an allergic reaction. After many trials they rate how strongly each food causes the reaction. The most common framing for contingency learning.
variations.justification: Canonical food-allergy prediction: participant judges cause-effect contingencies

variations.name: Blocking Paradigm
variations.description: First one cue (such as a food) is paired with the outcome on its own. Then that cue and a new cue are presented together with the outcome. The new cue receives low causal ratings because the outcome was already explained.
variations.justification: Pre-training on one cue blocks learning about second cue; distinct compound conditioning procedure

variations.name: Outcome Density Manipulation
variations.description: How often the outcome occurs overall is varied while the actual relationship between cue and outcome is held at zero. When the outcome is common, participants rate the cue as causal even though it makes no difference.
variations.justification: Systematically varies base rate of outcomes; changes the statistical environment

variations.name: Trial-by-Trial Prediction
variations.description: Before seeing each trial's outcome, the participant predicts whether it will occur. The sequence of predictions tracks learning as it happens, in addition to any rating at the end.
variations.justification: Participant predicts on each trial before feedback; different response requirement from summary judgment

variations.name: Summary vs. Sequential Presentation
variations.description: In the summary version the counts of all four combinations (cue present or absent, outcome present or absent) are shown at once in a table and the participant rates the causal link from it. In the sequential version the same information arrives one trial at a time.
variations.justification: Summary table vs. trial-by-trial presentation; changes information format and cognitive demand

variations.name: Multi-Cause (Relative Validity)
variations.description: Several candidate causes appear in different combinations, some of which predict the outcome perfectly while others predict it only partially. The partially predictive cue receives lower ratings when a perfect predictor is present than when it is not.
variations.justification: Multiple competing cues; relative validity procedure changes causal inference structure

variations.name: Causal Direction Manipulation
variations.description: The same trials are presented but the participant is asked either to predict the effect from the cause (does this food cause the reaction?) or to diagnose the cause from the effect (given the reaction, which food was eaten?).
variations.justification: Manipulates whether participant judges cause->effect or effect->cause; different reasoning direction

variations.name: Backward Blocking / Retrospective Revaluation
variations.description: Two cues are first presented together with the outcome. Then one of them is presented alone with the outcome. Ratings for the other cue, which was never presented again, drop, showing that earlier learning was revised in the light of later information.
variations.justification: Post-training devaluation of compound changes prior learning; distinct temporal structure

families.rationale: Judge causal strength from cue-outcome pairings

short_definition: Synchronous multisensory stimulation of a participant's hidden body part and a visible fake or virtual counterpart induces illusory ownership of the artificial body part; proprioceptive drift, subjective ratings, and threat responses index the strength of the illusion.
description: Body ownership illusion tasks exploit multisensory integration to induce the experience that an artificial body part (or whole body) belongs to the participant. In the classic Rubber Hand Illusion (Botvinick & Cohen, 1998), a participant's real hand is hidden behind a screen while a realistic rubber hand is placed in an anatomically plausible position. Synchronous stroking of both hands with paintbrushes for 1-2 minutes typically produces a vivid sense of ownership over the rubber hand, accompanied by a proprioceptive shift (pointing error toward the rubber hand) and autonomic responses to threats directed at the rubber hand (elevated skin conductance). Asynchronous stroking serves as the critical control condition. The paradigm demonstrates that body ownership is a dynamic, multisensory construction rather than a fixed perceptual given. The illusion depends on spatial, temporal, and anatomical congruence of visual, tactile, and proprioceptive signals, and is modulated by top-down factors (body schema, visual realism, postural plausibility). Computational accounts frame the illusion as Bayesian causal inference over multisensory signals (Samad, Chung, & Shams, 2015). The paradigm has been extended to the whole body (Petkova & Ehrsson, 2008), to faces (enfacement illusion; Tsakiris, 2008), and to virtual reality environments (Slater et al., 2008). Clinical applications include phantom limb pain treatment, eating disorder body image interventions, and assessment of body representation disturbances in schizophrenia and depersonalization.

procedure: A participant's real body part is hidden while a visible artificial (rubber, virtual, or video-displayed) counterpart is placed in a plausible position.
Synchronous multisensory stimulation (typically visuotactile stroking) is applied to both the real and artificial body parts, with asynchronous stimulation as a control.
manipulations: Body part (hand, arm, face, full body)
Realism of the artificial body part (rubber, wooden, virtual, incongruent object)
Spatial congruence (anatomically plausible vs. rotated position)
Temporal delay between seen and felt touch
measurements: Proprioceptive drift (pointing error toward the artificial body part, pre- vs. post-stimulation)
Skin conductance response to threat directed at the artificial body part
Skin temperature change of the real hand
Grip force or other motor measures

variations.name: Classic Rubber Hand Illusion
variations.description: The participant's real hand is hidden behind a screen and a rubber hand is placed in view where the real hand would be. The experimenter strokes both hands with brushes at the same time for a minute or two. Most people begin to feel the rubber hand is their own. When the strokes are out of time with each other, the feeling does not arise. Afterwards the participant points to where they feel their hand is and answers questions about the experience.
variations.justification: Synchronous brush strokes on rubber hand and hidden real hand; canonical embodiment paradigm

variations.name: Full Body Illusion (Body Swap)
variations.description: The participant wears a head-mounted display showing the view from cameras on a mannequin's head, so they see the mannequin's body where their own should be. The experimenter touches the participant's body and the mannequin's body at the same time, and the participant comes to feel the mannequin's body is theirs.
variations.justification: Full-body camera-to-HMD setup creates whole-body ownership; different from hand-only paradigm

variations.name: Virtual Hand / Virtual Body Illusion
variations.description: A virtual hand or body is shown in virtual reality and moves when the participant moves, or is touched in time with touches to the real body. The appearance, delay and position of the virtual body can be changed at will.
variations.justification: Virtual avatar hand in VR; different sensory integration conditions

variations.name: Enfacement Illusion
variations.description: The participant watches a video of another person's face being stroked with a brush while their own face is stroked in the same place at the same time. Afterwards they are more likely to judge faces morphed between their own and the other person's as their own.
variations.justification: Synchronous touch to face and rubber face; different body part and social dimension

variations.name: Somatosensory Rubber Hand Illusion
variations.description: The participant is blindfolded. The experimenter guides the participant's one hand to stroke the rubber hand while stroking the participant's other, hidden hand in the same way. The illusion arises from touch and position sense alone, without vision.
variations.justification: Tactile stimulation without visual component; isolates tactile-proprioceptive integration

variations.name: Kinesthetic Mirror Illusion
variations.description: A mirror is placed between the participant's hands so that the reflection of one hand appears where the other hand is. When the visible hand moves, the participant feels the hidden hand moving too, even if it is still.
variations.justification: Proprioceptive/kinesthetic basis without visual rubber hand; different sensory modality

variations.name: Threat Response Paradigm
variations.description: After the illusion has been induced, the experimenter suddenly stabs toward or bends back the rubber hand. The participant's skin conductance rise or brain response to the threat measures how much the rubber hand has been taken as their own.
variations.justification: Threatening stimulus applied to rubber hand; measures embodiment via threat response

variations.name: Incongruent Object Control
variations.description: A wooden block, a rubber ball or a rubber hand in an impossible position is used in place of the properly placed rubber hand, with the same synchronous stroking. The illusion normally fails, showing that the object must look like a hand in a plausible place.
variations.justification: Non-hand object used instead of rubber hand; tests specificity of body-form requirement

families.rationale: Induced ownership of a fake limb

short_definition: Execute an instructed finger movement while observing a congruent or incongruent action performed by another person; the congruency effect (faster responses on congruent trials) indexes automatic imitation and the cost of inhibiting observed-action representations.
description: The Imitation-Inhibition Task (Brass, Bekkering, Wohlschlager, & Prinz, 2000) measures the involuntary tendency to copy observed actions and the executive cost of suppressing that tendency. Participants are cued to perform a simple action (e.g., lift the index finger when a number '1' appears) while simultaneously viewing a task-irrelevant video of another person's hand performing either the same action (congruent), a different action (incongruent, e.g., lifting the middle finger), or no action (neutral/static hand). The congruency effect -- faster and more accurate responses on congruent than incongruent trials -- indexes automatic imitation, while the interference effect (incongruent minus neutral) specifically indexes the inhibitory cost of suppressing the observed action. The paradigm is grounded in common-coding / ideomotor theory (Prinz, 1997): perceiving an action activates the same motor representations as executing it, creating response conflict when the observed and instructed actions differ. The task has become a standard probe of the human mirror system and self-other distinction. The automatic imitation effect is modulated by animacy (stronger for human than robotic agents), social context (in-group vs. out-group models), empathy, and developmental stage (weaker in young children, inverted-U trajectory). Clinical applications include autism spectrum conditions (mixed findings on reduced automatic imitation) and schizophrenia (impaired self-other distinction).

procedure: Participants perform an instructed action (e.g., finger lift) in response to a symbolic cue while simultaneously observing a task-irrelevant video or animation of another agent performing a congruent, incongruent, or neutral action.
manipulations: Congruency (observed action matches vs. mismatches instructed action)
Agent type (human hand, robotic hand, non-biological stimulus)
Action type (finger lift, hand open/close, whole-arm movement)
Spatial compatibility control (orthogonal spatial arrangement to dissociate imitative from spatial compatibility)
measurements: Congruency effect (RT and error rate difference: incongruent minus congruent)
Congruency effect magnitude as individual-difference measure
EEG mu-suppression as neural index of motor simulation

variations.name: Classic Finger-Lift Paradigm (Brass et al.)
variations.description: The participant rests their hand on a table and watches a video of another hand. A number appears (1 or 2) telling them to lift the index or middle finger, while the hand on screen lifts either the same finger or the other one. Responses are slower when the observed movement differs from the instructed one.
variations.justification: Canonical: respond to number cue, observe incongruent finger lift

variations.name: Kinematic Paradigm (Kilner Task)
variations.description: The participant makes repeated arm movements, for example side to side, while watching another person (or a robot) move their arm either in the same direction or up and down. The participant's movements become more variable when the observed movement conflicts with their own.
variations.justification: Perform arm movement while observing congruent/incongruent arm; different motor effector

variations.name: Hand Open/Close Variant
variations.description: The instructed action is to open or close the whole hand, and the observed hand opens or closes at the same time, so that the imitation effect is measured with a larger movement than a finger lift.
variations.justification: Open/close hand in response to/despite observed hand action

variations.name: Animacy Manipulation
variations.description: The observed movement is performed by a human hand, a robotic hand, or a non-biological object such as a moving bar, to see whether the tendency to copy depends on seeing a living agent.
variations.justification: Animate vs. inanimate observed movement; tests social specificity of imitation

variations.name: Goal-Directed Imitation Variant
variations.description: The observed hand grasps an object, and the design separates how the hand moved from what it was trying to do, for example by having the same movement achieve different goals. Shows whether the participant copies the movement or the goal.
variations.justification: Imitate goal vs. means; tests level of imitative representation

variations.name: Vocal Stimulus-Response Compatibility
variations.description: The participant hears a syllable such as 'pa' while being instructed to say either 'pa' or 'ba'. Saying a syllable that differs from the one heard is slower, the speech version of the finger task.
variations.justification: Vocal response to observed action; different response modality

variations.name: Controlled Imitation Task (Reverse)
variations.description: On some trials the participant is told to imitate the observed movement and on others to make the instructed movement regardless of what they see. Tests the ability to choose when to copy and when not to.
variations.justification: Instructed to imitate or not; tests explicit voluntary control

variations.name: Counter-Imitation Training
variations.description: Before the test, the participant practices many trials of responding to an observed index-finger lift with a middle-finger lift and vice versa. After such training the usual tendency to copy is reduced or reversed.
variations.justification: Training to suppress imitation; tests plasticity of imitative tendencies

families.rationale: Observed action congruent or incongruent with the instructed movement

short_definition: Participants judge the perceived time of a voluntary action and/or its sensory effect using a Libet clock; the temporal compression between action and effect (intentional binding) indexes the implicit sense of agency.
description: The Intentional Binding Task (Haggard, Clark, & Kalogeras, 2002) measures the implicit sense of agency through perceived temporal shifts between voluntary actions and their sensory consequences. Participants watch a rotating clock hand (Libet clock) and make voluntary key presses that produce a tone after a fixed delay (typically 250 ms). In separate blocks, they report either the perceived time of their action (action binding: judged time shifts toward the tone) or the perceived time of the tone (effect binding: judged time shifts toward the action). The net temporal compression between action and effect - intentional binding - is taken as an implicit, pre-reflective marker of the sense of agency. Involuntary actions (e.g., TMS-induced movements) or externally triggered tones produce temporal repulsion rather than binding, establishing the specificity of the effect to voluntary agency. The paradigm has become the standard implicit measure of sense of agency, complementing explicit agency judgments. It is sensitive to disorders of agency including schizophrenia (reduced binding, especially in patients with passivity experiences), functional neurological disorder, and anarchic hand syndrome. Computational accounts link binding to motor prediction: the forward model predicts sensory consequences of voluntary actions, and the match between prediction and outcome generates the binding effect.

procedure: Participants make voluntary actions (key presses) that produce delayed sensory effects (tones) while monitoring a Libet clock.
They report the perceived time of either the action or the effect in separate blocks.
manipulations: Action type (voluntary vs. involuntary/TMS-induced vs. passive observation)
Causal belief (participant told action causes vs. does not cause effect)
Outcome valence (positive vs. negative vs. neutral tone)
measurements: Action binding (shift of perceived action time toward the effect)
Effect binding (shift of perceived effect time toward the action)
Overall intentional binding (action binding + effect binding)
Interval estimation (judged action-effect interval vs. actual)

variations.name: Libet Clock Method (Standard)
variations.description: A clock hand sweeps around a small clock face once every 2.5 seconds. The participant presses a key whenever they like, and a tone sounds 250 ms later. On some blocks they report where the hand was when they pressed; on others, where it was when the tone sounded. Compared with blocks with only a press or only a tone, the press is judged later and the tone earlier, as if the two were drawn together.
variations.justification: Canonical: estimate action or tone time on rotating clock

variations.name: Interval Estimation Method
variations.description: No clock is used. After each press and tone the participant estimates in milliseconds how long the gap between them was, or reproduces it. Shorter estimates for voluntary actions than for passive ones indicate the same binding.
variations.justification: Estimate delay between action and outcome; different timing judgment task

variations.name: Involuntary Action Control (TMS)
variations.description: The finger movement is produced by a magnetic pulse to the motor cortex rather than by the participant's own decision. The involuntary movement and its tone are judged as further apart rather than closer together.
variations.justification: TMS-induced involuntary movement instead of voluntary action; different action type

variations.name: Outcome Probability Manipulation
variations.description: The tone follows the key press only some of the time, for example on 50 or 75 percent of trials, rather than always. The binding effect is weaker when the tone is less predictable.
variations.justification: Vary probability that action produces tone; tests contingency on binding

variations.name: Causal Belief Manipulation
variations.description: The participant is told either that their press causes the tone or that the tone is produced independently, while the actual timing is the same in both cases. Tests whether believing one is the cause is enough to produce binding.
variations.justification: Instructions manipulate whether action causes outcome; tests belief on binding

variations.name: Social Intentional Binding
variations.description: Either another person presses the key and the participant judges the timing of that person's action and its tone, or two people act together so that one person's press produces an effect the other experiences.
variations.justification: Another person performs action; tests social extension of binding

variations.name: Outcome Valence Manipulation
variations.description: The key press produces a pleasant, unpleasant or neutral sound, or wins or loses money, and the amount of binding is compared across outcomes.
variations.justification: Aversive vs. pleasant outcomes; tests valence effect on temporal binding

families.rationale: Judge the time of a voluntary action and its effect

short_definition: Participants press a key to reveal each word or phrase of a sentence/passage; reading time per region indexes online processing difficulty and is sensitive to syntactic, semantic, and discourse-level manipulations.
description: Self-Paced Reading is the primary behavioral paradigm for studying online language comprehension at the sentence and discourse level. Participants read text presented one word or phrase at a time by pressing a button to advance; the time between button presses at each region is the dependent measure. In the non-cumulative (moving-window) variant, each new word replaces the previous one; in the cumulative variant, words accumulate on screen. Reading time elevations at critical regions reveal processing difficulty caused by syntactic ambiguity (garden-path effects), semantic anomaly, coherence breaks, anaphor resolution, predictability violations, and discourse-level inference demands. The paradigm was developed as an accessible alternative to eye-tracking that preserves the temporal dynamics of incremental comprehension while requiring minimal equipment. Spillover effects (elevated reading times on words following the critical region) are routinely analyzed. Comprehension questions after each trial ensure participants are reading for meaning. Self-paced reading has been central to testing models of sentence processing (surprisal theory, expectation-based parsing), discourse representation theory (situation models), and cross-linguistic processing differences.

procedure: Participants read sentences or passages presented one word or phrase at a time, advancing by button press.
Reading time at each region is recorded.
Comprehension questions follow each trial.
manipulations: Syntactic ambiguity at the critical region (reduced relative clause, garden-path)
Anaphor type (pronoun, repeated name, definite NP)
Word predictability (high vs. low cloze probability)
measurements: Reading time at the critical region (ms)
Reading time differences between conditions at the critical region

variations.name: Non-Cumulative (Moving Window)
variations.description: A sentence is shown as a row of dashes. Each key press reveals the next word and turns the previous word back into dashes, so only one word is visible at a time. The time between presses is the reading time for each word.
variations.justification: Canonical word-by-word presentation without previous words visible

variations.name: Cumulative Self-Paced Reading
variations.description: Each key press reveals the next word and earlier words stay on screen, so the reader can look back at what came before. Reading times are less tightly tied to the current word.
variations.justification: Words accumulate on screen; different visual context during reading

variations.name: Phrase-by-Phrase Presentation
variations.description: Each key press reveals a group of words, such as a noun phrase or a clause, rather than a single word, and reading time is measured for each group.
variations.justification: Phrases instead of words; different chunking of presentation

variations.name: Maze Task
variations.description: At each position in the sentence two words are shown side by side, one that continues the sentence correctly and one that does not. The participant must pick the correct one to go on. Choice time at each position replaces reading time.
variations.justification: Word-by-word forced choice between correct and anomalous continuation; different response structure

variations.name: Cross-Modal Self-Paced Listening
variations.description: The sentence is spoken rather than written, in segments, and each key press plays the next segment. Listening time per segment is measured.
variations.justification: Auditory presentation instead of visual; different sensory modality

variations.name: Passage-Level Self-Paced Reading
variations.description: The text is a passage of several sentences rather than an isolated sentence, revealed word by word or sentence by sentence, so that effects of earlier sentences on reading later ones can be measured.
variations.justification: Full passages instead of sentences; different text-level processing

families.rationale: Reveal a sentence word by word

short_definition: A rapid stream of visual items is presented at a single location (typically 6-20 items/second); participants detect one or more targets among distractors. Target detection accuracy, especially for a second target shortly after a first (attentional blink), indexes temporal attention allocation.
description: Rapid Serial Visual Presentation (RSVP) is a paradigm for studying the temporal dynamics of visual attention. A stream of visual items (letters, digits, words, images, or complex scenes) is presented sequentially at a single spatial location at rates of 6-20 items per second. Participants must detect, identify, or categorize one or more targets embedded among distractors. The signature finding is the attentional blink (Raymond, Shapiro, & Arnell, 1992): when two targets appear in the stream, detection of the second target (T2) is severely impaired when it follows the first target (T1) by approximately 200-500 ms (lag 2-5), recovering at longer lags. Lag-1 sparing (intact T2 detection when T2 immediately follows T1) is a robust exception. The attentional blink reveals fundamental bottlenecks in temporal attention and has generated competing theoretical accounts: the two-stage model (Chun & Potter, 1995), the episodic simultaneous type/serial token model (Bowman & Wyble, 2007), and the boost-and-bounce model (Olivers & Meeter, 2008). Beyond the attentional blink, RSVP is used to study categorical perception (rapid scene gist extraction), emotion-attention interactions (emotion-induced blindness), and rapid image triage. Applications include brain-computer interfaces (RSVP-based P300 spellers and image triage systems, including satellite imagery analysis), clinical assessment of temporal attention in ADHD and dyslexia, and speed-reading technologies.

procedure: A rapid serial stream of visual items is presented at a single location.
Participants detect, identify, or categorize one or more targets embedded among distractors.
Presentation rate is typically 6-20 items per second.
manipulations: Target category (letter among digits, face among objects, scene category)
Emotional content of targets or distractors
measurements: Attentional blink magnitude (T2 accuracy deficit at short lags, conditional on correct T1 detection)
P300 ERP amplitude for detected targets

variations.name: Dual-Target Attentional Blink
variations.description: Letters or pictures flash at one spot about ten per second. Two of them are targets, for example two letters among digits or a white letter among black ones. At the end the participant reports both targets. The second target is often missed when it comes 200 to 500 ms after the first.
variations.justification: Canonical AB: T2 missed when presented shortly after T1

variations.name: Single-Target RSVP
variations.description: Only one target is placed in the stream, and the participant reports it at the end. Measures how well a single item can be picked out at high presentation rates and serves as a baseline.
variations.justification: Detect or identify one target in stream; no AB protocol

variations.name: Emotion-Induced Blindness
variations.description: The stream is made of pictures, and an emotionally arousing picture (such as a violent or erotic scene) appears shortly before the target picture that must be reported. The emotional distractor makes the following target harder to see.
variations.justification: Emotional T1 causes blindness to T2; retained per section 5.1 (EMOT retired)

variations.name: Rapid Scene Categorization
variations.description: Photographs of natural scenes are shown at very high rates (down to about 20 ms per picture), and the participant reports whether a picture from a target category, such as an animal, appeared. Shows how quickly the gist of a scene is extracted.
variations.justification: Categorize natural scenes at rapid presentation rates; different stimulus class

variations.name: RSVP Image Triage (BCI)
variations.description: Images such as satellite photographs are shown in a rapid stream while electroencephalography is recorded, and the brain response to target images is used to flag them, without the participant pressing anything. Used in brain-computer interface research for screening large image sets.
variations.justification: Brain-computer interface using RSVP for rapid image tagging; different application and response structure

variations.name: Triple-RSVP (Multiple Streams)
variations.description: Three streams run at once at different positions on the screen, and a target may appear in any of them. The participant must monitor all three, which adds spatial demands to the rapid timing.
variations.justification: Three simultaneous streams; different attentional load structure

variations.name: Whole-Report RSVP
variations.description: A short stream of four to eight items is shown and the participant reports all of them, not just designated targets. Measures how many rapidly shown items can be captured and held.
variations.justification: Report all items seen; different response requirement

variations.name: RSVP with Task Switch
variations.description: The two targets require different judgments, such as naming the first and reporting whether the second was present, so the participant must change what they are doing between the targets.
variations.justification: Task changes within or between streams; adds switching demand

variations.name: Detection vs. Identification
variations.description: For the second target the participant either just reports whether it was there or has to say which item it was. The blink is measured with each kind of report.
variations.justification: Detect presence vs. identify identity; different judgment type

variations.name: Three-Target Variant
variations.description: Three targets are placed in the stream rather than two, and the participant reports all three, to probe how attention recovers across a longer sequence of targets.
variations.justification: Three targets in stream; extends AB to three-target scenario

variations.name: Cross-Modal Attentional Blink
variations.description: The first target is in one sense and the second in another, for example a spoken target followed by a visual one, to test whether the blink occurs when the two targets use different senses.
variations.justification: T1 and T2 in different modalities; tests cross-modal attentional resources

variations.name: Emotional Attentional Blink
variations.description: The targets themselves are emotional, such as emotional words or faces that must be reported, rather than emotional distractors. Emotional second targets are missed less often than neutral ones.
variations.justification: Emotional T2; retained per section 5.1 (EMOT retired)

variations.name: Spatial Two-Stream RSVP
variations.description: Two streams run at once at different positions, and the two targets may appear in the same stream or in different ones. Separates the costs of shifting attention in time from the costs of shifting it in space.
variations.justification: Two streams at different spatial locations; tests spatial attention in RSVP

families.rationale: Targets in a rapid stream; the attentional blink could argue for visual search and tracking

short_definition: Participant stays awake, still and unoccupied for a block of several minutes while spontaneous activity is recorded; the block is a baseline for task blocks or a resting-state recording in its own right.
description: The participant is asked to remain awake and relaxed, to keep still, and to do nothing in particular while the recording runs, typically for three to ten minutes. No stimulus is presented for processing and no response is required. Rest blocks appear at the start or end of a session as a baseline, between task blocks as a recovery period, or as the whole recording in resting-state studies of spontaneous brain activity and functional connectivity. Eye state is the standard manipulation: eyes closed removes visual input and raises occipital alpha; eyes open is often paired with a fixation cross to limit eye movement. When a cross is merely provided and the instruction is to rest, the block is a Rest Task; when the instruction is to hold gaze on the target and gaze is monitored or required, it is a Fixate Task. With no task to direct it, thought wanders: participants report thinking about themselves, their own past and their plans, and recent experience is replayed in a way that supports later memory. What the participant was thinking can be sampled afterwards by asking.

procedure: Participant remains awake, still and relaxed with no stimulus to process and no response to make, for a block typically lasting 3 to 10 minutes.
manipulations: Position relative to task blocks (before, between, after)
Instruction to let the mind wander versus to stay alert
measurements: Spontaneous EEG or MEG spectra and microstates
Self-reported drowsiness or thought content after the block

variations.name: Eyes-Open Rest
variations.description: The participant sits or lies still for several minutes with eyes open, usually looking at a fixation cross or a blank screen, with nothing to do.
variations.justification: Eye state changes visual input and the EEG alpha rhythm; a different postural state for the whole block

variations.name: Eyes-Closed Rest
variations.description: The participant sits or lies still for several minutes with eyes closed and nothing to do, while staying awake.
variations.justification: Eye state changes visual input and the EEG alpha rhythm; removes eye-movement artifact and raises the risk of drowsiness

families.rationale: No task is set; thought is left to arise on its own

short_definition: Participant holds gaze on a fixation target. It is used in two ways: as a block of its own with nothing else to do, as a baseline or control, and as a job held throughout another task so that the eyes stay still while that task is performed.
description: A fixation target, usually a cross or dot at the centre of the screen, is shown and the participant is instructed to keep looking at it for the duration of the block. Nothing else is presented and no response is made. Fixation blocks serve as the implicit baseline in block-design fMRI, as the inter-block interval in many EEG designs, and as the control condition for localizers. Gaze may be monitored with an eye tracker, but that is a matter of measurement and does not make a different task. The distinction from an eyes-open Rest Task is the instruction: here fixation is the required activity, not a convenience. Fixation is also held throughout other tasks, as in spatial cueing, where attention moves to the cued location while the eyes stay on the cross; there it is a second job done alongside the main one. In both uses the participant keeps attention on the target and holds back the urge to look away.

procedure: Participant maintains gaze on a fixation target for the block, with no other stimulus to process and no response to make.
Or, participant holds gaze on the target throughout the trials of another task while performing that task.
manipulations: Whether gaze is monitored and fed back
measurements: Baseline neural activity for contrast with task blocks
Fixation stability (gaze dispersion, saccade and blink counts) when eye-tracked
Fixation breaks during the other task's trials

families.rationale: Eye movements away from the target are withheld throughout
Held throughout cueing tasks so that attention moves while the eyes stay still
Held throughout tracking tasks so that items are followed by attention, not by gaze

short_definition: Participant reads or hears a series of questionnaire items and records a response to each; the instrument administered is a parameter of the block, not a variation.
description: A self-report instrument is administered as a block of the session, before, between or after task blocks. Items are presented on paper, on screen or read aloud, and the participant answers each in the instrument's response format. There is no time pressure and no stimulus other than the items themselves. The Catalog does not list instruments as tasks; answering one is this task, and which instrument was used is a parameter of it. Each item is a stimulus and each answer a response, but no answer is correct. To answer, the participant reads and understands the item, recalls what is relevant from their own experience, judges how it applies to them, and picks the response option that fits. A computerized administration records when each item was shown and answered.

procedure: Participant reads or hears each item of a questionnaire and records a response to it, in the instrument's format, with no time pressure.
manipulations: The instrument administered (a parameter, not a variation)
Response format (Likert, forced choice, free text)
measurements: Item responses and derived scale scores
Physiological recording during completion is incidental

variations.justification: Different response modality and one recorded event per item

variations.name: Interviewer-Administered Questionnaire
variations.description: An interviewer reads each item aloud and the participant answers in speech, with the interviewer recording the answers.
variations.justification: Different sensory and response modality

families.rationale: Each item asks the participant about themselves; no answer is correct
